title: Full Stack Developer: 1000+ Interview Questions with Answers

questions.question: Tell me about yourself.
questions.answer: Sure. I'm a full stack developer from Pune with about three years of experience. I work mostly with Python and JavaScript — my day job has been building custom ERPNext/Frappe modules like HRMS, CRM, inventory, and real estate, plus frontends in Vue.js and Angular. I've shipped over eight custom modules and automated workflows that handle more than 500 transactions a day. On the infrastructure side, I've deployed containerized apps on AWS with Docker on Ubuntu servers. Before this, I did my MCA from ASMA Institute Pune. What I enjoy most is taking a business problem, automating it end to end, and seeing it actually get used every day by real users.

questions.question: Why do you want to work here / what attracts you to this role?
questions.answer: I've built a lot of ERP and automation products, and from what I've seen about your company, you solve exactly those kinds of real business problems. I like the idea of my code directly improving how people work. Also, your stack overlaps a lot with what I do daily — Python, TypeScript, and modern frontends — so I can contribute from day one instead of spending months learning.

questions.question: What are your strengths as a full stack developer?
questions.answer: I'd say three things. First, I can see a feature end to end — I can design the database, build the API, and then build the UI myself, which saves a lot of handoff friction. Second, I'm strong at ERP and workflow automation, which is a niche skill most generalist developers don't have. And third, I care about reliability — I've done containerization and deployment, so I don't write code and throw it over the wall; I get it running on a server properly.

questions.question: What is your biggest weakness?
questions.answer: I used to spend too long polishing things that didn't matter — like tweaking UI details that users never noticed. I've learned to time-box that and ask myself: does this move the business forward? Another one is that I can be eager to jump into code before fully understanding the requirements, so I now force myself to write things down and confirm before building.

questions.question: Walk me through your typical day as a full stack developer.
questions.answer: I start by checking what's pending in the ticket board and any errors from overnight. Usually there's a mix of feature work — say a new Frappe doctype for a client — and bug fixes. I'll spend the morning on backend logic and database changes, the afternoon on frontend with Vue or Angular, and late afternoon I do code reviews or deployment prep. Since we deploy to Docker on AWS, I make sure my containers build clean and nothing breaks the staging environment.

questions.question: What's the most interesting project you've worked on and why?
questions.answer: The MSS — Master Production Scheduling tool. It took a messy paper-based manufacturing process and turned it into one module that calculates shift capacity against the Bill of Materials, checks mold availability, and auto-generates sales orders from blanket orders. It was interesting because it wasn't just coding — I had to understand how a factory actually plans production, and then translate that into a system that people trusted. It's still running for the client today.

questions.question: Why did you choose to specialize in full stack development?
questions.answer: Because I'm curious how the whole thing fits together. When I was doing my MCA I realized I didn't just want to write SQL or just write a button — I wanted to connect them. Being full stack means I understand tradeoffs: where to put the business logic, how to shape the data, and what the user sees. It also means I'm not blocked waiting on another person for every change.

questions.question: What kind of company or work culture brings out your best?
questions.answer: I do best in teams that move fast but still care about quality — where there's ownership and trust. I like having clear ownership of a feature and being accountable for it end to end. I also appreciate teams that do code reviews and share knowledge, because I've learned a lot from seniors who took the time to explain why.

questions.question: Where do you see yourself in five years?
questions.answer: In five years I see myself as a senior full stack engineer or a technical lead — still hands-on, but also helping design architecture and mentoring juniors. I'd love to deepen my ERP/enterprise experience because I find it genuinely interesting, and maybe lead a product line rather than just deliver features.

questions.question: Do you have any questions for us?
questions.answer: Yes, a few. What does the first 90 days in this role look like? How does the team handle code reviews and deployments? And is there a chance to work on architecture and design decisions, or is it mostly ticket-based? I also like to know what the team sees as the biggest technical challenge in the next year.

questions.question: What are the main differences between a list, tuple, and set in Python?
questions.answer: A list is ordered, mutable, and allows duplicates — like a dynamic array. A tuple is ordered and immutable, which makes it great for fixed data or as dictionary keys. A set is unordered, mutable, and only stores unique values, so it's perfect for deduplication and fast membership checks. The big difference in daily use: lists when order matters, tuples when data shouldn't change, sets when uniqueness is the point.

questions.question: What is the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy?
questions.answer: A shallow copy copies the container but keeps the same references to the inner objects — so if the inner objects change, both copies see it. A deep copy recursively copies everything, so the copies are fully independent. In Python, `copy.copy()` gives you a shallow copy and `copy.deepcopy()` gives you a deep one. This bit me once with nested lists in Frappe code where I mutated a child table by accident.

questions.question: Explain Python's GIL. How does it affect threading?
questions.answer: The GIL is a mutex in CPython that lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time. That means pure Python code doesn't get true parallel speedup across multiple CPU cores with threads. So for CPU-bound work you use multiprocessing or tools like NumPy that release the GIL; for I/O-bound work threads are fine because they spend most time waiting. In my work, threading for I/O tasks worked well; heavy number crunching I pushed to multiprocessing or SQL.

questions.question: What are decorators and how do you use them?
questions.answer: A decorator is just a function that takes another function and extends its behavior without modifying it. You write `@decorator` above a function. A common example in my work is a helper that wraps API endpoints to check authentication or log execution time. They're great for cross-cutting concerns like logging, caching, validation, and access control.

questions.question: What is a generator and why is it useful?
questions.answer: A generator is a function that yields values lazily one at a time instead of building the whole list in memory. You write `yield` instead of `return`. This is a big deal when you process large data — like iterating over thousands of records from a Frappe query — because memory stays flat. I've used generators to stream bulk export data so we didn't blow up the server RAM.

questions.question: What is the difference between `*args` and `**kwargs`?
questions.answer: `*args` collects extra positional arguments into a tuple, and `**kwargs` collects extra keyword arguments into a dictionary. They let you write flexible functions and wrappers. I use them a lot when writing generic validation helpers or when overriding Frappe hooks where the signature can vary.

questions.question: How does Python handle memory management?
questions.answer: Python uses reference counting plus a garbage collector for cyclic references. Each object tracks how many references point to it; when it hits zero it's freed immediately. For circular references — like two objects pointing at each other — the cyclic GC detects and cleans them up. In long-running services I keep an eye on memory growth and make sure I'm not holding onto large lists or DB cursors.

questions.question: What is the difference between `==` and `is` in Python?
questions.answer: `==` compares values, `is` compares identity — whether two names point to the same object in memory. For small integers and interned strings Python may reuse objects, which is why `a is b` sometimes looks true, but you should never rely on that. In practice, use `==` for comparing values and `is None` for checking None.

questions.question: Explain `try`, `except`, `finally`, and `else` in exception handling.
questions.answer: `try` holds the code that may fail. `except` catches specific exceptions. `finally` always runs — even if an exception happened — so it's for cleanup like closing connections. `else` runs only if no exception was raised, which is handy to separate the success path from error handling. In my APIs I catch specific exceptions, log them, and return proper HTTP error codes instead of a 500.

questions.question: What is the difference between a function and a lambda?
questions.answer: A function is a named, reusable block defined with `def`. A lambda is a small anonymous one-liner that returns an expression. Lambdas are fine for short throwaway operations like `sorted(items, key=lambda x: x['date'])`, but anything more complex should be a proper function for readability.

questions.question: How do you optimize slow Python code?
questions.answer: First, I profile rather than guess — I use `cProfile` or simple timing to find the actual bottleneck. Common wins: moving work out of loops, using list comprehensions over raw loops, caching repeated computations, switching data structures (e.g., a dict lookup instead of a linear search), and pushing heavy logic into SQL. One real case: we were calling the database inside a loop; moving to a single batch query cut the runtime dramatically.

questions.question: What is the `with` statement and when should you use it?
questions.answer: The `with` statement uses context managers to guarantee resources get cleaned up even when errors happen. The classic cases are opening files and database connections. Instead of manually calling `close()`, `with` does it for you. I use it heavily with SQLAlchemy sessions and file reads so I never leak connections.

questions.question: What's the difference between `range` in Python 2 and Python 3?
questions.answer: In Python 2, `range()` returned a list and `xrange()` was the lazy version. In Python 3, `range()` is lazy — it returns a range object that generates numbers on demand — and `xrange()` is gone. So in Python 3, iterating over a huge range doesn't allocate a giant list.

questions.question: Explain mutability. What does that mean for how you pass data around?
questions.answer: Mutable types — lists, dicts, sets — can change in place; immutable types — ints, strings, tuples — cannot. This matters because when you pass a mutable object to a function and modify it, the caller sees the change. I've had bugs where a helper function silently modified a list the caller still needed. A safe habit is to copy data before transforming it unless mutation is intentional.

questions.question: What is a classmethod vs a staticmethod?
questions.answer: A classmethod receives the class as its first argument (`cls`), so it can access class state and is often used as an alternative constructor. A staticmethod receives nothing special — it's just a function grouped inside the class for organization. In Frappe code you see `@staticmethod` a lot on controller helpers that don't need instance or class data.

questions.question: How do you handle circular imports in Python?
questions.answer: Circular imports happen when module A imports module B and B imports A. Fixes: import inside the function rather than at module top, move the shared dependency into a third module, or use lazy imports. I prefer moving shared models into a common module — it keeps imports clean and predictable.

questions.question: What's the difference between `requests` and `urllib`? When would you use each?
questions.answer: `requests` is a clean, high-level HTTP library with a nice API — `requests.get()`, timeouts, sessions, JSON handling built in. `urllib` is standard library and more low-level and awkward. Unless you can't install packages, use `requests`. In my Frappe integrations I use `requests` with session reuse for hitting external REST APIs.

questions.question: How do you work with dates and times in Python?
questions.answer: I use the standard `datetime` module and treat everything as timezone-aware. `datetime.utcnow()` is deprecated in favor of `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`. When storing timestamps I use UTC and convert to local time only for display. `strftime` and `strptime` handle formatting and parsing. For anything complex — recurring schedules, timezone math — I'd bring in `pytz` or `dateutil`.

questions.question: What is the Global Interpreter Lock doing when you run multiple processes instead of threads?
questions.answer: Each process gets its own interpreter and its own GIL, so multiple processes can actually run Python in parallel across cores. `multiprocessing` lets you spawn workers, each with independent memory. The tradeoff is overhead — inter-process communication is heavier than threads sharing memory. So the rule of thumb: threads for I/O, processes for CPU-bound work.

questions.question: Explain `enumerate`, `zip`, and `map` with quick examples.
questions.answer: `enumerate` gives you index and value while looping: `for i, item in enumerate(items)`. `zip` pairs two or more iterables element by element: `zip(names, ages)`. `map` applies a function to every item: `list(map(str, nums))`. These are bread-and-butter Python that make loops cleaner and usually faster.

questions.question: What is the difference between `var`, `let`, and `const`?
questions.answer: `var` is function-scoped and gets hoisted with a default of `undefined` — it's the old way and causes subtle bugs. `let` is block-scoped and can be reassigned but not redeclared in the same scope. `const` is block-scoped and can't be reassigned at all. I default to `const` and only use `let` when I truly need to reassign. I never use `var` in new code.

questions.question: Explain event bubbling and event delegation.
questions.answer: Event bubbling means when you click a child element, the event propagates up through its ancestors. Event delegation is the technique of putting one listener on a parent to handle events from many children. That's useful when you have a dynamic list — like rows that get added to a table — because you don't have to attach listeners to each row. In Angular I mostly get this for free with click bindings, but in vanilla JS I rely on it.

questions.question: What is the difference between `==` and `===`?
questions.answer: `==` does type coercion, so `'5' == 5` is true. `===` compares both value and type, so `'5' === 5` is false. I always use `===` unless I have a deliberate reason to coerce. Coercion surprises are one of the top sources of bugs in JavaScript.

questions.question: Explain closures with an example.
questions.answer: A closure is a function that remembers the variables from the scope where it was created, even after that scope has finished running. A classic example is a counter: `function makeCounter(){ let count=0; return () => ++count; }` — each call to the returned function still sees `count`. Closures power a lot of JS patterns like module patterns and partial application. In my Vue code, closures let me capture state in callbacks cleanly.

questions.question: What is `this` in JavaScript and how is it determined?
questions.answer: `this` is determined by how a function is called, not where it's defined. In a normal function it depends on the caller; in an arrow function it's inherited lexically from the surrounding scope. That's why arrow functions are handy for callbacks — they keep `this` pointing at the component instead of the DOM element. Understanding `this` was one of those things that clicked for me only after a few bugs.

questions.question: What is hoisting?
questions.answer: Hoisting is JavaScript moving declarations to the top of their scope during compile. Function declarations are fully hoisted, so you can call them before they appear. `var` declarations are hoisted but initialized to `undefined`. `let` and `const` are hoisted into a temporal dead zone — you get an error if you use them before the declaration line. I avoid relying on hoisting except for function declarations.

questions.question: What's the event loop and how does it relate to promises?
questions.answer: The event loop is how JavaScript handles async without threads. The main thread runs synchronous code, then checks the microtask queue (promises) and then the macrotask queue (setTimeout, I/O). Promises and `async/await` resolve as microtasks, so they run before timers. When I write code that does a fetch, the event loop keeps the UI responsive while the network request is pending, then the callback runs when it's done.

questions.question: Explain `async/await` vs promises.
questions.answer: Promises give you `.then()` and `.catch()` chains. `async/await` is syntactic sugar on top that reads like synchronous code. `await` pauses the function until the promise resolves, and errors are caught with try/catch. I use `async/await` almost always because it's more readable, especially when I need to await multiple API calls in sequence.

questions.question: What is `Promise.all` and when would you use it?
questions.answer: `Promise.all` takes an array of promises and resolves with an array of their results, but only after all of them succeed — if any rejects, the whole thing rejects. I use it to fetch independent data in parallel, like loading user info and settings at once instead of sequentially, which cuts loading time. For fault tolerance, `Promise.allSettled` is better when I want results even if some fail.

questions.question: What are the differences between `null`, `undefined`, and `NaN`?
questions.answer: `undefined` means a variable was declared but has no value assigned. `null` is an explicit value meaning 'nothing' — you set it intentionally. `NaN` means 'not a number' and comes from failed numeric operations like `parseInt('abc')`. Checking for `NaN` needs `isNaN` or `Number.isNaN` because `NaN !== NaN` is true. These seem small but they cause real bugs when you default values.

questions.question: What is TypeScript and why do you use it?
questions.answer: TypeScript is a typed superset of JavaScript that compiles to plain JS. The value is catching bugs at compile time instead of runtime — typos, wrong argument types, missing properties. In a large Angular app, types make refactoring safe and act as living documentation. I genuinely don't like going back to untyped large codebases now because the compiler catches so many silly mistakes.

questions.question: What is the difference between `interface` and `type` in TypeScript?
questions.answer: Both define shapes, but there are differences. Interfaces can be extended and merged (declaration merging), and they're better for object shapes that get implemented by classes. Type aliases can represent unions, tuples, and mapped types, which interfaces can't. In practice, I use interfaces for objects and `type` when I need unions or complex combinations.

questions.question: What are generics in TypeScript?
questions.answer: Generics let you write a function or class that works with any type while keeping type safety. For example, `function identity<T>(arg: T): T` — the caller decides what `T` is, and the compiler enforces consistency. I use generics for reusable utilities like API response wrappers where I don't want to duplicate code for every entity type.

questions.question: Explain `type` narrowing and type guards.
questions.answer: Type narrowing is TypeScript shrinking a union type to a more specific one based on runtime checks — like `if (typeof x === 'string')` or `if (item instanceof Error)`. Type guards are functions that perform those checks and tell TypeScript the type, like `function isUser(obj: unknown): obj is User`. This lets me safely handle mixed data, especially when parsing API responses.

questions.question: What is the difference between `any`, `unknown`, and `never`?
questions.answer: `any` disables type checking entirely — the escape hatch, but it defeats TypeScript's purpose. `unknown` is the safe counterpart: you must narrow it before using it, which is what you want for external data. `never` means a value can never occur — used for exhaustive checks, like making sure a switch over a union covers every case. I avoid `any` and prefer `unknown` for unvalidated input.

questions.question: How does TypeScript handle compile-time vs runtime types?
questions.answer: TypeScript types only exist at compile time — they're erased when it compiles to JavaScript. That's why you can't rely on `instanceof` for interfaces at runtime. When I need runtime checks, I either write manual type guards or use a library like zod to validate and type external data in one shot. This distinction matters for API boundaries.

questions.question: What is a module in JavaScript, and what's the difference between CommonJS and ES modules?
questions.answer: A module is a file that exports and imports pieces of code. CommonJS uses `require`/`module.exports` and is what Node used historically — it's synchronous. ES modules use `import`/`export` and are the standard, supported natively in Node and browsers, with static analysis for tree shaking. I write ES modules in frontend code; in older Node/Frappe server code I've worked with CommonJS.

questions.question: What is the spread operator and how is it useful?
questions.answer: The spread operator `...` expands an iterable into its elements. You can copy objects and arrays: `const copy = { ...obj }` or `const arr = [...items]`, merge them, or pass array elements as function arguments. It's also great for immutability — creating new arrays instead of mutating state, which fits React and Vue reactivity patterns.

questions.question: What is `fetch` and how do you handle errors with it?
questions.answer: `fetch` is the browser API for making HTTP requests that returns a promise. One gotcha: it only rejects on network errors, not on HTTP error status like 404 or 500 — you have to check `response.ok` yourself. My pattern is `const res = await fetch(url); if (!res.ok) throw new Error(...); return res.json();` wrapped in a try/catch, and I map that to a user-friendly message.

questions.question: Explain `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, and cookies.
questions.answer: `localStorage` persists across sessions with no expiry — good for preferences. `sessionStorage` lives only for the browser tab session. Cookies are sent automatically with every request to the domain, which makes them right for auth tokens but also means they add request overhead and have size limits. I store non-sensitive UI state in localStorage and keep auth in httpOnly cookies or an auth token in memory.

questions.question: What is Angular and how does it differ from a plain JavaScript app?
questions.answer: Angular is a full framework — it gives you component architecture, dependency injection, routing, forms, HTTP client, and change detection out of the box. A plain JS app is you wiring everything yourself. The tradeoff is Angular has a learning curve and more boilerplate, but for a large enterprise app — which is what I usually build — the structure pays off. It also makes cross-team consistency easier.

questions.question: Explain components, modules, and services in Angular.
questions.answer: A component is a UI building block — template, styles, and class. A module (`NgModule`) groups related components, directives, pipes, and services and controls what's exported and imported — though newer Angular pushes standalone components. A service is an injectable class for shared logic and data access. My habit: keep components thin and put HTTP calls and business logic in services.

questions.question: What is dependency injection and why does Angular use it?
questions.answer: Dependency injection is a pattern where a class receives its dependencies from outside instead of creating them itself. Angular's DI system resolves services from an injector hierarchy, so a service can be singleton at the app level or scoped to a feature. It makes code testable — you can swap a real HTTP service for a mock — and it's how I share a common API service across components without singletons scattered around.

questions.question: What is Angular's change detection and how does it work?
questions.answer: Angular checks whether component bindings changed and updates the DOM. By default it runs change detection on every event, async call, and timer from the top of the tree. It's efficient but can be wasteful in large apps. I use `OnPush` strategy on heavy components so Angular only checks them when their inputs change, plus `trackBy` in `*ngFor` to avoid rebuilding entire lists.

questions.question: What is the difference between `*ngIf` and `[hidden]`?
questions.answer: `*ngIf` removes the element from the DOM entirely when the condition is false — the node doesn't exist, so no rendering cost. `[hidden]` only sets the CSS `display: none`, so the element stays in the DOM. Use `*ngIf` for things you don't need in the DOM at all, and `[hidden]` when you want the element present, like to preserve state. I default to `*ngIf`.

questions.question: How does routing work in Angular, and what is lazy loading?
questions.answer: Angular Router maps URLs to components. You define routes, and you can guard them and pass data. Lazy loading means a feature module is only loaded when its route is first visited, instead of bundling everything upfront. That's a big performance win — in my e-commerce app the admin section loads only when an admin opens it, which shrunk the initial bundle.

questions.question: What are Angular lifecycle hooks, and which do you use most?
questions.answer: Lifecycle hooks let you react to a component's life. The ones I use most: `ngOnInit` for initialization after inputs are set, `ngOnDestroy` to clean up subscriptions and prevent memory leaks, `ngOnChanges` when inputs change, and `ngAfterViewInit` for code that needs the view. The most important habit is cleaning up in `ngOnDestroy` — leaking subscriptions is a common Angular bug.

questions.question: What is a reactive form vs a template-driven form?
questions.answer: Template-driven forms put the form logic in the HTML with directives like `ngModel`. Reactive forms build the model in the TypeScript class with `FormGroup` and `FormControl`. Reactive forms are more powerful and testable — you can do dynamic validators and complex nesting — so for any non-trivial form I use them. They make validation logic visible and unit-testable.

questions.question: What are Observables and how are they different from Promises?
questions.answer: Observables come from RxJS and are a stream of values over time. A promise resolves once with one value; an observable can emit many values over time, can be cancelled, and has operators like `map`, `filter`, `switchMap`. Angular's HTTP client returns observables. This is great for things like search-as-you-type where I debounce and cancel in-flight requests using `switchMap`.

questions.question: What is `async` pipe and why use it?
questions.answer: The `async` pipe subscribes to an observable (or promise) in the template and automatically handles subscribing and unsubscribing, so I don't need to manage the subscription manually in the component. That prevents memory leaks and reduces boilerplate. Example: `{{ users$ | async }}` where `users$` is an observable of a user array. I combine it with `*ngIf` to handle loading states.

questions.question: What are Angular guards and what types exist?
questions.answer: Guards control whether a route can be activated, deactivated, loaded, or resolved. `CanActivate` checks access before entering a route — that's my go-to for auth. `CanLoad` prevents lazy modules from even loading. `CanDeactivate` prompts before leaving, like unsaved form warnings. `Resolve` prefetches data before the route activates so the page renders with data already available.

questions.question: What is an Angular service's `providedIn`? Explain `root` vs `any` vs `platform`.
questions.answer: `providedIn: 'root'` makes a service a singleton for the whole app — it's tree-shakable, so if nothing uses it, it's excluded from the bundle. `'any'` creates a new instance per injector, which can be useful for module-scoped services. `'platform'` is rare and shares one instance across multiple apps in the same platform. I use `root` by default and rarely need the others.

questions.question: How do you communicate between components in Angular?
questions.answer: The options are: parent-to-child via `@Input`, child-to-parent via `@Output` with EventEmitters, and shared state via a service — often with BehaviorSubject for reactive state. For distant or sibling components I prefer a service; for simple parent-child relationships, `@Input`/`@Output` is cleaner than adding a global service.

questions.question: What are pipes and how do you create a custom pipe?
questions.answer: A pipe transforms data in the template, like `{{ price | currency }}`. Built-ins cover date, uppercase, currency, and more. For a custom pipe I use `@Pipe({ name: 'myPipe' })` and implement `transform(value, args)`. One thing to note: pipes run on change detection, so they should be pure unless you mark `pure: false`, which I avoid for performance.

questions.question: Explain `ng-container` and `ng-template`.
questions.answer: `ng-container` is a wrapper that doesn't render its own DOM element — useful for grouping structural directives like `*ngIf` and `*ngFor` on the same element without adding a div. `ng-template` is a template that isn't rendered until you instantiate it, like with `*ngIf` or `ngTemplateOutlet`. These keep my markup clean without extra wrapper elements that break CSS layouts.

questions.question: What is content projection and how does it work?
questions.answer: Content projection is passing content into a component and rendering it inside — like Angular's version of slots. With `ng-content` the projected content lands at that spot, and with `ng-content select="[slot=...]"` or CSS selectors I can project content to multiple places. It's great for building reusable cards, modals, and layout components.

questions.question: What is the difference between `BehaviorSubject`, `Subject`, and `ReplaySubject`?
questions.answer: A `Subject` is a multicast observable; subscribers only get emissions after they subscribe. A `BehaviorSubject` also needs an initial value and replays the latest value to new subscribers immediately — my default for shared state. A `ReplaySubject` replays a buffer of past emissions to new subscribers. For an auth service, `BehaviorSubject` is perfect because a new subscriber immediately needs to know if the user is logged in.

questions.question: How do you handle authentication state in an Angular app?
questions.answer: I keep an `AuthService` with a `BehaviorSubject<boolean>` (or user object) for login state. On login, the token goes to an interceptor that attaches it to outgoing HTTP requests, and route guards check the state. On logout I clear state, redirect to login, and make sure guards re-evaluate. I've also handled 401 responses centrally in an HTTP interceptor to redirect to login automatically.

questions.question: What is an HTTP interceptor and what have you used it for?
questions.answer: An interceptor sits between the app and the HTTP backend — it can transform outgoing requests and incoming responses. I've used it to attach JWT tokens to every request, handle a shared loading spinner, log API calls, and catch 401 errors to redirect to login. It's a powerful cross-cutting tool that keeps components clean of repetitive HTTP concerns.

questions.question: How do you make an Angular app performant?
questions.answer: The wins I focus on: lazy-loading routes so initial bundle is small, using `OnPush` change detection, `trackBy` in lists, avoiding heavy expressions in templates, using the async pipe so subscriptions don't leak, building with `--prod`/`--optimization`, and using Angular's built-in tree shaking and code splitting. In my projects I saw meaningful load-time improvements from lazy loading alone.

questions.question: What is Vue.js and what are its core features?
questions.answer: Vue.js is a progressive JavaScript framework for building UIs. Its core ideas are a reactive data system, component-based composition, a virtual DOM, and an approachable learning curve. What I like is that you can use it as a drop-in for a single component or scale it to a full SPA with Vue Router and Pinia. Its template syntax feels natural if you know HTML.

questions.question: What is the difference between the Options API and the Composition API?
questions.answer: The Options API organizes code by `data`, `computed`, `methods`, `watch`, `lifecycle` options — familiar and clean for small components. The Composition API groups code by feature using `setup()` or `<script setup>` with `ref`, `computed`, and `watch`. Composition API is better for reuse via composables and for complex components where related logic lives together. I use the Composition API now, especially for components with more than a few pieces of state.

questions.question: What is reactivity in Vue and how does it work?
questions.answer: Vue reactivity tracks dependencies between your state and your template, then updates the DOM when state changes. In Vue 3 it's built on the Proxy API — when you access a property inside a component, Vue records that dependency, and when the property changes, Vue re-runs only the effects that depend on it. That's why updates are surgical instead of re-rendering the whole app.

questions.question: What is `ref` vs `reactive` in Vue 3?
questions.answer: `ref` wraps a single value — it can be a primitive or an object — and you access it with `.value` in script. `reactive` makes an object deeply reactive and you access its properties directly. I default to `ref` for primitives and simple values, and use `reactive` when I have a structured object where the `.value` everywhere would be noisy. When I destructure from reactive I wrap it in `toRefs` to keep reactivity.

questions.question: What are computed properties and when do you use them?
questions.answer: A computed property derives a value from other reactive state and caches it — it only recomputes when its dependencies change. I use them instead of putting logic in the template, like `const total = computed(() => items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price, 0))`. They keep templates clean and avoid recalculating on every render.

questions.question: What is a watcher (`watch`) and how is it different from computed?
questions.answer: A watcher runs side effects when reactive state changes — like saving to the backend, logging, or debouncing a search. A computed property is pure: it derives and caches a value, no side effects. Rule of thumb: if you need to compute a value for display, use computed; if you need to react and do something, use watch. For immediate execution you pass `{ immediate: true }`.

questions.question: Explain Vue lifecycle hooks.
questions.answer: Vue components go through phases: creation, mounting, updating, and unmounting. Key hooks: `onMounted` for DOM work and initial data fetch, `onBeforeUnmount`/`onUnmounted` for cleanup like removing listeners or cancelling timers, and `onUpdated` rarely used. In a composition-API component I mostly use `onMounted` and `onUnmounted` — I'm careful to clean up anything I start in `onMounted`.

questions.question: What is v-model and how does it work?
questions.answer: `v-model` is two-way binding — it reads from the data property and updates it when the input changes. On a native input it's basically `:value` plus `@input`. On custom components it becomes `modelValue` prop plus `update:modelValue` event. It's how I bind form fields in Vue without writing the value-and-event boilerplate every time.

questions.question: What are Vue directives and what built-in ones do you use?
questions.answer: Directives are template attributes with `v-` prefix that apply behavior. The ones I use constantly: `v-if`/`v-else` and `v-show` for conditional rendering, `v-for` for lists (with `:key`!), `v-bind` (`:`) for binding, `v-on` (`@`) for events, `v-model` for two-way binding, and `v-html` for raw HTML when needed. A custom directive is sometimes the cleanest way to wrap third-party DOM behavior.

questions.question: `v-if` vs `v-show` — when do you pick which?
questions.answer: `v-if` conditionally renders the element — it's removed from the DOM when false. `v-show` always renders but toggles `display: none`. `v-if` is better when the condition rarely changes or the element is expensive to keep around; `v-show` when you toggle frequently and want instant show/hide. I use `v-if` by default and `v-show` for things like tab panels that toggle often.

questions.question: How do components communicate in Vue?
questions.answer: Parent to child via `props`, child to parent via `emit` events, and shared/complex state via a store like Pinia or a composable. For one-off sibling communication I often use a small event or a shared reactive object. I keep the rule simple: props down, events up, and anything multi-component goes to a store.

questions.question: What are slots and what are scoped slots?
questions.answer: Slots let a parent inject content into a child component — like Vue's version of children/transclusion. A default slot takes anything, named slots handle multiple locations, and scoped slots let the parent access data that lives inside the child, like a list item passed up for custom rendering. Slots make layout components flexible without prop explosion.

questions.question: What is Pinia and why do you use it for state management?
questions.answer: Pinia is the official Vue state store. It gives you reactive state, actions, and getters in a type-safe, devtools-friendly way, and it works with the composition API. I use it when multiple components share state — like a cart or user session — where passing props would get messy. It's simpler than Vuex was, with less boilerplate.

questions.question: What is `provide`/`inject` in Vue?
questions.answer: `provide` lets a parent component supply data to all descendants without prop drilling, and `inject` lets descendants access it. It's great for things like a theme or a shared config. The tradeoff is it can make data flow implicit, so I reserve it for app-wide concerns rather than regular feature state, where I'd prefer props or a store.

questions.question: How do you optimize Vue performance?
questions.answer: The things I check: ensure `v-for` has a stable `:key` so Vue can reuse DOM, avoid unnecessary reactivity depth, lazy-load route components with dynamic imports, debounce heavy user input, and move expensive computations to `computed` so they cache. In my projects I also kept the bundle lean by tree-shaking and code-splitting big dependencies.

questions.question: How does Node.js handle concurrency given it's single-threaded?
questions.answer: Node runs a single main thread but uses an event loop plus a thread pool for certain operations. I/O operations — files, network, databases — are non-blocking, so while one request waits on I/O, the event loop serves other requests. The async model means it handles thousands of concurrent connections with low memory compared to one-thread-per-request servers. The catch is CPU-bound code blocks the loop, so that should go to worker threads or external services.

questions.question: What is middleware in Express?
questions.answer: Middleware is a function that runs between the request arriving and the route handler — it can modify the request/response, run checks, or end the response. I've written middleware for logging, CORS, authentication, and error handling. Middleware order matters: auth goes before protected routes, error middleware has four arguments and goes last. It's the backbone of how Express apps are organized.

questions.question: How do you structure an Express app for a real project?
questions.answer: I separate concerns: a `routes` layer for endpoints, a `controllers` layer that orchestrates, a `services` layer for business logic, and a `models`/repository layer for data access. Configuration goes in environment variables, error handling is centralized, and I use async wrappers so errors flow to the error middleware. This layering is what lets the project scale without turning into a mess.

questions.question: How do you handle errors in an Express app?
questions.answer: I use a centralized error middleware: any thrown error, including from async handlers, gets passed to it via `next(err)`, and it maps errors to proper status codes and a consistent JSON shape. I also use an Express error handler with the four-argument signature, and I make sure to catch unhandled promise rejections. Consistent error responses make the frontend much easier to build.

questions.question: What is CORS and how do you handle it?
questions.answer: CORS is a browser security mechanism that blocks a page from calling APIs on a different origin unless the server allows it. On the server I configure the `cors` middleware with allowed origins, methods, and headers. If credentials are involved, `credentials: true` must pair with an explicit origin. This came up constantly when my Angular/Vue frontends talked to a separate backend on a different port.

questions.question: How do you authenticate requests in a Node/Express API?
questions.answer: The common approach is JWT: on login, the server issues a signed token; the client sends it in the `Authorization` header; a middleware verifies the signature and expiry and attaches the user to the request. I also make sure tokens aren't stored in insecure places and that secrets come from env vars. For higher security, refresh tokens and httpOnly cookies, but JWT-in-header covers most internal apps.

questions.question: What is FastAPI and what makes it different from Flask?
questions.answer: FastAPI is a modern Python framework built on Starlette and Pydantic. The big wins: automatic request validation using Python type hints, auto-generated OpenAPI docs at `/docs`, async support, and dataclass-like models. Flask is simpler and more flexible but leaves validation and serialization to you. For a new API in my stack I'd pick FastAPI for the validation and docs alone.

questions.question: How does FastAPI's dependency injection work?
questions.answer: FastAPI lets you declare dependencies as function parameters with type hints, and it resolves them for you. A classic use is a `get_db()` dependency that yields a database session and closes it after the request. It's also how you do auth — a `get_current_user` dependency that validates the token. It keeps endpoints clean and testable because you can override dependencies in tests.

questions.question: What is Pydantic and why does FastAPI use it?
questions.answer: Pydantic is a data validation library — you define models with Python type hints and it validates, converts, and serializes data. FastAPI uses it for request bodies and query params, so invalid input is rejected with a clear 422 error automatically. It also gives you rich error messages. I find it elegant that my validation logic is just the type definition.

questions.question: What is the difference between sync and async endpoints in FastAPI?
questions.answer: A sync `def` endpoint runs in a thread pool so it doesn't block the event loop, while an `async def` endpoint runs directly on the event loop. The rule I follow: use `async def` only when the endpoint does non-blocking async I/O; if it's blocking — like a synchronous DB driver or heavy computation — use a plain `def` and let FastAPI manage the thread. Mixing a blocking call inside an async endpoint would block everything.

questions.question: What is Flask and when would you use it over FastAPI?
questions.answer: Flask is a micro-framework — minimal, flexible, and easy to get started. I've used it for REST micro-services. Compared to FastAPI, Flask is lighter on magic and gives you more manual control, but you also write your own validation and you don't get auto docs. If the API needs lots of third-party ecosystem, Flask's mature extensions are a plus; for a clean validated API, I lean FastAPI.

questions.question: What is a REST API and what makes one well-designed?
questions.answer: REST uses HTTP verbs on resources: `GET /products`, `POST /products`, etc. Good REST design: nouns for resources, plural consistent naming, proper status codes (200, 201, 400, 404, 401, 500), pagination for lists, versioning (`/api/v1/`), and consistent JSON. I've built several — from e-commerce catalogs to Frappe REST endpoints — and consistency is what makes an API pleasant to consume.

questions.question: How do you secure a backend API?
questions.answer: Beyond auth, I look at: validating all input (never trust the client), rate limiting to prevent abuse, setting CORS carefully, using HTTPS, not logging secrets, sanitizing to prevent injection and XSS, and using environment variables for secrets rather than hardcoding. I also make sure error messages don't leak internals. Security is a habit, not a feature you bolt on at the end.

questions.question: How do you handle database access in Node.js — what libraries have you used?
questions.answer: I've used `pg` for PostgreSQL, `mysql2` for MySQL, and Mongoose for MongoDB. For small apps a raw driver with parameterized queries is fine — parameterization prevents SQL injection. For larger apps an ORM or query builder like Knex or Sequelize helps with migrations and reduces boilerplate. I always use parameterized queries; string-concatenating user input into SQL is a cardinal sin.

questions.question: What is session management in a Node app?
questions.answer: Sessions keep server-side state for a logged-in user, often stored in Redis or memory with a session ID cookie. It's the alternative to stateless JWT. Sessions are easy to revoke server-side; JWTs are easier to scale horizontally but harder to invalidate. For most of my apps JWT was enough; if I needed instant logout control, I'd switch to Redis-backed sessions.

questions.question: What is the difference between `process.nextTick`, `setImmediate`, and `setTimeout`?
questions.answer: `process.nextTick` queues a callback to run after the current operation but before the event loop continues — it's the highest priority. `setImmediate` runs after the current poll phase. `setTimeout` schedules for a minimum delay. The practical lesson: don't starve the loop with nextTick recursion; use it sparingly, like to guarantee certain ordering.

questions.question: How do you test a Node/Express API?
questions.answer: I use Jest or Mocha with Supertest to hit the endpoints. For unit tests I mock database calls; for integration tests I use a test database and run the real app. I test the happy path, validation failures, auth failures, and error responses. My rule is: test behavior, not implementation, so tests don't break on refactoring.

questions.question: What is `dotenv` and how do you manage environment config?
questions.answer: `dotenv` loads `.env` files into `process.env`, so config like DB URLs, JWT secrets, and ports aren't hardcoded. I keep `.env` out of version control and provide a `.env.example` so teammates know what to set. Secrets go in the deployment environment itself — like AWS or the container env — not committed to the repo.

questions.question: What are the differences between horizontal and vertical scaling?
questions.answer: Vertical scaling means a bigger machine — more CPU/RAM on the same server. It's simple but has a ceiling and a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling means more instances behind a load balancer — better for availability and elasticity, but you need shared state (a common DB, Redis for sessions) and stateless app design. I design apps to be stateless so they can scale horizontally on AWS.

questions.question: What is rate limiting and why is it important?
questions.answer: Rate limiting caps how many requests a client can make in a window. It protects your API from abuse, brute-force login attempts, and runaway clients that eat resources. In Express I use `express-rate-limit`, and at the platform level services like Nginx or AWS can enforce it too. Even internal apps benefit from a basic limit.

questions.question: What is Frappe and what is ERPNext?
questions.answer: Frappe is a full-stack, batteries-included web framework written in Python and JavaScript. ERPNext is the flagship open-source ERP built on Frappe — it covers accounting, HR, CRM, inventory, manufacturing, and more. The key idea is that ERPNext is just a set of Frappe apps, so you can build your own app on the same framework. That's exactly what I do for clients: extend ERPNext with custom modules.

questions.question: What is a DocType?
questions.answer: A DocType is the core data model in Frappe — it defines a document type with fields, and each record is a DocType instance. Think of it as Frappe's ORM model that also generates the database table, the form UI, and even the API. Custom DocTypes are how I build things like a Mold record or an Attendance Sync Log for clients. You can make it single, or child-table for sub-rows.

questions.question: What is a Child Table and when do you use it?
questions.answer: A Child Table is a DocType that's meant to be embedded inside a parent document, like line items on a Sales Invoice. It has its own fields and rows, and it's edited within the parent's form. I use child tables constantly — BOM items, gate entry line items, asset lists — because they model one-to-many relationships that live and die with the parent.

questions.question: Explain the Frappe server-side script approach — what are Server Scripts?
questions.answer: Server Scripts let you write Python that runs on the server without creating a full custom app — they can be attached to DocType events or run as API endpoints. They're a quick way to automate small workflows. But for anything substantial I prefer a proper custom app with controllers, because it's version-controllable, testable, and maintainable. Server scripts are great for quick wins though.

questions.question: What are hooks in Frappe?
questions.answer: Hooks is a Python file in the app that registers the app's behavior — DocType overrides, scheduler jobs, permissions, navigation, roles, and scripts. It's the wiring hub of a Frappe app. When I add a scheduler job for a nightly sync or override a method on Sales Order, it goes in hooks. Getting hooks right matters because it's where your app declares itself to the system.

questions.question: What is a Controller in Frappe?
questions.answer: A controller is a Python class for a DocType where you write business logic — validation, auto-calculation, and on-submit actions. Frappe calls the `validate` method before saving and `on_update`/`on_submit` after. For my MSS module, the controller calculates shift capacity and checks mold availability right before the document is saved, so invalid data never reaches the database.

questions.question: What is a workflow in Frappe and how do you use it?
questions.answer: A workflow is a defined state machine on a DocType — it lists states and transitions, and each transition can be restricted to certain roles. So a Sales Order can go from Draft to Submitted to Approved, with only authorized people allowed at each step. Frappe also has workflow actions and optional notifications. It's how I enforce approval chains for client processes without custom code.

questions.question: What is a workflow action and how does it differ from a document state?
questions.answer: A workflow action is the record of a transition step — like 'Approve' or 'Reject' — with the assigned role and the conditions. The document state is where the document currently sits in the workflow. They work together: actions drive transitions, transitions change states. Understanding this distinction helped me debug permission issues where users could see a document but couldn't act on it.

questions.question: What is the role-based permission system in Frappe?
questions.answer: Frappe permissions are role-based: you define roles, assign them to users, and then set read/create/write/delete/print/submit rules per DocType for those roles. There are also user-level and doc-level permissions. This is critical for multi-client ERP deployments — you don't want one client's staff seeing another's data. I set up permission rules carefully in every custom module.

questions.question: How do you customize an existing ERPNext DocType without breaking it?
questions.answer: The clean way is by extending it in a custom app: `override_doctype_class` in hooks plus `extends` in Python to add methods, or using `customize_form` for adding fields. That way upgrades to ERPNext don't clobber my customizations. I avoid editing core files directly — that's a maintenance nightmare on upgrade. Custom fields live separately from core.

questions.question: What is a custom field and how is it different from a custom DocType?
questions.answer: A custom field adds an individual field to an existing DocType — like adding 'Vendor Category' to a Supplier. A custom DocType creates a whole new document type with its own table. Custom fields are light and perfect for small additions; custom DocTypes are for new entities. Both can be managed via the UI or via code (using fixtures or doctype JSON) for version control.

questions.question: What is a report in Frappe and what types are there?
questions.answer: Frappe reports present data from the system. Query reports run raw SQL. Script reports run Python. Report Builder reports are drag-and-drop from the UI. I've built reports for production dashboards, gate logs, and HR data. For complex business metrics I write query reports with SQL and often expose them via dashboards.

questions.question: How do you create a dashboard in Frappe?
questions.answer: Frappe has a built-in Dashboard feature — you can build chart dashboards from report data, and also add dashboard tabs to DocTypes to show related metrics. My Gate Management extension included a dashboard showing daily entries, vehicle counts, and exceptions, so the client could see operations at a glance instead of exporting data.

questions.question: What are Frappe scheduler jobs?
questions.answer: Scheduler jobs are recurring tasks registered in hooks — like a cron. I've used them for nightly data syncs, email notifications, and cleanup tasks. You specify `cron` or interval in hooks and the job calls a Python method. Scheduler reliability matters for things like automated follow-ups, so I log failures and make jobs idempotent so they're safe to re-run.

questions.question: What is a Queue Job / background job in Frappe?
questions.answer: Frappe supports background jobs via RQ for long-running tasks, so a heavy export or a bulk import doesn't block a user request. You use `frappe.enqueue()` to push a function to the queue and track progress. This is how I handled bulk resume processing in the Resume Lens app — the parsing runs in the background and the user sees progress instead of a hanging request.

questions.question: What is `frappe.client.get_list` vs `frappe.get_all`?
questions.answer: They're basically the same — `frappe.get_all` is a low-level optimized way to fetch a list of DocTypes with only the fields you need, no permission checks, and limited conversions. `frappe.client.get_list` is the API wrapper used by the frontend which goes through permissions. On the server I use `frappe.get_all` for speed; on the client side I use `frappe.client.get_list` so permissions apply.

questions.question: What is `frappe.db.sql` and when do you use raw SQL?
questions.answer: `frappe.db.sql` runs raw SQL against the database, which is useful for complex aggregations that the ORM can't express cleanly. I use it for performance-critical reports and bulk operations. The tradeoff is you bypass some Frappe layers, so I keep the SQL simple, use parameters to avoid injection, and prefer the ORM for normal CRUD. In the MSS module I used a raw query for the shift capacity computation.

questions.question: What is a Webhook in Frappe?
questions.answer: A webhook in Frappe fires an HTTP request to an external URL when a DocType event occurs — like on submit of a Sales Order. It's configured in the Frappe UI. I've used it to notify external systems of document changes. For more complex integrations with logic on the Frappe side, I write a custom endpoint and call it from the external system instead.

questions.question: How do you create a REST API endpoint in Frappe?
questions.answer: I create a new Python file in the app, decorate the function with `@frappe.whitelist(allow_guest=True)` when it must be accessible without auth (otherwise default logged-in), and register the route with `route()` or configure it in hooks via `website_route_rules` or app routes. Then the frontend calls it via `frappe.call` or a normal HTTP request. `allow_guest` must be used with care for security.

questions.question: What is `frappe.call` and how is it used from the frontend?
questions.answer: `frappe.call` is the JavaScript method to call a whitelisted server method from the client. You pass the method name, args, and callbacks. It's the standard way to run server logic from ERPNext forms and custom components. I use it to fetch computed data or trigger server actions that go beyond simple form saves, with proper handling of success and failure callbacks.

questions.question: What is a Form Script in Frappe?
questions.answer: A Form Script is JavaScript attached to a DocType's form for client-side behavior — field dependencies, show/hide logic, computed display values, and calls to server methods. It runs on page load. I write form scripts to make client forms feel responsive — like auto-filling fields or enabling a field only when a certain state is selected.

questions.question: How do you handle document submission and cancellation logic in Frappe?
questions.answer: Submission typically sets `docstatus` to 1 and triggers `on_submit` logic — like posting accounting entries. Cancellation sets it to 2 and runs `on_cancel` to reverse those effects. The key is making your logic reversible. For the MSS module, when a production order is cancelled I make sure the capacity and mold bookings are released, so nothing gets double-booked.

questions.question: What is a `validate` method and why is it important?
questions.answer: `validate` is a controller method that runs before the document is saved. It's where I enforce business rules — checking required values, preventing invalid combinations, computing fields. If it raises a `frappe.ValidationError`, the save is blocked and the user sees a friendly message. It's the first line of defense for data integrity in any custom module.

questions.question: What are named and default properties in a DocType?
questions.answer: Named properties define a unique, human-readable name for each record — like a serial number — and become the record's `name`. Default properties are just default field values on new documents. I always give important DocTypes a good named property because it makes references and search work naturally, and I set defaults to reduce data entry errors.

questions.question: How do you do one-to-many and many-to-many relationships in Frappe?
questions.answer: One-to-many is a Child Table inside a parent DocType — the standard pattern. Many-to-many I usually model with a link plus a child table, or a dedicated mapping DocType with links to both sides. For example, a Mold might have many linked machines via a child table of links. I avoid raw many-to-many table design and keep it explicit in Frappe's model.

questions.question: How do you enable and configure notifications/email alerts in Frappe?
questions.answer: Frappe has Notification records where you define a trigger event on a DocType, the condition, recipients (fixed or from fields), and the email/notification template with Jinja placeholders. You can also use `frappe.sendmail` in code for more control. In my HR module I set up automated notifications when attendance or leave requests change status.

questions.question: How do you update Frappe/ERPNext without breaking customizations?
questions.answer: The safe process: keep customizations in a custom app, never edit core files, take a DB backup and snapshot before upgrading, test on staging first, and review release notes for breaking changes. Since my client work is largely custom apps on top of ERPNext, this discipline means upgrades are routine instead of scary. I also pin versions and use benchmarks for manageability.

questions.question: What is the difference between a primary key and a unique key?
questions.answer: A primary key uniquely identifies a row, is automatically indexed, can't be null, and there's only one per table. A unique key also enforces uniqueness but can be null (multiple nulls allowed in most DBs) and you can have several. I use a primary key on the ID column and unique constraints on things like email or serial numbers.

questions.question: What is an index and when should you add one?
questions.answer: An index is like a lookup table that lets the database find rows quickly without scanning the whole table. I add indexes on columns used in `WHERE`, `JOIN`, and `ORDER BY` clauses. But they're not free — they slow writes and take space, so I don't index everything. In my internship I indexed large PostgreSQL tables used in queries and the latency drop was dramatic.

questions.question: Explain a JOIN and the different types.
questions.answer: A JOIN combines rows from two tables based on a related column. `INNER JOIN` returns only matching rows. `LEFT JOIN` returns all rows from the left table plus matches from the right (nulls where no match). `RIGHT JOIN` is the mirror. `FULL OUTER JOIN` returns everything from both. I use INNER for strict relationships and LEFT when I want all left-side records even without matches, like showing all customers even with zero orders.

questions.question: What is the difference between `GROUP BY` and `DISTINCT`?
questions.answer: `DISTINCT` removes duplicate rows from the result. `GROUP BY` groups rows and lets you run aggregate functions per group — like `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`. You can use `GROUP BY` without an aggregate to behave like distinct, but the point of `GROUP BY` is aggregation. For daily transaction reports I'd use `SELECT date, COUNT(*) FROM transactions GROUP BY date`.

questions.question: What is a subquery and when is it better than a JOIN?
questions.answer: A subquery is a query inside another query, often in the `WHERE` or `FROM` clause. It's good for single-value comparisons — like finding employees whose salary is above the average. Generally, joins are more efficient and readable for pulling columns from related tables, while subqueries shine for filtering based on an aggregate or one-off computation.

questions.question: What is normalization and can you explain 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF?
questions.answer: Normalization organizes tables to reduce redundancy. 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups. 2NF: 1NF plus no partial dependency on part of a composite key. 3NF: no transitive dependency — non-key columns depend only on the key. In practice I aim for 3NF for transaction data, then selectively denormalize for reporting tables where joins get too heavy.

questions.question: What is denormalization and why would you do it?
questions.answer: Denormalization adds redundant data to avoid expensive joins, at the cost of consistency. I use it for read-heavy, analytics-style tables — like storing a denormalized daily summary in the dashboard tables instead of joining five tables on every load. The rule: normalize for correctness in writes, denormalize deliberately for reads, and keep the sync logic explicit.

questions.question: What is a transaction and what are ACID properties?
questions.answer: A transaction is a group of database operations that succeed or fail together. ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (constraints preserved), Isolation (transactions don't interfere), Durability (once committed, it's permanent). In ERPs this matters a lot — an order and its stock deduction must be atomic. I've relied on transactions in Frappe and Node to avoid partial updates.

questions.question: What is isolation level and what is the default in most databases?
questions.answer: Isolation levels control how much one transaction can see another's uncommitted changes. From strict to loose: Serializable, Repeatable Read, Read Committed, Read Uncommitted. PostgreSQL defaults to Read Committed; MySQL/InnoDB defaults to Repeatable Read. Lower isolation gives more concurrency but more anomalies. I rarely need to touch this, but I check it when I see phantom-read bugs.

questions.question: What is SQL injection and how do you prevent it?
questions.answer: SQL injection is when user input is crafted to alter the meaning of your SQL — like `' OR 1=1 --`. Prevention: always use parameterized queries or an ORM, never concatenate input into SQL strings. I also validate and sanitize input, use least-privilege DB users, and escape where a dynamic identifier is unavoidable. This is non-negotiable in any API I write.

questions.question: What is the difference between MySQL and PostgreSQL?
questions.answer: PostgreSQL is more feature-rich — advanced indexing (GIN/GIST), full-text search, richer data types, and better standards compliance. MySQL is widely used, simpler, and had a reputation for speed in web read workloads. In my work I've used both plus MariaDB. For complex relational logic I prefer PostgreSQL; for a straightforward web app with the LAMP-style ecosystem, MySQL/MariaDB is fine. Both are rock solid for production.

questions.question: What is MongoDB and when is it a good fit?
questions.answer: MongoDB is a document database — data is stored as BSON documents in collections. It's schema-flexible and great when data is naturally hierarchical or the shape changes often, like content and user profiles. I used it in the TechIT platform for content storage. It's a poor fit when you need heavy multi-table relational queries and strict transactions — then a relational DB is better.

questions.question: What is a NoSQL document vs a relational row?
questions.answer: A relational row lives in a table with a fixed schema — columns are defined up front. A document is a self-contained JSON-like object, and different documents in the same collection can have different fields. That flexibility is powerful but shifts integrity responsibilities to the application. I pick based on the data's shape and how it's queried.

questions.question: What is Redis and what do you use it for?
questions.answer: Redis is an in-memory key-value store. Its killer uses: caching (store computed results or hot data), sessions, rate limiting, and pub/sub or message queues. I've used it to cache frequently-read data so the database load drops, and for storing short-lived state. Because it's in memory, it's fast but you must design for eviction and persistence carefully.

questions.question: What is caching and what strategies do you use?
questions.answer: Caching stores frequently-used data so you don't recompute or re-query. Strategies: cache-aside (check cache, miss → query DB → fill cache), write-through, and TTL-based invalidation. My practical approach: cache reads that are expensive and don't change often, invalidate on write, and set TTLs so stale data is bounded. In my internship I saw API latency drop noticeably once I cached hot queries.

questions.question: What is Firebase and what do you use it for?
questions.answer: Firebase is Google's BaaS — it offers Firestore (a NoSQL document DB), Auth, hosting, storage, and real-time sync. I've used it for auth and real-time data in quick prototyping. It's great when you want to move fast without managing infrastructure, but for complex relational data and custom backend logic I prefer running my own API.

questions.question: What is the difference between `WHERE` and `HAVING`?
questions.answer: `WHERE` filters rows before grouping; `HAVING` filters groups after aggregation. So `WHERE` can't use aggregate functions, but `HAVING` can — `HAVING COUNT(*) > 10`. Classic mistake: trying to filter aggregated results in `WHERE`. I use HAVING for things like 'categories with more than 100 products'.

questions.question: What is an aggregate function? Name a few.
questions.answer: Aggregate functions compute a single value from a set of rows: `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`, and grouping ones like `GROUP_CONCAT`/`string_agg`. I use them constantly in reports and dashboards — like total daily transactions or average order value. They work with `GROUP BY` to summarize per group.

questions.question: What is `LIMIT` and pagination, and how do you implement it efficiently?
questions.answer: `LIMIT` restricts how many rows a query returns; pagination pages through results with `LIMIT n OFFSET m`. The catch: deep offsets get slow because the DB still scans skipped rows. For large sets I use keyset pagination — filtering on the last seen ID — which is much faster. For APIs I always paginate list endpoints so a client can't request the whole table at once.

questions.question: What is a foreign key and what does `ON DELETE CASCADE` do?
questions.answer: A foreign key links a column in one table to a primary key in another, enforcing referential integrity. `ON DELETE CASCADE` means when the parent row is deleted, the dependent rows are deleted automatically. I use CASCADE for child tables that make no sense without their parent, but I avoid it where accidental mass deletion could occur — preferring RESTRICT or a soft delete.

questions.question: What is a deadlock and how do you resolve it?
questions.answer: A deadlock happens when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, and neither can proceed. Databases detect it and abort one. To reduce deadlocks I keep transactions short, lock rows in a consistent order (e.g., always sort IDs), and retry the aborted transaction once. This came up in stock-level updates where two processes deducted inventory simultaneously.

questions.question: What is EXPLAIN and how do you use it for query optimization?
questions.answer: `EXPLAIN` shows the database's execution plan for a query — how it scans, which indexes it uses, where the cost is. I use it when a query is slow: I look for seq scans on big tables (meaning a missing index), verify the index is actually used, and check row estimates. It turned query tuning from guesswork into evidence. Then I add indexes or rewrite the query based on what it reveals.

questions.question: What is a connection pool and why is it important?
questions.answer: A connection pool reuses database connections instead of opening a new one per request — opening connections is expensive. Without pooling, a burst of traffic can exhaust the database's connection limit and crash the app. I configure pools in Node and Python apps, set a sane max size, and make sure connections are released back after use. This is standard in every production app I've deployed.

questions.question: What is ACID vs BASE, and where does each apply?
questions.answer: ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) is for relational databases where correctness is critical — like orders, payments, inventory. BASE (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent) describes many NoSQL systems — they prioritize availability and scale over strict consistency. I choose ACID for anything financial or transactional and consider BASE only when I truly need massive scale and can tolerate eventual consistency.

questions.question: What is the difference between `DELETE` and `TRUNCATE`?
questions.answer: `DELETE` removes rows one at a time, fires triggers, can be filtered with `WHERE`, and can be rolled back — it's slower. `TRUNCATE` removes all rows in one shot, is much faster, doesn't fire per-row triggers, and in most DBs can't be rolled back easily. I use `TRUNCATE` only for clearing staging tables. And note: `DROP` removes the table entirely.

questions.question: What is Docker and how does containerization work?
questions.answer: Docker packages an app and everything it needs — code, runtime, libraries, config — into a container image. Containers share the host OS kernel but isolate the app, so 'it works on my machine' disappears. I write a `Dockerfile`, build an image, and run it consistently on any machine. Images are built in layers, which makes them efficient to share and update. This is the backbone of how I deploy apps.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?
questions.answer: An image is the immutable blueprint — a snapshot of the filesystem and config. A container is a running instance of that image — it has its own writable layer and lifecycle. You can run many containers from one image. I build the image once, then run/stop containers from it for dev, staging, and production.

questions.question: What is a Dockerfile and what are the common instructions?
questions.answer: A Dockerfile is the recipe to build an image. Common instructions: `FROM` (base image), `WORKDIR`, `COPY`/`ADD`, `RUN` (build commands), `ENV`, `EXPOSE` (document ports), `CMD`/`ENTRYPOINT` (how the container starts), and `VOLUME`. I keep images lean — multi-stage builds let me compile and then copy only artifacts, dropping the toolchain from the final image.

questions.question: What is Docker Compose?
questions.answer: Docker Compose defines and runs multi-container apps with a YAML file — services, networks, volumes, environment. Instead of a dozen `docker run` commands, I write `docker-compose.yml` and run `docker compose up`. For my projects that meant one command to start the app, its database, Redis, and a reverse proxy together, which made local dev and staging reproducible.

questions.question: What is the difference between Docker and a virtual machine?
questions.answer: A VM virtualizes hardware — it runs a full guest OS on a hypervisor, which is heavy. A container virtualizes at the OS level — it shares the host kernel and packages just the app and its dependencies. Containers start in seconds and use far less memory. That's why I use containers for application services. VMs still make sense for isolating workloads that need a full OS or different kernels.

questions.question: What is AWS and what services have you used?
questions.answer: AWS is Amazon's cloud platform. I've used EC2 for running servers, ECR/EBS around containers and storage, S3 for object storage and backups, and things like IAM for permissions, plus related services for deployment. My pattern was Ubuntu EC2 instances running Docker containers, with S3 for backups and Nginx for proxying. Knowing the core services — compute, storage, networking, security — covers most needs.

questions.question: What is EC2 and how do you secure one?
questions.answer: EC2 is AWS's virtual server service. To secure an instance: use a restrictive Security Group (only needed ports), SSH key pairs instead of passwords, no public access on admin ports, keep the OS and images patched, use IAM roles rather than hardcoded keys, and enable backups. I also put a reverse proxy like Nginx in front and only expose 80/443 publicly.

questions.question: What is S3 and what do you use it for?
questions.answer: S3 is object storage — buckets of files with URLs and lifecycle policies. I use it for storing uploads, static assets, backups, and logs. It's durable, cheap, and scales infinitely. In the HR module, documents like resumes could live in S3 while the ERP stores just the metadata. I also set lifecycle rules to archive or expire old backups.

questions.question: What is IAM and why is it important on AWS?
questions.answer: IAM is identity and access management — it controls who can do what on AWS via users, groups, roles, and policies. The key principles: least privilege (give only what's needed), prefer roles over long-lived keys for services, and use MFA. Getting IAM wrong is how AWS accounts get compromised. I keep credentials out of code and use environment-based or role-based access.

questions.question: What is Nginx and what do you use it for?
questions.answer: Nginx is a high-performance web server and reverse proxy. I use it to: route requests from port 80/443 to app containers, serve static files, terminate TLS/HTTPS, do load balancing across instances, and add basic security headers. It also handles gzip and caching. Putting Nginx in front of Node/Python apps is the standard production topology I use.

questions.question: What is a reverse proxy vs a forward proxy?
questions.answer: A forward proxy sits in front of clients — it fetches the web on behalf of them, like a corporate proxy or VPN. A reverse proxy sits in front of servers — it receives client requests and forwards them to backend apps. Nginx as a reverse proxy is how I expose multiple services on one server without exposing app ports directly. It also lets me terminate TLS in one place.

questions.question: What are some basic Linux commands you use daily?
questions.answer: The ones I use constantly: `ls`, `cd`, `pwd`, `cp`, `mv`, `rm`, `cat`, `grep`, `find`, `ps`, `top`/`htop`, `df -h`, `free -h`, `netstat`/`ss`, `systemctl`, `journalctl`, `curl`, `chmod`, `chown`, and `tar`. For debugging a slow server I start with `top`, `free`, and `df`, then check logs with `journalctl`. Being comfortable in a shell is essential for deployment work.

questions.question: How do you check disk space and memory on a server?
questions.answer: `df -h` shows disk usage per filesystem and `free -h` shows memory with a line for swap. If disk is full I find the culprit with `du -sh */` or `du -x -h / | sort -h | tail`. Memory pressure shows as swap usage climbing. I also set up monitoring/alerting so I hear about these before users do.

questions.question: What is `systemctl` and how do you manage services with it?
questions.answer: `systemctl` manages systemd services. Common commands: `systemctl start/stop/restart myapp`, `systemctl enable myapp` (start on boot), `systemctl status myapp`, and `journalctl -u myapp` for logs. Whether it's systemd or a Docker restart policy, making services auto-start and auto-restart is table stakes for production reliability.

questions.question: How do you secure an Ubuntu server for production?
questions.answer: My checklist: SSH keys only (no password auth), fail2ban, firewall (ufw) allowing only 22/80/443, automatic security updates, non-root user for daily work, keep Docker images patched, Nginx with TLS, and regular backups with tested restores. I also disable unused services and review open ports. These basics prevent most real-world compromises.
