questions.question: What is Git and what's your branching strategy?
questions.answer: Git is a distributed version control system. My branching strategy: `main` is production-ready, features live in feature branches off `develop`, code review happens via pull requests, and releases are tagged. I rebase or merge to keep history clean depending on team convention. The non-negotiables: commit logical changes with clear messages, never force-push shared branches, and resolve conflicts before they merge.

questions.question: What is CI/CD and how have you implemented it?
questions.answer: CI/CD automates building, testing, and deploying. CI runs on every commit — lint, typecheck, tests — and fails the build if something breaks. CD deploys automatically after a successful pipeline — to staging always, to production on merge or tag. I've used GitHub Actions to build Docker images and push them, then trigger deploys. It removes the human error from shipping and made releases routine.

questions.question: What is the difference between continuous integration and continuous delivery?
questions.answer: Continuous integration is the practice of merging code changes frequently and validating them automatically — every commit is tested, so the trunk is always deployable. Continuous delivery extends that: every validated change is automatically packaged and ready to deploy to production, but the actual production deployment might be a manual or gated click. Continuous deployment pushes to production automatically with no human gate.

questions.question: How do you monitor an application in production?
questions.answer: I look at three layers: logs (centralized, searchable), metrics (CPU, memory, request rates, error rates, latency), and uptime/alerting. Tools I've used range from simple `journalctl` and health-check endpoints to monitoring dashboards and alerting. I also add structured logging and error tracking in the app so a failure is diagnosable instead of a mystery.

questions.question: What is your approach to backups and disaster recovery?
questions.answer: I follow the 3-2-1 rule: three copies, two different media, one off-site. For databases, scheduled snapshots plus a tested restore procedure; for files, off-site storage like S3 with lifecycle rules. The critical part people skip is regularly testing restores — a backup you can't restore isn't a backup. I also document the runbook so a recovery isn't a panic.

questions.question: How would you design a system to handle 100k daily transactions?
questions.answer: Start with the data model — that's the foundation. I'd use a relational database for transactional integrity, with proper indexing on the hot query paths and child tables for line items. The API layer is stateless so it can scale horizontally behind a load balancer. Reads that don't need to be real-time go through caching (Redis) to protect the DB. Heavy work — exports, parsing, notifications — moves to background queues. Finally, monitoring and alerts so I know when something is trending bad. 100k daily is very manageable with a couple of app instances and a tuned DB.

questions.question: What is horizontal scaling and what do you need for it to work?
questions.answer: Horizontal scaling means adding more app instances behind a load balancer instead of one bigger server. For it to work, your app must be stateless — no user data stuck in local memory — so any instance can serve any request. Shared state goes to Redis or the database. Your deployment uses containers (Docker) so instances are identical, and the DB itself might need read replicas. Everything I deploy is designed this way from the start.

questions.question: How do you decide between SQL and NoSQL for a new project?
questions.answer: I look at the data: is it highly relational with joins and transactions? Then SQL — PostgreSQL or MySQL. Is it document-shaped, schema-flexible, with read-heavy workloads? Then NoSQL like MongoDB. I also consider the team's expertise and the query patterns. For ERPs the answer is almost always relational. My honest answer: default to SQL unless there's a concrete reason not to — most 'we need NoSQL for scale' projects don't actually have that scale.

questions.question: How would you architect a microservices split from a monolith?
questions.answer: Don't split everything at once. Start by identifying bounded contexts — natural seams like users, orders, inventory. Extract one service at a time, give it its own database, and expose a clean API. Until then, a modular monolith is honestly fine and much simpler to operate. When services exist, they communicate over HTTP or a message queue, and you need distributed tracing and resilient patterns (retries, circuit breakers) because networks fail.

questions.question: What is a message queue and when do you use one?
questions.answer: A message queue decouples producers from consumers — one side publishes, the other processes asynchronously. I use it for jobs that don't need an immediate response: sending emails, generating reports, parsing resumes, syncing data. It smooths traffic spikes and gives retry/failure handling. In Frappe that's RQ; in general stacks, RabbitMQ, Redis, or SQS. The classic win: the user gets a fast response while heavy work happens behind the scenes.

questions.question: How do you handle API rate limiting and what tools do you use?
questions.answer: Rate limiting protects the API from abuse and runaway clients. I've implemented it at the app level with middleware (like `express-rate-limit`) using Redis for distributed counting, and at the infra level with Nginx or cloud load balancers. Design decisions: per-IP and/or per-user limits, appropriate windows, and friendly 429 responses with a `Retry-After` header so clients can back off gracefully.

questions.question: What is a load balancer and how does it work?
questions.answer: A load balancer distributes incoming traffic across multiple servers so no single one is overwhelmed and a failing one doesn't take the service down. It can do round-robin, least connections, or health-based routing — checking each backend and removing unhealthy ones. In my architecture, Nginx or the cloud load balancer sits in front of Docker containers running the app, terminating TLS and routing requests.

questions.question: How do you design an idempotent API?
questions.answer: An idempotent endpoint means calling it multiple times with the same input has the same effect as calling it once — no duplicate orders, payments, or records. Techniques: use an idempotency key header (client sends a UUID), check if a record with that key already exists before creating, and make updates natural (setting a value rather than incrementing blindly). For my MSS module, preventing double-generated Sales Orders relied on exactly this.

questions.question: What are eventual consistency and strong consistency?
questions.answer: Strong consistency means every read sees the latest committed write — the app waits for confirmation. Eventual consistency means writes propagate asynchronously and reads may briefly see stale data, but will converge. Databases replicate with different tradeoffs. In practice: critical money flows need strong consistency; a 'recent notifications' feed can be eventual. I choose per-feature, not per-stack.

questions.question: How would you design a URL shortener or similar simple system?
questions.answer: Focus on the key decisions: the API (`POST` to create, `GET` redirect), the storage (relational with a unique code column and an index), the short-code generation (collision-safe, e.g., base-62 of a counter or random with retry), analytics capture, and caching hot URLs in Redis so the DB isn't hit on every redirect. Then scaling: the redirects are read-heavy, so caching and stateless app servers do most of the work.

questions.question: How do you approach database migrations?
questions.answer: I treat migrations as version-controlled code — each change is an incremental, reversible script. Before running: backup, review, test on staging. Order matters: add a column nullable first, backfill, then add the constraint. For Frappe, changes are in the DocType JSON; for raw SQL apps, migration files. The discipline is what keeps schema changes from breaking running systems.

questions.question: What is the difference between a monolith and microservices, and when would you choose each?
questions.answer: A monolith is one deployable unit — simpler to build, test, and operate, but gets hard to scale teams on. Microservices are independent deployables per business domain — great for large teams and independent scaling, but expensive: more ops, networking, and failure modes. My honest default: start modular monolith; split only when team size or scaling genuinely demands it. 'Microservices for everyone' creates more problems than it solves.

questions.question: How do you ensure high availability for a web app?
questions.answer: Remove single points of failure. Multiple app instances behind a load balancer, so instance loss is invisible. A managed or replicated database with failover. Health checks that remove unhealthy instances. Stateless design so any instance can take traffic. Backups with tested recovery. And monitoring + alerting so I find problems before users do. Perfection is impossible, but you can make every failure survivable.

questions.question: What is observability and how is it different from monitoring?
questions.answer: Monitoring tells you something is wrong — metrics, thresholds, alerts. Observability is the ability to ask why — to drill into any state using logs, traces, and metrics together. Concretely: monitoring says 'error rate is up'; observability lets me trace a specific failed request across the stack to find the cause. I add structured logs and correlation IDs so a user report can be traced end to end.

questions.question: How do you design an authentication system?
questions.answer: The basics: secure password storage (hash with salt via bcrypt/argon2, never plaintext), login that issues a signed token or session, and middleware that verifies it on protected routes. Add-ons: refresh tokens, token expiry, lockout after failed attempts, rate limiting on login, and MFA for sensitive actions. On the frontend, the token goes in an httpOnly cookie or memory with secure headers. For multi-app setups, a single sign-on gateway. I've built this both with JWT and with session stores.

questions.question: Tell me about the Production Scheduling & Mold Management Tool (MSS).
questions.answer: It was a custom ERPNext module for a manufacturer. The client planned production on spreadsheets and paper, and mistakes caused missed deliveries. I built a module that reads the Bill of Materials for planned production, computes shift capacity, checks mold availability and maintenance schedules, and auto-generates Sales Orders from Blanket Orders. The hard part was modeling the real factory rules — capacity, mold conflicts, maintenance windows — and then making the system reliable enough that planners trusted it. It's been running in production and cut planning time significantly.

questions.question: What was the biggest technical challenge in the MSS project?
questions.answer: The capacity calculation. It wasn't a simple sum — it had to combine shift schedules, machine availability, mold lifecycle, and BOM requirements, and detect conflicts like a mold booked on two machines at the same time. I solved it by modeling availability as a schedule with bookings, writing a server-side calculation in the controller, and using raw SQL for the heavy aggregation. I also made it idempotent so re-running the calculation didn't double-book capacity.

questions.question: How did you ensure the MSS tool didn't generate duplicate Sales Orders?
questions.answer: I designed it to be idempotent. Before generating a Sales Order from a Blanket Order, the code checks whether one already exists for that source — there's a link field recording the origin. I also ran generation inside a transaction so a failure rolled everything back cleanly. We tested the re-run scenario explicitly because a planner re-running a job is exactly when duplicates would sneak in.

questions.question: Explain the HRMS Biometric Integration Tool.
questions.answer: The client used physical biometric attendance machines, and HR was manually copying logs into ERPNext. I built a Python integration that reads attendance logs from the devices, matches them to employees, and syncs them into ERPNext with automatic shift mapping. I also built Resume Lens — a React-based recruitment tool that parses resumes and feeds candidates straight into the ERP. Together they cut a ton of manual data entry and the errors that came with it.

questions.question: How did you handle the real-time sync between biometric devices and ERPNext?
questions.answer: The sync ran on a schedule and on-demand, pulling new logs, transforming them into the ERP's attendance doctype, and flagging mismatches — like an employee ID with no match — for manual review instead of failing silently. I made the sync idempotent by tracking a last-synced marker and de-duplicating by device log ID, so re-syncs didn't double-count attendance. Every failure was logged and visible to the HR admin.

questions.question: What was the Resume Lens App and how did resume parsing work?
questions.answer: Resume Lens was a recruitment module built with React and Python inside ERPNext. Candidates upload or send resumes, and the tool extracts structured data — name, contact, experience, skills — and creates candidate records. Parsing used extraction logic in Python with fallbacks for different formats, and unresolvable fields went to a review queue rather than being silently wrong. Bulk imports ran as background jobs so the UI never froze.

questions.question: Tell me about the e-commerce platform you built.
questions.answer: It was a multi-stack showcase e-commerce build with Angular and TypeScript on the frontend and Flask/PHP micro-services behind REST APIs, with MySQL for data. I handled the responsive, component-driven UI with product filtering, the API layer for catalog and inventory, and the admin panel for managing categories and content. It was a great project for understanding the whole web: UI, API design, and relational schema in one codebase.

questions.question: How did you optimize the Vue.js frontend to get a 25% load speed improvement?
questions.answer: I attacked the usual culprits in order: bundle size first — lazy-loaded routes so users only download what they need; then rendering — stable keys in `v-for`, computed properties so expensive logic wasn't re-run on every render, and removing unnecessary reactivity; then network — caching API responses and parallelizing independent requests. I measured before and after with the browser performance tools, which is the important part — I changed things, verified each one actually helped, and kept the wins.

questions.question: How did you reduce database errors by 15% in the REST API layer?
questions.answer: The errors weren't one bug — they were a pattern of small data issues: missing required fields, wrong types, race conditions on updates. I fixed it by standardizing validation on the API layer (so bad input never reached the DB), adding proper transactions for multi-step operations, indexing the hot query paths, and adding error tracking so each failure was visible and fixed instead of happening silently in the dark. Measuring error rates before and after showed the drop.

questions.question: What did you learn from the TechIT cross-platform project (web + mobile)?
questions.answer: The big lesson was that 'shared backend, two clients' is a coordination problem as much as a technical one. I built the Angular web app, the Android app in Java/XML, and connected both to one REST API. I learned to keep the API clean and consistent because two frontends magnify every API inconsistency. Also SEO work — I applied content strategies that boosted traffic by 40%, which taught me that good engineering includes how users find the product.

questions.question: What was the Gate Management module and why was it useful?
questions.answer: It was a Frappe extension automating gate entry and exit for a client site — vehicle logs, visitor records, and approvals. Before, it was paper registers; now every entry is a doctype record, searchable and reported. I built a dashboard showing daily entries, vehicle counts, and exceptions. It was a good example of digitizing an operational process end to end — small in theory, high daily usage, and it visibly improved how the site ran.

questions.question: How do you approach a new client module from requirements to delivery?
questions.answer: I start by understanding the process, not the code — I ask how the work happens today, where the pain is, and what a win looks like. Then I design the data model (doctypes, fields, relationships) and get the user to confirm it against real examples. I build in small vertical slices — a working thing end to end early — and get feedback constantly. Then testing, migration of real data, training, and a rollout with support. The successful modules were the ones where I listened first and coded second.

questions.question: What was your most technically difficult bug and how did you fix it?
questions.answer: A sync job was intermittently missing records. The logs looked fine, but some records never arrived. The root cause turned out to be a race — two processes could process the same device log simultaneously, both saw 'not yet processed,' and both wrote, with one silently dropping due to a duplicate key. The fix had three parts: a unique constraint on the device log ID so duplicates couldn't slip through, an atomic 'claim before processing' step, and a reconciliation job that re-scanned for gaps. That experience shaped how I design sync systems now.

questions.question: If you were to rebuild one of your projects from scratch, what would you do differently?
questions.answer: For MSS, I'd spend more time on the data model upfront — some of the availability logic had to work around an awkward schema I'd have designed differently. I'd also build a proper test suite from day one; on client modules there was a lot of manual testing, and automated tests would have caught regressions earlier. And I'd set up monitoring for the sync jobs earlier so failures surfaced the day they happened, not the week after.

questions.question: How do you decide what technologies to use for a project?
questions.answer: I start from the problem and the team. If it's an ERP problem, Frappe/ERPNext — building it from scratch would be crazy. If it's a user-facing web product, the frontend follows what the team knows best and what the product needs. Backend: Python or Node based on the domain — Python for data-heavy logic, Node for I/O-heavy real-time. I keep the principle: choose boring, proven tech unless there's a concrete reason not to, because I'm paid to deliver, not to be adventurous.

questions.question: Reverse a string in Python.
questions.answer: There's the Pythonic way: `s[::-1]` — slicing with a negative step reverses it. If I had to do it manually, two pointers swapping from both ends. For a coding interview I'd first check edge cases — empty string, unicode. The Pythonic one-liner is usually what they want, but being able to explain the manual approach shows you understand the mechanics.

questions.question: How do you find the most frequent element in an array?
questions.answer: I'd use a dictionary to count occurrences in one pass — O(n) time — then track the max. `Counter` from collections does exactly this. The honest interview answer: hash map counting, then a single pass to find the max count. If there are ties you decide the tiebreak and state it.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of binary search?
questions.answer: Binary search is O(log n) because it halves the search space each step — assuming the data is sorted. I can write it iteratively or recursively; the iterative version avoids recursion depth issues. It's one of those algorithms I actually use in real life, like when searching a sorted dataset or debugging a range query.

questions.question: Explain big O notation in your own words.
questions.answer: Big O describes how an algorithm's time or space grows as the input grows — the trend, not exact numbers. O(1) is constant, O(n) linear, O(n log n) like good sorting, O(n²) quadratic, O(log n) like binary search. When I write code that might process large data — like a daily export — I think about whether the algorithm will blow up at scale. It's about choosing the right shape of solution, not micro-optimizing.

questions.question: How would you check if two strings are anagrams?
questions.answer: Two ways. The simple one: sort both and compare — O(n log n). The better one: count character frequencies in a dictionary and compare the counts — O(n). I'd also normalize whitespace and case first. The hash-map counting approach is the one I'd present in an interview because it's the more efficient and shows you think about complexity.

questions.question: What is a hash map and why are lookups fast?
questions.answer: A hash map (or dict) stores key-value pairs, and lookups average O(1) because it hashes the key to find the bucket directly instead of scanning everything. Collisions are handled by chaining or probing, which is why worst case is worse but average is constant. That's why I reach for dictionaries for deduplication and counting — near-instant lookups regardless of size.

questions.question: How do you find duplicates in an array?
questions.answer: Use a set — add elements as you iterate; if an element is already in the set, it's a duplicate. That's O(n) time and O(n) space. If space is constrained, sorting first then checking adjacent pairs is O(n log n) time with O(1) space. For most real cases, the set approach is the right one. In actual work this comes up all the time with import data.

questions.question: What is a stack vs a queue?
questions.answer: A stack is LIFO — last in, first out, like a pile of plates. A queue is FIFO — first in, first out, like a line at a counter. In Python a list can act as a stack (`append`/`pop`), and `deque` is a good queue. Stacks are great for undo operations and matching brackets; queues for processing things in order, like a job queue.

questions.question: Explain recursion and give an example.
questions.answer: Recursion is a function calling itself on a smaller piece of the problem until it hits a base case. The classic example is factorial or Fibonacci: `fact(n) = n * fact(n-1)` with `fact(0)=1`. The two rules: a clear base case that stops it, and progress toward that base case on every call. Missing either causes infinite recursion. I use recursion for tree traversal and directory walking, but I watch stack depth — Python has a recursion limit.

questions.question: How would you find the largest number in an array without using built-in max?
questions.answer: Initialize a variable to the first element, then loop through comparing — if the current element is bigger, update the variable. That's O(n), which is optimal since you have to look at every element. In an interview I'd write it manually to show the logic, then mention that in real code I'd just use `max()`. Edge cases: empty array — return None or raise, and decide it upfront.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to learn a new technology quickly.
questions.answer: At Assimilate I had to pick up Frappe and ERPNext in my first weeks because my first tasks were Frappe modules. I treated it like a directed learning project: I read the framework docs, built tiny experiments, and asked the senior devs the right questions. Within a couple of months I was delivering custom modules on my own. The lesson that stuck: you don't need to know everything upfront, you need to know how to learn the next thing.

questions.question: Describe a time you dealt with a difficult client or stakeholder.
questions.answer: We had a client who kept asking for changes mid-development and the scope was growing. Instead of getting defensive, I set up a short weekly demo where they saw the latest build and I showed what each change cost in the schedule. Once they could see the impact of every request, they became more deliberate. We shipped on time and they still use the module. The lesson: a visible process beats arguing about scope.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate.
questions.answer: I remember a disagreement about whether to use a raw SQL report or build it with the framework's reporting tools. I argued for raw SQL because the aggregation was complex and the framework version was getting awkward. We sat down, I built a small prototype of both, and compared — mine was faster and simpler. The senior agreed, but I learned to lead with evidence and prototypes, not opinions.

questions.question: How do you handle a bug that's urgent but you can't reproduce it?
questions.answer: First, I don't guess — I gather data. I check logs, error tracking, and recent deployments, and ask the reporter for the exact steps, environment, and data involved. I add targeted logging at the likely paths to catch it next time. If it's urgent, I look for a safe mitigation — like a validation or a retry — while continuing to investigate. The goal is to reduce the blast radius first, then find the root cause.

questions.question: How do you prioritize when you have multiple tasks and deadlines?
questions.answer: I look at impact and urgency. Anything that blocks other people or is heading to an external deadline goes first; small internal things wait. I also communicate — if two deadlines collide, I say so early and propose a tradeoff rather than silently dropping something. Practically, I keep a short written list and update it, because 'what am I working on' should be answerable in one sentence.

questions.question: What do you do when you don't know the answer to a problem?
questions.answer: I say I don't know — no one expects you to know everything — and then I immediately do something about it: I research, reproduce the issue in a small test, read the docs or source, and if it's blocking I ask a teammate with context. The worst thing you can do is pretend and guess in production. I've also found that explaining the problem out loud to someone often surfaces the answer.

questions.question: How do you give and receive feedback?
questions.answer: I give feedback promptly and privately, focused on the behavior and its impact, not the person — 'when X happened, it caused Y, here's what I'd suggest.' I receive feedback by listening, asking clarifying questions, and saying thank you rather than defending. Then I actually do something with it, because repeated feedback you ignore is worse than no feedback.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you made a mistake at work.
questions.answer: Early on, I deployed a change without testing a migration against real data, and it caused a data issue for a client. I owned it, restored from the backup, fixed the migration, and added a step to my checklist: always test schema changes against a copy of production data. The incident changed my process, and that's the part I emphasize — mistakes are fine if they make the system better.

questions.question: How do you stay updated with new technologies?
questions.answer: I balance depth and breadth. For depth, I follow the frameworks I actually use — Frappe, Angular, Vue, FastAPI — by reading their release notes and changelogs. For breadth, I keep a few trusted sources and communities and do hands-on experiments rather than just reading. But I'm also a bit skeptical of hype — I want to know what's genuinely useful for my work, not just what's trending.

questions.question: Why should we hire you over other candidates?
questions.answer: I bring a combination that's genuinely rare: strong full stack fundamentals AND deep ERP/Frappe automation experience. I can design the database, build the API, and ship the frontend, and I've delivered real modules that process hundreds of transactions daily for actual clients. I also care about the full lifecycle — testing, deployment, monitoring — so I don't just write code, I make it work reliably in production.

questions.question: Describe your ideal working relationship with your manager.
questions.answer: I work best with a manager who gives clear priorities and context — the 'why' — and then trusts me to figure out the how. I like check-ins where I can show progress and flag risks early, and I want honest feedback so I can grow. I'm comfortable with autonomy, but I'll never surprise a manager with a problem they should have known about earlier.

questions.question: How do you handle working under pressure?
questions.answer: Pressure doesn't change what good work looks like, it changes how I sequence it. I break the problem into the smallest deliverable that unblocks people, do that first, and then build on it. I communicate status honestly, even when it's bad news — a clear early warning beats a late surprise. And I make sure the fundamentals don't break under pressure: no hacks, no skipped backups, no uncommitted work.

questions.question: What are your salary expectations?
questions.answer: I'm looking for a fair market rate for my experience level — a full stack developer with three years, ERP/automation specialization, and production deployment experience in Pune. I'd rather talk about the full package — including learning and growth opportunities — than a single number. If you share the range for this role, I can tell you whether it aligns.

questions.question: What do you like most about being a full stack developer?
questions.answer: The end-to-end ownership. I like that I can take a real business problem, shape the data, build the logic, design the screen, and deploy it — and then watch people use it every day. There's an instant feedback loop that keeps me motivated. I also like that full stack work keeps me honest: when you own the whole path, you can't blame 'the other side' for integration problems.

questions.question: Do you prefer working on new features or fixing bugs?
questions.answer: I'd say I prefer new features, because building something useful is the rewarding part, but I've learned to genuinely appreciate good debugging — it's detective work, and the systems I've designed (syncs, ERP modules) made me better at it. The honest answer for a team is: I'll do both well, and I understand that a healthy product needs both.

questions.question: What is HTML and what does it do?
questions.answer: HTML, HyperText Markup Language, is the skeleton of every web page. It defines the structure and content — headings, paragraphs, links, images, forms. It's not a programming language; it's markup. In my daily work I rarely hand-write plain HTML because frameworks like Angular and Vue generate it, but understanding it deeply is what makes framework-generated markup debuggable.

questions.question: What is the difference between HTML and HTML5?
questions.answer: HTML5 is the modern version. The big additions: semantic tags like `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<section>`, `<article>`, `<footer>`; native audio and video; canvas and SVG; local storage and session storage; new form input types and validation; and better accessibility and mobile support. Older HTML relied on divs and third-party plugins for media. When I mark up a page today, HTML5 semantics are the default.

questions.question: What are semantic HTML tags and why do they matter?
questions.answer: Semantic tags describe what the content means, not just how it looks — `<article>` means an article, `<nav>` means navigation. They matter for three reasons: accessibility (screen readers understand structure), SEO (search engines understand the page), and maintainability (developers understand the code). A blind comparison of a page made of divs versus one made of semantic tags shows exactly why semantics matter.

questions.question: What is the difference between block and inline elements?
questions.answer:
A block element takes the full width available and starts on a new line — like `
`, `

`, `

`, `
`. An inline element sits within the line flow and only takes as much width as it needs — like ``, ``, ``, ``. You can change this with CSS `display`, but understanding the default matters for layout. This distinction is the first thing that clicked for me about why pages lay out the way they do.

questions.question: What is the difference between `<div>` and `<span>`?
questions.answer: A `<div>` is a block-level container used to group larger sections or layout blocks. A `<span>` is an inline container used to group small pieces of text or inline elements for styling. Neither carries any semantic meaning by itself — that's why HTML5 added semantic tags. In practice, I reach for a div when I need a layout wrapper and a span when I need to style a fragment of text.

questions.question: What is the difference between `id` and `class` in HTML/CSS?
questions.answer: An `id` is unique — one element per page — and is great for anchor links and JavaScript hooks. A `class` can be reused on many elements and is the workhorse for CSS styling. In CSS, `#id` has higher specificity than `.class`, so it's harder to override. My habit: use classes for anything reusable and reserve ids for truly one-of-a-kind elements or JS targets.

questions.question: What are meta tags and which ones matter for SEO?
questions.answer: Meta tags live in the `<head>` and give the browser and search engines information about the page. The ones that matter most: `<title>` (the page title in search results), `<meta name="description">` (the snippet), `<meta name="viewport">` (mobile responsiveness), and Open Graph tags for social sharing. I worked on SEO for the TechIT platform, and getting title and description right measurably improved click-through.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the `<!DOCTYPE html>` declaration?
questions.answer: It tells the browser to render the page in standards mode rather than quirks mode. In quirks mode, browsers emulate old, buggy behavior; in standards mode, your CSS behaves predictably across browsers. It has to be the very first thing in the document. This tiny declaration is the difference between consistent cross-browser layouts and mysterious inconsistencies.

questions.question: What is the DOM?
questions.answer: The DOM, Document Object Model, is the browser's tree representation of an HTML document — each element, attribute, and text node becomes an object. JavaScript manipulates the DOM to change what users see without reloading the page. Frameworks like Angular and Vue work by efficiently syncing the DOM with your state. Understanding the DOM is understanding where your UI actually lives.

questions.question: What is the difference between HTML elements and tags?
questions.answer:
A tag is the raw markup — like `

` and `

`. An element is the tag plus everything between the opening and closing tag — the content included. So the opening tag, closing tag, and content together form an element. It's a small distinction but interviewers like precision, and it clarifies how browsers parse documents.

questions.question: What is the difference between `<strong>` and `<b>`? And `<em>` vs `<i>`?
questions.answer: `<strong>` and `<em>` carry semantic meaning — strong importance and emphasis, which screen readers announce differently. `<b>` and `<i>` are purely visual — bold and italic — with no semantic weight. Accessibility best practice says use the semantic ones. On modern browsers they look the same, but meaning matters for assistive technology.

questions.question: What are void elements in HTML? Give examples.
questions.answer:
A void element is an element that has no content and no closing tag — it's self-contained. Examples: ``, `
`, `
`, ``, ``, ``. There's nothing to put between tags because the element itself is the content. Knowing which tags are void prevents the classic mistake of writing `` and getting confused why it doesn't validate.

questions.question: What are attributes and which common ones do you use?
questions.answer: Attributes provide extra information or behavior on an element — they go in the opening tag as name/value pairs. Common ones: `href` on links, `src` and `alt` on images, `class` and `id` for styling, `type` on inputs, `data-*` for custom data, `disabled`, `placeholder`, and `target`. The `alt` attribute is important — it's both accessibility and SEO, and a broken image without alt is a broken experience.

questions.question: What is the difference between `href` and `src`?
questions.answer: `href` establishes a link to another resource or location — used by ``, ``, and in some cases as a reference. `src` embeds the resource directly into the page — used by ``, `

questions.question: What are the heading tags and why is hierarchy important?
questions.answer: `<h1>` through `<h6>` define headings with decreasing importance. The hierarchy matters for SEO and accessibility — a page should have one `<h1>` that represents its main topic, then subheadings in order. Jumping from `<h1>` to `<h4>` confuses both screen readers and search crawlers. I treat the heading structure like a document outline.

questions.question: What is a form in HTML and what are its key parts?
questions.answer: A form collects user input and sends it to a server. Key parts: `action` (where to send), `method` (`get` or `post`), input fields with `name` attributes (the name becomes the data key), labels for accessibility, and a submit button. `name` is critical — without it, the browser doesn't know what key to send the value under. Almost every app I've built starts with a form somewhere.

questions.question: What is the difference between GET and POST forms?
questions.answer: GET appends the form data to the URL as query parameters — it's visible, has length limits, and is good for search and filters. POST sends data in the request body — it's not visible in the URL, has no practical size limit, and is used for creating or updating data. I use GET for anything that should be bookmarkable and POST for anything that changes state.

questions.question: What is `localStorage` vs `sessionStorage` vs cookies?
questions.answer: `localStorage` persists until you clear it — data survives browser restarts. `sessionStorage` survives only while the tab/session is open. Cookies are sent automatically with every request to the domain and have a size limit around 4KB, but they work cross-tab and are needed for session-based auth. I use localStorage for non-sensitive preferences and reserve cookies for auth where the server needs them.

questions.question: How do you make a website responsive?
questions.answer: The three pillars: fluid layouts using relative units and flexbox/grid, media queries to adjust at breakpoints, and flexible images that scale within their container. Mobile-first means writing base styles for small screens and enhancing upward. In my Vue and Angular work I build with responsive design from the first component rather than bolting it on later, because retrofitting is painful.

questions.question: What are media queries and how do they work?
questions.answer: Media queries apply CSS only when certain conditions are true — most commonly a viewport width range. Example: `@media (max-width: 768px) { .sidebar { display: none; } }`. They're the core mechanism of responsive design, letting you define breakpoints where the layout reorganizes for different screen sizes.

questions.question: What is the box model in CSS?
questions.answer: The box model says every element is a box made of content, padding, border, and margin — inside to outside. Understanding it explains why elements are sized the way they are. With `box-sizing: border-box`, width includes padding and border, which makes layout math far easier. I set `box-sizing: border-box` globally on every project — it removes a whole class of sizing bugs.

questions.question: What is the difference between `margin` and `padding`?
questions.answer: Margin is the space outside the border — it pushes other elements away. Padding is the space inside the border — it pushes the content away from the border. Margins can collapse (adjacent vertical margins merge), padding never does. This is one of those fundamentals that causes subtle layout differences, so I always think about which one I actually mean.

questions.question: What is the CSS cascade and specificity?
questions.answer: The cascade determines which rule wins when multiple rules target the same element. Specificity ranks selectors — IDs beat classes, classes beat element selectors — and inline styles beat all of them, while `!important` overrides everything. The practical lesson: write low-specificity, well-organized CSS and you won't need `!important` battles. I've debugged plenty of 'why is this style not applying' — it's always specificity or order.

questions.question: What is the difference between `display: none` and `visibility: hidden`?
questions.answer: `display: none` removes the element from the layout entirely — it takes up no space and isn't rendered. `visibility: hidden` keeps the space but makes the element invisible. `opacity: 0` also keeps space but remains clickable. So the choice depends on whether you want space preserved and whether interaction should remain. Angular's `*ngIf` uses DOM removal, which is the `display: none` equivalent.

questions.question: What is the difference between `position: relative`, `absolute`, `fixed`, and `sticky`?
questions.answer: `relative` positions the element relative to its normal spot and creates a containing block for absolute children. `absolute` positions relative to the nearest positioned ancestor and removes it from flow. `fixed` positions relative to the viewport, so it stays on scroll. `sticky` is like relative until a threshold, then acts fixed. These are the building blocks of overlays, modals, and headers — I use them almost daily.

questions.question: What is z-index and how does stacking work?
questions.answer: `z-index` controls the stacking order of positioned elements — higher values appear on top. But it only works on positioned elements (relative, absolute, fixed, sticky) or flex/grid items, and it's scoped to the nearest stacking context. The classic bug: a z-index that doesn't work because a parent creates its own stacking context. Understanding stacking contexts fixes a whole family of overlay problems.

questions.question: What is Flexbox and when do you use it?
questions.answer: Flexbox is a one-dimensional layout model — it lays items out along a row or a column and handles alignment and distribution elegantly. It's perfect for navbars, centering content, card rows, and distributing items with `justify-content` and `align-items`. I use flexbox for almost any single-axis arrangement because it removes the hacks we used to need for centering.

questions.question: What is the difference between `justify-content` and `align-items`?
questions.answer: `justify-content` aligns items along the main axis (the direction of the flex row/column). `align-items` aligns along the cross axis (perpendicular). So in a horizontal row, `justify-content` controls left-right spacing and `align-items` controls vertical alignment. Mixing these up is the most common flexbox mistake I see — including in my own early projects.

questions.question: What is CSS Grid and when is it better than Flexbox?
questions.answer: Grid is a two-dimensional layout model — it handles rows and columns simultaneously with explicit placement. It's better for full-page layouts, dashboards, and any design where items need to align both horizontally and vertically. Flexbox handles one axis at a time; Grid handles both. For a dashboard of widgets or a product grid, Grid is the right tool. My rule: flex for alignment along one axis, grid for overall page structure.

questions.question: What is the difference between CSS Grid `grid-template-columns` and `grid-auto-rows`?
questions.answer: `grid-template-columns` defines the explicit columns and their sizes. `grid-auto-rows` sets the size for rows that aren't explicitly defined — the implicit ones created when content overflows. So you define the structure explicitly with template properties, and auto properties handle the overflow rows and columns. This matters when you have dynamic content, like a growing list of dashboard widgets.

questions.question: What is a pseudo-class and a pseudo-element? Give examples.
questions.answer: A pseudo-class targets an element based on state or position — `:hover`, `:focus`, `:first-child`, `:nth-child(2)`. A pseudo-element targets a specific part of an element — `::before`, `::after`, `::first-letter`. Pseudo-elements let you add decorative content with CSS instead of HTML. I use `::before`/`::after` for icons and accents, and `:hover`/`:focus` for interaction states.

questions.question: What are CSS combinators?
questions.answer: Combinators describe relationships between selectors: descendant (space, `div p`), child (`>`), adjacent sibling (`+`), and general sibling (`~`). So `div > p` selects paragraphs that are direct children, while `div p` selects any paragraph inside. They let you target precisely without adding classes. Understanding combinators reduces the amount of class noise in your markup.

questions.question: What is `em` vs `rem` in CSS?
questions.answer: `rem` is relative to the root font size — predictable, consistent, and unaffected by nesting. `em` is relative to the parent's font size — it compounds as you nest, which can get unpredictable. My rule: use `rem` for almost everything, especially spacing and font sizes, and reserve `em` for things that should scale with their own context, like padding inside a component with a varying font size.

questions.question: What is `vh` and `vw`? When would you use them?
questions.answer: `vh` and `vw` are viewport-relative units — `100vh` is the full viewport height, `50vw` is half the viewport width. They're great for hero sections that fill the screen or elements sized to the browser window. The caveat: mobile browsers handle dynamic toolbars differently, so `100vh` can be slightly off — `100dvh` (dynamic viewport height) fixes that on modern browsers.

questions.question: What is the difference between `min-width`, `max-width`, and `width`?
questions.answer: `width` sets a fixed size, `min-width` sets a floor the element won't shrink below, and `max-width` sets a ceiling it won't grow beyond. Using `max-width` with percentage widths gives fluid-but-bounded layouts — like content that fills 90% but caps at 1200px. This combo is the backbone of most responsive containers I write.

questions.question: How do you center an element both horizontally and vertically?
questions.answer: The modern clean ways: with flexbox, `display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center` on the parent. With grid, `place-items: center`. The classic way is `position: absolute; top: 50%; left: 50%; transform: translate(-50%, -50%)`. For text, `text-align: center` and `line-height`. Flexbox centering is what I reach for almost every time.

questions.question: What is `overflow` and what values does it take?
questions.answer: `overflow` controls what happens when content exceeds the element's box. Values: `visible` (content spills out), `hidden` (clipped), `scroll` (always shows scrollbars), `auto` (shows scrollbars only when needed). `overflow: hidden` on a parent is also the classic fix for floating-children issues. In modern layout I use `auto` for scrollable containers and `hidden` to clip content like carousels.

questions.question: What is a CSS transition and how does it differ from an animation?
questions.answer: A transition animates from one state to another when a property changes — like `transition: all .3s` on hover. An animation defines keyframes with `@keyframes` and runs them, including repeating and controlling intermediate steps. Transitions are for simple state changes; animations are for complex multi-step motion. I use transitions for hover effects and subtle feedback, animations for loading spinners and entrance effects.

questions.question: What is the CSS `float` property and why is it less used today?
questions.answer: Float pushed elements left or right so text wraps around them — it was the original layout tool. But it takes elements out of normal flow, causing the parent-height-collapse problem that needed the `clearfix` hack. Flexbox and Grid replaced it for layout. Today I only see float used for the niche case of wrapping text around an image — which is actually its one remaining legitimate use.

questions.question: What is `clearfix` and when do you need it?
questions.answer: Clearfix is a hack to fix the problem where a container's height collapses because its floated children are out of normal flow. You add a pseudo-element with `clear: both` or the container `overflow: hidden` to make it contain its floats. I rarely need it now because flexbox and grid handle containment naturally, but knowing it explains a lot of old CSS code.

questions.question: What is the difference between `opacity`, `visibility`, and `display` for hiding?
questions.answer: `opacity: 0` makes it invisible but it still occupies space and is clickable, and it can be transitioned smoothly. `visibility: hidden` keeps space but disables interaction. `display: none` removes it from layout completely. So for a fade-out effect use opacity; for keeping layout space use visibility; for removing entirely use display. The choice depends on what you want to happen to the space.

questions.question: What are CSS variables (custom properties) and how do you use them?
questions.answer: CSS variables are custom properties defined with `--name` and used with `var(--name)`. They're defined on an element and inherited by descendants, and they can be changed with media queries or classes. They're perfect for theming — define a palette once and reference it everywhere. In my projects I put the color and spacing scale in `:root` variables so a theme change is one-line.

questions.question: What is the `!important` rule and when should you use it?
questions.answer: `!important` forces a declaration to win over everything else regardless of specificity. It's a last resort — overusing it destroys the cascade and makes styles impossible to override later. My rule: avoid it entirely in normal code; only use it to override third-party styles you can't control or in edge-case utilities. If I reach for `!important` often, the CSS architecture has a problem.

questions.question: What is the difference between relative units and absolute units?
questions.answer: Absolute units — `px`, `cm`, `in` — are fixed measurements. Relative units — `%`, `em`, `rem`, `vw`, `vh` — depend on context like the parent, root font, or viewport. Relative units make layouts adapt to different screens and user font settings, which is why responsive design is built on them. I default to relative units and use pixels sparingly for things like borders that shouldn't scale.

questions.question: How do you handle fonts on a website?
questions.answer: Modern approach: self-host or use a font service with `@font-face`, load only the weights you need with `font-display: swap` to avoid invisible text, and use `system-ui` fallbacks so text shows instantly if the webfont is slow. I also respect users' accessibility needs — I don't hard-code font sizes so small they break browser zoom, and I test line-height and letter-spacing for readability.

questions.question: What is a responsive image and how do you implement it?
questions.answer: A responsive image adapts to the viewport. Techniques: `max-width: 100%` with `height: auto` so it scales down; `srcset` with `sizes` so the browser downloads the appropriately sized file; and `picture` with `source` for art direction or format selection. In the Toptal example I studied, the point was to load the smallest image that still fills the space — `srcset` and `sizes` do exactly that and save bandwidth.

questions.question: What is the `picture` element and when do you use it?
questions.answer: `` lets you provide multiple image sources and let the browser pick based on conditions — viewport width, resolution, or format support like WebP/AVIF. It's for art direction (different crops for different screens) and modern formats. When you just need scaling, `srcset` on a plain `` is enough. I use `picture` when a design genuinely needs different images, not just different sizes.

questions.question: What is `loading="lazy"` on images and why use it?
questions.answer: `loading="lazy"` tells the browser to defer loading images until they scroll near the viewport, saving bandwidth and speeding up initial page load. Combined with `decoding="async"`, images don't block rendering. On image-heavy pages this is a big win — I've used it in portfolio and e-commerce-style pages to cut initial payload meaningfully. Just don't lazy-load the hero image above the fold.

questions.question: What is the difference between inline styles and external CSS?
questions.answer: Inline styles use the `style` attribute on the element — high specificity, hard to reuse, and they mix presentation with markup. External CSS lives in `.css` files linked from the head — reusable, cacheable, and maintainable. Internal styles use a `<style>` block in the document, fine for single-page demos. Best practice is external stylesheets, and for frameworks, scoped component styles.

questions.question: What is BEM and why do people use it?
questions.answer: BEM, Block Element Modifier, is a CSS naming convention: `block__element--modifier`. Like `.card__title--active`. It makes class names self-documenting, prevents specificity wars, and clarifies relationships. I don't use it with Angular/Vue scoped styles since those give encapsulation for free, but for plain CSS projects BEM is a solid, honest convention.

questions.question: What is the CSS `calc()` function and when do you use it?
questions.answer: `calc()` lets you compute values at runtime by combining units — like `width: calc(100% - 240px)` for a layout with a fixed sidebar. It's especially useful when mixing relative and absolute units. It's supported everywhere modern, so I use it freely for things like full-bleed sections or offsetting fixed headers.

questions.question: What is `background` shorthand and how do you use it?
questions.answer: The `background` shorthand sets color, image, position, size, repeat, and attachment in one line — like `background: url(img) center/cover no-repeat #222`. The order has some flexibility but `size` must come right after `position` with a slash. It's convenient but I spell out `background-color` and `background-image` when I want clarity, and use shorthand for the common 'cover an element with an image' case.

questions.question: What is the difference between `relative` and `absolute` sizing?
questions.answer: Relative sizing uses units like `%`, `em`, `rem`, `vw` that depend on something else. Absolute sizing uses `px` or fixed values. For example, a container that's `50%` of its parent versus a fixed `400px`. Relative sizes make layouts adapt; absolute give exact control. The tension between them is central to responsive design — you use absolute for things that must stay constant and relative for everything that should flow.

questions.question: What is the `viewBox` attribute in SVG?
questions.answer: `viewBox` defines the coordinate system of an SVG — `viewBox="0 0 100 100"` sets a 100x100 canvas. It lets SVG scale cleanly to any display size because the drawing coordinates stay relative to the viewBox, not the rendered pixel size. Without it, SVGs scale unpredictably. When I embed icons or charts, setting a proper viewBox and `preserveAspectRatio` is the difference between crisp and stretched.

questions.question: What is the difference between `<canvas>` and SVG?
questions.answer: SVG is vector — it draws shapes as DOM-like elements, scales perfectly at any resolution, and each shape can be styled and scripted individually. Canvas is raster — it paints pixels on a drawing surface, is faster for many thousands of items, but doesn't scale and redraws as a whole. For interactive charts with few elements, SVG; for complex animations or game-like rendering, canvas.

questions.question: What is a web component and how does it promote reuse?
questions.answer: A web component is a self-contained custom element built with custom elements, shadow DOM, and templates — like `<my-card>`. Because it's based on standard browser APIs, it works across frameworks. It promotes reuse because you encapsulate markup, styles, and behavior together and use it anywhere. Frameworks have similar ideas — Angular components and Vue components — but web components are the platform-native version.

questions.question: What is the shadow DOM?
questions.answer: The shadow DOM is a scoped DOM tree attached to an element — its styles and markup are isolated from the main document, so an ID or class inside doesn't collide with the page. That's how web components get style encapsulation. Angular's emulated encapsulation and Vue's scoped styles are different mechanisms trying to solve the same problem: preventing cross-component CSS leakage.

questions.question: What is the CSS specificity calculation?
questions.answer: Specificity is a weight computed from selectors: inline styles count 1000, IDs 100, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes 10, and element/pseudo-element 1. When two rules conflict, the higher total wins. If equal, the later in the stylesheet wins. I've spent hours on 'why isn't my style applying' and it's almost always a specificity calculation. Keeping selectors shallow avoids the whole class of bug.

questions.question: What is `aspect-ratio` in CSS and when is it useful?
questions.answer: `aspect-ratio` sets a fixed width-to-height ratio for an element — `aspect-ratio: 16/9` keeps a video or image frame proportional regardless of width. It replaced the old padding-top hack for maintaining ratios. I use it for embeds, hero images, and placeholders that must keep their shape during load. Combined with `width: 100%`, it's an elegant way to keep media boxes stable.

questions.question: What is `object-fit` and how does it differ from `background-size`?
questions.answer: `object-fit` controls how an `` or `

questions.question: How do you implement a sticky header or sidebar?
questions.answer: Use `position: sticky` with `top: 0` (or a pixel offset) on the element. Sticky keeps the element in flow until it would scroll out of view, then pins it. It avoids the layout jump that `position: fixed` causes, because the space is preserved. My topbar in this very interview tool uses sticky — it's the modern way and handles the scrolling logic for free.

questions.question: What is `filter` in CSS and what can you do with it?
questions.answer: `filter` applies visual effects like `blur()`, `grayscale()`, `brightness()`, `contrast()`, and `drop-shadow()`. It's great for image hover effects, duotone looks, and darkening overlays. Performance-wise it's GPU-friendly in most cases. I use subtle filters like `grayscale(1)` on hover-to-color effects and `brightness()` on image overlays.

questions.question: What is a CSS grid `fr` unit?
questions.answer: `fr` stands for fraction — it distributes available space proportionally. `grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr` makes the second column twice the first. Unlike percentages, `fr` handles gaps and free space gracefully. It's the natural unit for grid layouts, and I use it for dashboards and split layouts constantly.

questions.question: What is the difference between `auto-fit` and `auto-fill` in CSS grid?
questions.answer: Both let a grid auto-place columns of a min size: `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr))`. `auto-fit` collapses empty tracks so items stretch to fill the row; `auto-fill` keeps the empty tracks, preserving column count. So with one item, auto-fit makes it full width while auto-fill keeps the empty columns. For responsive card grids, auto-fit is usually what I want.

questions.question: How do you create a tooltip with pure CSS?
questions.answer: Use a `::after` pseudo-element positioned absolutely over the parent, hidden with `opacity: 0` and shown on `:hover` with a transition. Set the parent `position: relative` as the anchor. Add `white-space: nowrap` and a z-index so it sits above content. It's a classic demonstration of positioning plus pseudo-elements, and it shows you understand the box model and states.

questions.question: What is `prefers-reduced-motion` and why should you respect it?
questions.answer: It's a media query matching users who've requested reduced motion in their OS. I use it to disable or tone down animations — `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { * { animation-duration: .01ms; } }`. It's an accessibility courtesy that matters to people with vestibular disorders, and it signals you care about the whole audience, not just the average user.

questions.question: What is `content-visibility` and how does it help performance?
questions.answer: `content-visibility: auto` tells the browser to skip rendering work for content outside the viewport, dramatically speeding up initial page render for long pages. It's like a browser-level version of lazy rendering. I'd use it on long article or list pages. The caveat is scrollbar sizing jumps, fixed with `contain-intrinsic-size`. It's one of the modern CSS performance features I keep an eye on.

questions.question: What are accessibility (a11y) best practices in HTML?
questions.answer: The essentials: semantic tags so structure is understood, `alt` text on images, labels on every form field, proper heading hierarchy, keyboard navigation support (focus states visible, tab order logical), `aria` attributes where semantics aren't enough, sufficient color contrast, and `lang` attributes. Accessibility isn't a feature — it's the baseline, and it also happens to improve SEO. I build forms with labels from the start.

questions.question: What is `aria-label` and when do you use it?
questions.answer: `aria-label` provides an accessible name for an element that has no visible text — like an icon-only button. Screen readers announce the label instead of reading nothing. Example: a close button with an × glyph gets `aria-label="Close"`. I use it whenever the visual element is purely iconic, because a screen reader user otherwise hears 'button' with no clue what it does.

questions.question: What is the difference between `aria-label` and `aria-labelledby`?
questions.answer: `aria-label` supplies the name directly as a string. `aria-labelledby` references the id of another element whose text becomes the name — useful when the accessible name should come from visible text on the page. The rule: prefer visible text via `aria-labelledby` when possible, fall back to `aria-label` when there's no visible label.

questions.question: What is the `role` attribute and how does it relate to semantic HTML?
questions.answer: `role` tells assistive technology what an element's purpose is when the HTML semantics don't convey it — like `role="dialog"` on a custom modal. Good practice is to use native semantic elements first and reserve roles for cases where you're building custom widgets. Duplicating a role on a semantic element is redundant — that's why I keep it minimal.

questions.question: How do you make a custom modal accessible?
questions.answer: Set `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`, give it an accessible name with `aria-labelledby`, trap focus inside while it's open, return focus to the trigger on close, close on Escape, and keep the background from being read by screen readers (often `aria-hidden`). These details turn a visually-nice modal into one everyone can use, and interviewers notice when you mention focus management.

questions.question: What is `tabindex` and how does it affect keyboard navigation?
questions.answer: `tabindex="0"` makes an element keyboard-focusable in the natural order; `-1` makes it programmatically focusable but not in the tab order (used to move focus for modals); positive values force an order but are an anti-pattern. Managing `tabindex` is how you control keyboard flow — important for custom widgets and single-page apps where tab order can break.

questions.question: What is `lang` attribute and why is it important?
questions.answer: `lang` declares the language of the document — `lang="en"` on the `<html>` tag. It matters for screen readers (correct pronunciation), translation tools, and spell-checkers. This is a tiny attribute that's easy to forget but genuinely affects assistive technology quality. I treat it as part of the page's basic setup, like the doctype.

questions.question: What are the advantages of CSS `min()`, `max()`, and `clamp()`?
questions.answer: They're math functions that resolve to a value in context. `clamp(min, preferred, max)` is the star — `font-size: clamp(1rem, 2vw, 1.5rem)` gives fluid type that scales with the viewport but stays within bounds. `min()` and `max()` pick the smaller or larger of values. They reduce the need for media-query breakpoints by letting values be fluid. I use clamp for font sizes and container widths.

questions.question: What is a CSS reset and why is it useful?
questions.answer: A reset removes default browser styles — margins on `body`, padding on lists, font sizes — so your styles start from a clean slate. Different browsers apply different defaults, which is exactly the inconsistency a reset removes. Alternatives like Normalize.css make defaults consistent instead of removing them. On every project I start with either a reset or normalize so cross-browser behavior is predictable.

questions.question: What is the difference between a `<section>` and an `<article>`?
questions.answer: `<section>` groups related content under a theme and should have a heading. `<article>` represents a self-contained composition — a blog post, a news story — that could stand alone and be syndicated. A page can contain articles, and articles can contain sections. In practice, think: does this content make sense on its own? Then it's an article; otherwise it's a section.

questions.question: What is the `<nav>` element and when should it be used?
questions.answer: `<nav>` marks a block of navigation links — the primary site menu. It tells screen readers and search engines 'this is navigation,' letting users jump straight to it. You typically have one main `<nav>`. Not every group of links is nav — footer link groups often aren't. Using it correctly improves keyboard accessibility because assistive tech exposes a navigation landmark.

questions.question: What is the `<figure>` element and what's in it?
questions.answer: `<figure>` wraps self-contained content like images, diagrams, or code snippets, with an optional `<figcaption>` for its caption. It's semantically different from a plain `<div>` because it explicitly associates the caption with the content. It also helps SEO and screen readers. I use it whenever an image or code block deserves a labeled caption.

questions.question: What is the difference between `<head>` and `<header>`?
questions.answer: `<head>` is the document's metadata section — title, meta tags, stylesheet links, scripts — and it's not rendered visually. `<header>` is a content element — the visible top section of a page or article with the logo, heading, and nav. They sound alike but one is invisible plumbing and the other is visible structure. Getting them straight is a small sign of care in an interview.

questions.question: What is the `<footer>` element?
questions.answer: `<footer>` marks the bottom of a page or section — copyright, contact, legal links, secondary navigation. It's a semantic element, so it contributes to page structure for screen readers. A `<footer>` can appear inside an `<article>` too, representing the article's footer. Using it is more meaningful than another generic `<div>`.

questions.question: What is the `<time>` element and why is it useful?
questions.answer: `<time>` marks dates and times with a machine-readable `datetime` attribute: `<time datetime="2026-08-20">Aug 20, 2026</time>`. That machine-readable value helps search engines and browsers understand chronology, and lets you style date content separately. It's a small semantic win I use for event dates and article publish dates.

questions.question: What is a data attribute and how do you use it?
questions.answer: A `data-*` attribute stores custom data directly in the HTML: `<button data-user-id="42">`. JavaScript reads it with `getAttribute('data-user-id')` or `dataset.userId`. It's the clean way to carry small bits of data with elements without inventing fake classes or ids. In vanilla JS I use it for event delegation — attaching one handler and reading `data-*` from the clicked target.

questions.question: How does the browser render a webpage, in order?
questions.answer: First it parses the HTML into a DOM tree and builds the CSSOM from stylesheets. Then it combines them into the render tree, computes layout (where each box goes), then paints to the screen. This is why render-blocking resources matter — CSS blocks render, `defer` scripts don't. Understanding this pipeline is how I reason about why a page is slow and where to fix it.

questions.question: What is the critical rendering path?
questions.answer: It's the sequence of steps the browser takes from receiving HTML to painting pixels — parsing HTML, building CSSOM, compiling JavaScript, computing layout, and painting. Optimizing it means: minimize render-blocking CSS/JS, inline critical styles, defer non-critical scripts, and reduce resource size. Every performance question I answer ties back to the critical rendering path.

questions.question: What is the difference between `defer` and `async` on a script?
questions.answer: Both make scripts non-blocking. `defer` downloads in parallel and runs in order after the document is parsed — good for scripts that depend on the DOM. `async` downloads in parallel and runs as soon as it's ready, out of order — good for independent scripts. For most app code I use `defer`; `async` is for third-party scripts that don't depend on anything. The distinction matters for load-time bugs.

questions.question: What is a service worker and what can it do?
questions.answer: A service worker is a script the browser runs in the background, separate from the page, that can intercept network requests, cache responses, and enable offline functionality and push notifications. It's the engine behind progressive web apps. I've used the concept for caching static assets so repeat visits load fast even with a weak connection. It's powerful but needs careful cache-invalidation design.

questions.question: What is a PWA?
questions.answer: A progressive web app is a web app that behaves like a native app: installable, offline-capable via service workers, with push notifications and an app-like UI. It uses a web manifest, HTTPS, and service workers. PWAs are a good story for cost-conscious product owners because one codebase reaches all devices. I've studied PWA patterns as the natural evolution of the responsive sites I build.

questions.question: What is the difference between `innerHTML`, `textContent`, and `innerText`?
questions.answer: `textContent` returns all text including hidden elements, as-is, no parsing — safe. `innerText` respects rendering and excludes hidden text. `innerHTML` parses HTML, which is why setting it with untrusted data is an XSS vector. My rule: use `textContent` for text, `innerHTML` only when the HTML is from trusted sources or deliberately sanitized.

questions.question: What is DOM manipulation and how do frameworks relate to it?
questions.answer: DOM manipulation is changing the DOM with JavaScript — creating, updating, removing nodes. Frameworks like Angular and Vue wrap this with reactivity: you change state, and the framework efficiently updates the DOM for you. Understanding raw DOM manipulation explains the value of frameworks — they automate the boring, error-prone part while I focus on data and behavior.

questions.question: What is event delegation and how does it improve performance?
questions.answer: Event delegation attaches one listener to a parent and catches events from all children via bubbling. Instead of adding a listener to each of 1000 rows, one listener on the container checks which child was clicked. It improves performance (fewer listeners) and handles dynamically added elements automatically. In vanilla JS work, especially dynamic tables, delegation is my default.

questions.question: What is the difference between `querySelector` and `getElementById`?
questions.answer: `getElementById` is fast and specific — it looks up by id only. `querySelector` accepts full CSS selectors — `.class`, `[attr]`, `div > p` — which is more flexible but slower. For single elements with an id, `getElementById`; for everything else with complex selection, `querySelector`. In modern code I mostly use `querySelector` for flexibility and reserve getElementById for hot paths.

questions.question: What is `closest()` and when do you use it?
questions.answer: `element.closest('selector')` walks up from the element to find the nearest ancestor matching the selector, returning it or null. It's the modern replacement for the old parent-node walking in event delegation. Example: in a delegated click handler, `event.target.closest('tr')` finds the row. It makes delegation code much cleaner than manual `parentNode` loops.

questions.question: What is the `dataset` property?
questions.answer: `element.dataset` gives you an object mapping `data-*` attributes to properties — `data-user-id` becomes `dataset.userId`. It's the modern, readable way to read data attributes compared to `getAttribute`. It's read-write, so you can also set data with it. I use it constantly for dynamic UI logic that needs small bits of element-bound data.

questions.question: What is the difference between `scrollTop`, `clientHeight`, and `offsetHeight`?
questions.answer: `clientHeight` is the visible height including padding; `offsetHeight` is the visible height plus borders; `scrollTop` is how far the element is scrolled from the top. The classic 'am I near the bottom' check is `scrollTop + clientHeight >= scrollHeight`. I've used these for infinite scroll and sticky behavior. They're the practical geometry properties of scrolling.

questions.question: What is `requestAnimationFrame` and why use it over `setTimeout` for animations?
questions.answer: `requestAnimationFrame` schedules a callback before the next repaint, syncing with the display refresh rate. `setTimeout` doesn't sync, which causes jank. It also pauses when the tab is hidden, saving battery. For smooth animations, especially in canvas or custom JS, `requestAnimationFrame` is the correct tool. I mention it whenever a scroll- or animation-related performance question comes up.

questions.question: What is the Intersection Observer API?
questions.answer: It's a browser API that asynchronously watches when elements enter or leave the viewport. It's efficient because the browser does the work natively. Uses: lazy-loading images, infinite scroll, triggering animations on scroll, and tracking ad visibility. It replaced scroll-listener hacks. I'd use it for lazy loading and scroll-triggered effects.

questions.question: What is the difference between `onerror` and `onload` on an image?
questions.answer: `onload` fires when the image finishes loading successfully; `onerror` fires when it fails — like a broken URL. Handling `onerror` with a fallback image and `onload` to reveal the image avoids showing broken-image icons and layout flashes. In image-heavy UIs, I set both handlers so users always see something sensible.

questions.question: What is responsive typography and how do you implement it?
questions.answer: Responsive typography scales text with the viewport so it reads well on phone and desktop. Implementation: `clamp()` with a minimum, preferred fluid value, and maximum — like `font-size: clamp(1.2rem, 2.5vw, 2rem)`. Plus `rem` units so it respects user font settings. This avoids the awkward 'tiny on phone, huge on desktop' text and reduces breakpoint fiddling.

questions.question: What are CSS container queries?
questions.answer: Container queries let styles respond to the size of a container instead of the viewport — `@container (min-width: 400px) { ... }`. That's a big deal for reusable components: a card can adapt based on where it's placed, not the screen size. It's the modern answer to 'component-level responsiveness.' I see it as the natural upgrade over viewport-only media queries for component libraries.

questions.question: What is the difference between `hover` and `focus` states?
questions.answer: `:hover` matches when the pointer is over an element; `:focus` matches when it's the keyboard/user target — clicked, or tabbed to. Touch users never hover, so relying only on hover hides affordances for them. Best practice: make hover and focus states visible and often identical. That's why I style `:focus-visible` for keyboard users specifically.

questions.question: What is `:focus-visible` and why is it important?
questions.answer: `:focus-visible` styles focus only when the browser determines it should be visible — usually keyboard navigation — and not for mouse clicks. That lets you keep a clean look for mouse users while still giving keyboard users a clear focus indicator. It's the modern accessibility pattern for focus styles, and I apply it wherever I'd previously have dimmed `:focus`.

questions.question: How do you handle the `:root` selector?
questions.answer: `:root` matches the document root — the `<html>` element — but with higher specificity than `html`. It's the standard place to define CSS variables for global theming: `:root { --primary: #4f8cff; }`. Because variables inherit, defining them at the root makes them available everywhere, and overriding on a subtree enables scoped theming.

questions.question: What is `line-height` and how does it affect layout?
questions.answer: `line-height` controls the vertical space between lines of text. A unitless value like `1.5` is best because it scales with font size. It affects readability and vertical rhythm, and it's the old trick for centering single-line text vertically. I set sensible line-height on body text first, then tune headings — it's one of the highest-impact readability settings.

questions.question: What is the difference between `font-weight: bold` and `font-weight: 700`?
questions.answer: Nothing functionally — `bold` maps to `700` numerically. The numeric scale lets you request intermediate weights like `500` or `600` that named keywords can't. The catch: the font must actually include those weights, otherwise the browser synthesizes a fake bold. When choosing a web font, I load the specific weights I use.

questions.question: What is `letter-spacing` and when should you use it?
questions.answer: `letter-spacing` adjusts the space between characters. Use it sparingly — for uppercase labels, small headings, or to improve legibility at large sizes. Overusing it hurts readability. I apply tiny amounts on uppercase text (like the 'Required Skills' labels in this tool) where it adds polish without sacrificing legibility.
