questions.question: What is the difference between `text-align` and `vertical-align`?
questions.answer: `text-align` aligns inline content horizontally within its container — left, center, right, justify. `vertical-align` aligns inline elements vertically relative to the line — top, middle, baseline. A classic confusion: `vertical-align` doesn't vertically center block content; flexbox does that. I use `text-align` for text and flexbox for block centering.

questions.question: What is `white-space` and what values are useful?
questions.answer: `white-space` controls how whitespace and line breaks are handled. `nowrap` prevents wrapping — useful for button labels and tooltips. `pre` preserves spaces and newlines like a `<pre>` block. `pre-wrap` preserves whitespace but wraps. I use `nowrap` for pills and tags so they don't break awkwardly, and `pre-wrap` for monospace output.

questions.question: What is `text-overflow: ellipsis` and how do you enable it?
questions.answer: `text-overflow: ellipsis` shows '…' when text overflows, but it needs three things: the element must have `overflow: hidden`, `white-space: nowrap`, and a constrained width. That's a common CSS gotcha — the property silently does nothing without its siblings. I use it for titles and table cells that must stay on one line.

questions.question: What is the difference between `currentColor` and `inherit`?
questions.answer: `currentColor` means the value of the element's `color` property — so `border-color: currentColor` matches the text color automatically. `inherit` takes the computed value of the property from the parent. `currentColor` is a great trick for icons that should match text color without duplicating the value.

questions.question: What is `pointer-events` and when would you use it?
questions.answer: `pointer-events: none` makes an element ignore pointer interactions — clicks pass through it to elements below. It's useful for decorative overlays, or to disable buttons without the clumsy `disabled` styling. The caveat: it also disables hover and can affect accessibility if misused. I use it deliberately, mainly for overlay elements.

questions.question: What is `user-select` and when would you disable text selection?
questions.answer: `user-select: none` prevents users from selecting text — useful for UI chrome like buttons, drag handles, and emoji that shouldn't be copied accidentally. But disabling it on body text is an anti-pattern that hurts users who copy content. I apply it only to interactive chrome, never to readable content.

questions.question: What is the `@supports` rule?
questions.answer: `@supports (property: value) { ... }` applies CSS only if the browser supports that feature — feature detection in CSS. It lets you use modern features with graceful fallbacks. Example: apply `backdrop-filter` only where supported. It's cleaner than guessing with JS. I use it for progressive enhancement of nice-to-have visual features.

questions.question: What is the difference between `min-height` and `height: auto`?
questions.answer: `height: auto` lets the element size to its content — the default. `min-height` sets a floor: the element is at least that tall but grows with content. This is the trick for equal-height sections and sticky footers — content can grow without breaking the layout. A common layout pattern: `main { min-height: calc(100vh - header - footer) }`.

questions.question: What is the CSS `writing-mode` property?
questions.answer: `writing-mode` sets the direction of text flow — `horizontal-tb` (default), `vertical-rl`, `vertical-lr`. It matters for languages like Japanese and for creative layouts like vertical headings. Supporting it correctly matters if you build internationalized products. It also interacts with RTL support. I mention it when asked about i18n/l10n or multilingual layouts.

questions.question: What is RTL support and how do you implement it?
questions.answer: RTL (right-to-left) is for languages like Arabic and Hebrew. Implementation: `dir="rtl"` on the document, logical properties (`margin-inline-start` instead of `margin-left`) so layouts mirror automatically, and testing with real RTL text. Tools like Tailwind include RTL variants. Getting RTL right is a sign of mature internationalization thinking, which is why I bring it up on i18n questions.

questions.question: What are logical properties in CSS?
questions.answer: Logical properties replace physical ones with direction-agnostic equivalents: `margin-inline-start` instead of `margin-left`, `padding-block` instead of `padding-top/bottom`, `border-inline-end`. They follow the text direction, so the same CSS works for LTR and RTL layouts automatically. Modern CSS encourages them. I use them in components meant to be internationalized.

questions.question: What is `inset` in CSS positioning?
questions.answer: `inset` is the shorthand for `top`, `right`, `bottom`, `left` together — `inset: 0` pins an absolutely-positioned element to all four edges of its containing block, which is how you make a full-bleed overlay or a stretched element. It's cleaner than writing four properties. I use `inset: 0` for full-screen modals and overlay backdrops.

questions.question: What is `place-items` and `place-content` in grid?
questions.answer: `place-items` is shorthand for `align-items` and `justify-items` — how grid items align within their cells. `place-content` is shorthand for `align-content` and `justify-content` — how the grid tracks themselves align within the container. `place-items: center` centers items; `place-content: center` centers the whole grid. Understanding the distinction prevents centering confusion.

questions.question: What is the difference between `gap` in flexbox and grid?
questions.answer: `gap` creates space between items — in grid it's `column-gap` and `row-gap` shorthand, and since 2021 flexbox also supports `gap` natively. So the modern answer is: `gap` works in both now. It's cleaner than margins because it never adds unwanted outer spacing. I use `gap` everywhere instead of margin-hacks for spacing between cards and items.

questions.question: How do you build a card component in CSS?
questions.answer: A card is a `position: relative` container with a background, border or shadow, `border-radius`, padding, and an `overflow: hidden` for image headers. The image uses `object-fit: cover`, the title and text sit in the body, and the footer holds actions. Layout-wise I put cards in a grid with `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(...))`. It's a template I reuse in nearly every UI.

questions.question: What is a skeleton screen and how do you build one?
questions.answer: A skeleton screen is a placeholder shown while content loads — grey blocks mimicking the layout. You build it with a few divs styled to match the final structure, plus a shimmer animation via CSS. It feels faster than a spinner. In Angular/Vue I conditionally render a skeleton until the async data arrives. I used this pattern to keep ERP pages from feeling empty during loads.

questions.question: What is `preconnect` and how does it help performance?
questions.answer: `<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com">` tells the browser to start the connection handshake early so the first request to that origin is faster. It shaves real milliseconds off third-party resource loads. I add preconnect to critical origins like font and CDN hosts. The caveat: don't preconnect to everything — only the 2-3 origins you actually need.

questions.question: What is the difference between `preload` and `prefetch`?
questions.answer: `preload` fetches a resource the current page will definitely need soon — like the hero font or a critical script — with high priority. `prefetch` fetches resources for the next navigation with low priority. So preload is for now, prefetch is for later. Misusing them wastes bandwidth, so I use preload sparingly and only for genuinely critical resources.

questions.question: What is Core Web Vitals and how do you measure them?
questions.answer: Core Web Vitals are the three performance signals Google uses for ranking: LCP (largest contentful paint — load speed), INP (interaction to next paint — responsiveness), and CLS (cumulative layout shift — visual stability). I measure with Lighthouse, PageSpeed Insights, or the web-vitals library. In my Vue optimization work, tracking these gave me concrete numbers to show improvement.

questions.question: What is CLS and how do you avoid it?
questions.answer: CLS, cumulative layout shift, measures how much visible content jumps around while loading. Causes: images without dimensions, ads, fonts swapping, injected content. Prevention: reserve space for images with width/height or `aspect-ratio`, load fonts with `font-display: swap`, avoid injecting content above the fold. Low CLS is a sign of polish — it's one of the things I check before calling a UI done.

questions.question: What is LCP and how do you improve it?
questions.answer: LCP is when the largest visible element — usually a hero image or heading — finishes rendering. To improve it: make the server respond fast, prioritize the hero resource, preload it, compress images, and avoid render-blocking scripts. It's the first thing I check when a page feels slow. Good LCP is under 2.5 seconds.

questions.question: What is INP and how does it differ from FID?
questions.answer: INP, interaction to next paint, measures the latency of all interactions on the page, replacing FID (first input delay). FID only measured the first interaction; INP measures the worst-case across the session. Improving it means keeping the main thread free — no long tasks, no huge synchronous re-renders, efficient event handlers. Modern performance questions center on it.

questions.question: What is the difference between `static` and `dynamic` content?
questions.answer: Static content is fixed — same for every user — like a product description or a stylesheet, so it can be cached and served from a CDN. Dynamic content is generated per request — like a user's dashboard — and comes from the server. Knowing the split drives architecture: static goes to CDN/S3, dynamic to your app server. I used this split when deploying e-commerce pages.

questions.question: What is SSG vs SSR vs CSR?
questions.answer: SSG, static site generation, builds HTML at build time — fastest, best for content sites. SSR, server-side rendering, renders HTML per request — good for SEO and dynamic data. CSR, client-side rendering, sends a shell and renders in the browser — best for apps but weaker for SEO. Angular and Vue can do all three. My honest default for a marketing page is SSG, for a data-heavy app CSR, and SSR when SEO and dynamic data both matter.

questions.question: What is hydration in the context of SSR?
questions.answer: Hydration is when server-rendered HTML is already on the page and the client framework attaches event handlers and state to it, making it interactive. The trick is matching the server HTML with what the client expects to avoid mismatches. Frameworks like Angular Universal and Next.js handle this. It's the price you pay for SSR's SEO benefit.

questions.question: What is code splitting and how do you do it in CSS/JS?
questions.answer: Code splitting breaks one big bundle into pieces loaded on demand. In JS, dynamic imports and route-based lazy loading; in CSS, splitting per-route styles and inlining critical CSS. The win: users download only what the current page needs. In Angular I do this with lazy-loaded route modules; in Vue, with dynamic component imports.

questions.question: What is minification and why is it important?
questions.answer: Minification removes unnecessary characters from code — whitespace, comments, newlines, shortening variable names — without changing behavior. It shrinks file size and speeds up downloads and parsing. Build tools do it automatically. I've seen minified bundles a fraction of the source size. It's a free, standard part of the build pipeline.

questions.question: What is tree shaking?
questions.answer: Tree shaking is dead-code elimination — the bundler removes exported functions and modules you never import, shrinking the bundle. It works with ES module static analysis: the bundler sees what's actually used and drops the rest. I look for tree-shakable libraries and avoid barrel files that defeat it. It's why importing one utility from a large library is cheaper than importing the whole thing.

questions.question: What is a bundle and why does its size matter?
questions.answer: A bundle is the combined output of all your JS/CSS/assets after the build. Size matters because it directly affects load time and parsing time — a 2MB bundle can make a page feel broken on mobile. Techniques to control it: code splitting, tree shaking, minification, and gzip/brotli at the server. Measuring bundle size is a routine part of my frontend performance checklist.

questions.question: What is gzip and brotli compression?
questions.answer: gzip and brotli are compression algorithms the server uses to shrink responses before sending them, and the browser decompresses. Brotli compresses better than gzip at comparable speed. Most web servers compress text by default. The gain is dramatic — 70-80% smaller HTML/CSS/JS. It's one of the cheapest performance wins, and I always confirm compression is on in my deployments.

questions.question: What is a CDN and why is it useful?
questions.answer: A CDN, content delivery network, caches your static assets on servers worldwide so users download from a nearby edge instead of your origin. That slashes latency for global users and offloads your servers. It's standard for images, JS bundles, and CSS. In my deployments, static assets on S3/CDN while the API stays on the origin is the typical split.

questions.question: What is the `cache-control` header and how do you use it?
questions.answer: `Cache-Control` tells the browser (and proxies) how long to reuse a response — `max-age=3600` caches for an hour; `no-cache` requires revalidation; `no-store` forbids caching. Static assets get long max-age with immutable; HTML and API responses get short or no-cache. Getting this right is the difference between instant repeat loads and wasted requests.

questions.question: What is ETag and how does it work?
questions.answer: An ETag is a fingerprint the server sets for a response. On revalidation, the browser sends `If-None-Match: <etag>`; if unchanged, the server replies 304 without resending the body. It's efficient — no full download when nothing changed. Combined with Cache-Control, ETags handle the 'is it still the same' question cheaply.

questions.question: What is the difference between `304` and `200` responses?
questions.answer: A `200` returns the full resource. A `304 Not Modified` tells the browser its cached copy is still valid — no body. So a cached page hits the server for revalidation but only gets bytes when something changed. That's why properly-cached sites feel fast on repeat visits.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a favicon and how do you include one?
questions.answer: A favicon is the small icon in the browser tab and bookmarks. Include it with `<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.ico">` or use SVG/PNG variants for different contexts. A missing favicon produces a 404 noise request, so I always include one. It's small, but it's part of a polished, complete page.

questions.question: What is Open Graph and why does it matter?
questions.answer: Open Graph (`og:`) meta tags control how your page appears when shared on social platforms — the title, description, and image. `<meta property="og:title" content="...">`. Without them, platforms guess and usually show something ugly. For the TechIT platform I set OG tags so shared links looked professional. It's a small thing with real marketing value.

questions.question: What is the `<iframe>` element and what are its risks?
questions.answer: `<iframe>` embeds another document inside your page — used for videos, maps, third-party widgets. Risks: it can load heavy content, and if not sandboxed it can run scripts you don't control, creating security surface. `sandbox` attribute limits its capabilities, and `loading="lazy"` defers it. I use iframes deliberately and always sandbox third-party embeds.

questions.question: What is the difference between `<iframe>` and `<embed>`?
questions.answer: `<iframe>` embeds an entire HTML document with its own browsing context. `<embed>` is for embedding plugins or binary content like PDFs and applets, and `<object>` is similar. Iframes are the common, flexible choice; embed/object are legacy and rarely used now. In modern web, iframe is what you'll actually see in code.

questions.question: How do you embed a YouTube video in a page?
questions.answer: Use an `<iframe>` with the embed URL (`https://www.youtube.com/embed/VIDEO_ID`) and set `loading="lazy"`, `frameborder="0"`, `allow="autoplay; encrypted-media; picture-in-picture"`, and an aspect-ratio wrapper so it's responsive. In the TechIT Android app I integrated YouTube APIs for streaming, and on the web side the iframe approach is the standard for embeds.

questions.question: What is `srcdoc` on an iframe?
questions.answer: `srcdoc` provides the iframe's document content as a string instead of loading from a URL. It's used when you want to sandbox untrusted HTML in an isolated frame. Combined with `sandbox`, it can safely render user-generated content. It's a niche but powerful tool for safe HTML previews.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the `<template>` element?
questions.answer: `<template>` holds markup that isn't rendered but can be cloned and inserted via JavaScript. The browser parses it once and you instantiate it repeatedly. It's the raw material for web components and templating. Angular's `<ng-template>` and Vue's `<template>` slots are similar concepts built into the frameworks.

questions.question: What is the `<noscript>` element?
questions.answer: `<noscript>` provides fallback content that displays only when JavaScript is disabled. Modern apps assume JS, but a basic message or a fallback link in `<noscript>` is good hygiene. SEO crawlers that don't execute JS also read it. I include a minimal noscript message on apps whose content depends entirely on JS.

questions.question: What is ARIA and what problem does it solve?
questions.answer: ARIA, Accessible Rich Internet Applications, is a spec of attributes that add accessibility semantics to HTML — `role`, `aria-label`, `aria-live`, `aria-expanded`. It solves the problem that custom widgets and complex apps have semantics native HTML can't express. The guideline is: use native elements first, ARIA when there's no native equivalent. I keep ARIA focused and minimal.

questions.question: What is `aria-live` and when do you use it?
questions.answer: `aria-live` makes a region announce content changes to screen readers automatically — useful for status messages, toasts, and dynamic updates. `aria-live="polite"` announces when idle; `assertive` interrupts immediately. Without it, dynamic content updates are invisible to screen reader users. I add it to toast and notification containers.

questions.question: What is `aria-expanded`?
questions.answer: `aria-expanded` tells assistive tech whether a collapsible element — an accordion, a menu — is open or closed. It must be toggled by JavaScript as the state changes. It's one of those attributes that's easy to forget but genuinely affects screen reader UX. When I build accordions or dropdowns, I wire aria-expanded in from the start.

questions.question: What is the difference between a `<button>` and an `<a>` used as a button?
questions.answer: A `<button>` performs an action — submits a form, opens a dialog — and is keyboard-accessible with Space/Enter. An `<a>` navigates. Using an `<a>` as a button breaks semantics and keyboard behavior unless you add roles and handlers. The right answer: if it navigates, use `<a>`; if it acts, use `<button>`. Styling buttons to look like links or vice versa is fine as long as the element matches behavior.

questions.question: What is the `autofocus` attribute and when should you use it?
questions.answer: `autofocus` moves focus to an element when the page loads — like a search box. Use it sparingly: on login pages it's convenient, but forcing focus can scroll the page unexpectedly and confuse screen reader users. I use it only where it genuinely speeds up the primary task, like a search or login field.

questions.question: What is the `required` attribute and how does browser validation work?
questions.answer: `required` marks a form field as mandatory; the browser validates it on submit and shows a native error without a server round trip. You pair it with `type` validation — `type="email"`, `type="number"`, and patterns via `pattern`. Browser validation is a first line, but I always re-validate on the server because client validation is trivially bypassed.

questions.question: What is the `pattern` attribute in forms?
questions.answer: `pattern` lets you specify a regex the input value must match — like `pattern="[0-9]{10}"` for a phone number. The browser enforces it client-side. It's a quick win for structured inputs, but the regex must be escaped correctly and you still need server validation. I use it for common structured fields.

questions.question: What is the difference between `type="number"` and `type="tel"`?
questions.answer: `type="number"` restricts to numeric input and shows a numeric keypad on mobile, but it has quirks with leading zeros and scientific notation. `type="tel"` is for phone numbers — it brings up the phone keypad but accepts any characters, which is actually right for phone numbers with symbols. For phone fields I use `tel`; for true numeric quantities, `number`.

questions.question: What is the `name` attribute's role in forms?
questions.answer: `name` is what the browser sends to the server as the data key — `name="email"` sends `email=value`. Without a name, the field's value isn't submitted at all. It's also how JavaScript reads form data via `FormData`. I always give every form field a meaningful name; it's the contract with the backend.

questions.question: What is `autocomplete` and why does it matter?
questions.answer: `autocomplete` tells the browser what kind of data a field contains — `autocomplete="email"`, `autocomplete="current-password"`, `autocomplete="off"`. Correct values enable password managers and speed up form filling, and `off` on sensitive fields avoids suggestions. Poor autocomplete config is why users abandon forms. It's a small attribute with big UX payoff.

questions.question: What is the `<label>` element and how does it connect to inputs?
questions.answer: `<label>` describes a form control, and you connect them either by nesting the input inside the label or using `for` matching the input's `id`. Clicking a label focuses its input — bigger hit target — and screen readers announce the label when the field gets focus. Unlabeled inputs are an accessibility failure. Every form field I build gets a label.

questions.question: What is a fieldset and legend?
questions.answer: `<fieldset>` groups related form controls together, and `<legend>` gives the group a name. Screen readers announce the legend when entering the group, which is essential for radio groups. Example: a set of radio buttons for payment methods inside a fieldset with 'Payment method' as legend. It's the semantically correct way to group options.

questions.question: How do radio buttons differ from checkboxes?
questions.answer: Radio buttons are for selecting one option from a group — selecting one deselects the others, and they share the same `name`. Checkboxes are independent toggles — each can be checked or not. Both are common interview gotchas. In forms I use radios for single-choice and checkboxes for multi-select or toggles.

questions.question: What is the `select` element and what is `multiple`?
questions.answer: `<select>` creates a dropdown; each option is an `<option>`. The `multiple` attribute turns it into a multi-select list. For long lists you also have `<optgroup>` for grouping. Dropdowns save space but are worse for many-option search — that's when I build a combobox instead. It's a bread-and-butter form control.

questions.question: What is a datalist?
questions.answer: A `<datalist>` provides suggested values for an input, letting users either pick a suggestion or type their own — the input stays editable. It's wired by `list` attribute on the input pointing to the datalist's id. It's a lightweight autocomplete without a JS library. I use it for fields like city or department where suggestions help but free text is allowed.

questions.question: What is a progress bar vs a meter?
questions.answer: `<progress>` represents the completion of a task — a known amount done toward a total, like a file upload. `<meter>` represents a scalar measurement within a range — like a battery or a score, with `min`, `max`, `low`, `high`, `optimum`. They look similar but semantically different. For upload progress in my apps, `<progress>` is the right element.

questions.question: What is `contenteditable`?
questions.answer: `contenteditable` makes an element editable directly in the browser — like a mini rich-text area. It's the basis for WYSIWYG editors, but it's notoriously inconsistent across browsers for complex content, which is why most editors use libraries. I'd use it for simple inline editing, and a library for anything serious.

questions.question: What is `draggable` and HTML5 drag and drop?
questions.answer: `draggable="true"` makes an element draggable; HTML5 DnD fires events like `dragstart`, `dragover`, `drop`. It's the native way to build drag-and-drop UIs, though it can be finicky on mobile, which is why libraries like SortableJS exist. I know the API but reach for a library for production DnD.

questions.question: What is the `<picture>` element's `media` attribute?
questions.answer: `media` inside a `<source>` child of `<picture>` applies a media query — so different images load at different breakpoints. Example: a wide banner on desktop, a square crop on mobile. Combined with `type` for format fallbacks, it's full art-direction control for images.

questions.question: What is the `loading` attribute on iframes?
questions.answer: `loading="lazy"` on an iframe defers its load until near the viewport, like images. Embedded videos and maps are heavy, so lazy-loading them improves page load. The attribute is supported in modern browsers and is a one-line performance win for iframe-heavy pages.

questions.question: What is the `referrerpolicy` attribute?
questions.answer: `referrerpolicy` controls what URL information is sent in the `Referer` header when navigating or fetching — `no-referrer`, `origin`, `strict-origin-when-cross-origin`. The default strict mode sends full URL same-origin and just origin cross-origin. It's a privacy and security control. I set `no-referrer` on links that shouldn't leak the page URL.

questions.question: What is the `target` attribute and the `rel` requirement?
questions.answer: `target="_blank"` opens a link in a new tab. Security best practice: always add `rel="noopener noreferrer"` so the new page can't access the opener (tabnabbing protection). Modern browsers default some protections, but the attribute is still standard. I write `target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"` every time without thinking.

questions.question: What is a `<bdo>` element?
questions.answer: `<bdo>` overrides the text direction for its content — `dir="rtl"` or `dir="ltr"`. It's used for mixed-direction text like embedding an English phrase inside Arabic content. It's niche, but it shows depth on i18n questions.

questions.question: What is the `<address>` element?
questions.answer: `<address>` marks contact information — the author of a page or article: email, physical address, links. It's semantic, so search engines and screen readers understand it as contact info. It's not for every street address on a page, just contact info for the document's author or the organization.

questions.question: What is the difference between `<ol>`, `<ul>`, and `<dl>`?
questions.answer: `<ul>` is an unordered list with bullets; `<ol>` is an ordered list with numbers; `<dl>` is a description list with `<dt>` (term) and `<dd>` (description) pairs — like a glossary. Semantic choice matters for accessibility. For step-by-step instructions I use `<ol>`, for feature lists `<ul>`, for term definitions `<dl>`.

questions.question: What is the `<blockquote>` element?
questions.answer: `<blockquote>` marks a quoted block from another source. The `cite` attribute can point to the source URL. It renders indented by default. Inline quotes use `<q>`. Using it semantically matters because plain indented divs don't tell readers or crawlers it's a quote.

questions.question: What is the `<pre>` element?
questions.answer: `<pre>` renders whitespace and line breaks exactly as written — it's for preformatted text like code blocks. Browsers render it monospace by default. For code you often combine `<pre><code>`. I use it for any output where spacing matters, like logs or code samples.

questions.question: What is the `<code>` element vs `<pre>`?
questions.answer: `<code>` marks a fragment of code inline — like a variable name in a sentence. `<pre>` preserves formatting for blocks. Best practice: inline code uses `<code>`, multi-line code uses `<pre><code>` together. The distinction matters for both semantics and rendering.

questions.question: What is the `<details>` and `<summary>` element?
questions.answer: `<details>` is a native, no-JS disclosure widget; `<summary>` is its clickable heading. Clicking expands/collapses the content. It's a great building block for FAQ and collapsible sections without custom code. One nuance: to keep a details open, add the `open` attribute. I'd use it for FAQ pages to avoid writing accordion JS.

questions.question: What is the `<mark>` element?
questions.answer: `<mark>` highlights text as relevant — like a search-term highlight. It's semantically different from a span with a yellow background because it conveys relevance, and its default styling is a yellow highlight. Screen readers can announce it. I'd use it for search results highlighting.

questions.question: What is the `<abbr>` element?
questions.answer: `<abbr>` marks an abbreviation or acronym, with the full form in the `title` attribute: `<abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr>`. Hovering shows the title, and screen readers read it. It adds polish and semantic value to documentation-heavy content.

questions.question: What is the `<kbd>`, `<samp>`, and `<var>` elements?
questions.answer: They're the technical text elements: `<kbd>` for keyboard input (`Ctrl+C`), `<samp>` for sample program output, `<var>` for variables. Together with `<code>` and `<pre>`, they give technical content real semantics instead of relying on styling. Documentation pages use them; knowing them shows depth in content-markup awareness.

questions.question: What is Git and why is version control essential?
questions.answer: Git is a distributed version control system that tracks every change to your codebase over time. Each developer has a full copy of history locally, so you can work offline, branch freely, and recover from anything. Version control is essential because it gives you history, collaboration, experimentation via branches, and a safety net — I've undone bad merges more times than I can count.

questions.question: What is the difference between Git and GitHub?
questions.answer: Git is the tool — the version control system that runs locally. GitHub is a hosting platform for Git repositories — remote storage, pull requests, issue tracking, CI/CD. You can use Git without GitHub (GitLab, Bitbucket, or a plain remote). In practice they work together: Git is the engine, GitHub is the team's shared dashboard.

questions.question: What is a repository?
questions.answer: A repository is a folder tracked by Git containing your project's files and the full commit history — the `.git` directory holds all the version data. There are local repositories on your machine and remote ones on a server. The repo is the unit of version control: everything inside is tracked, everything outside isn't.

questions.question: What is a commit?
questions.answer: A commit is a snapshot of the project at a point in time — a record of changes with a message, author, timestamp, and a parent reference. Commits form the history graph. A good commit is small, focused, and has a clear message. My rule: each commit is one logical change, so bisecting and reverting stay easy.

questions.question: What is the difference between `git add`, `git commit`, and `git push`?
questions.answer: `git add` stages changes — moves them into the staging area. `git commit` records the staged snapshot into local history. `git push` uploads local commits to the remote. So: stage, then commit locally, then push. Missing that commit happens before push is a classic beginner confusion — and a common interview starter.

questions.question: What is the difference between `git pull` and `git fetch`?
questions.answer: `git fetch` downloads commits and refs from the remote but does NOT update your working branch. `git pull` fetches AND merges the remote branch into your current branch. So `pull` = `fetch` + `merge`. I use fetch when I want to inspect changes first and pull when I'm ready to integrate.

questions.question: What is a branch and how do you create one?
questions.answer: A branch is a movable pointer to a commit — a line of development you can diverge on without affecting the main line. `git branch feature` creates one; `git checkout -b feature` creates and switches. Branches are cheap in Git, which is why branch-based workflows are standard.

questions.question: What is the difference between `git merge` and `git rebase`?
questions.answer: Both integrate branches. Merge creates a merge commit preserving the full history — safe, non-destructive, and honest about what happened. Rebase rewrites history by replaying your commits on top of another branch — cleaner, linear history, but it rewrites commits and can be dangerous on shared branches. My rule: merge for shared branches, rebase for local cleanup before pushing.

questions.question: What is a merge conflict and how do you resolve it?
questions.answer: A conflict happens when two branches change the same lines differently and Git can't merge automatically. Git marks the file with `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>` sections. I resolve by reading both versions, deciding the correct outcome, removing the markers, then `git add` and completing the merge. The skill is understanding the intent of both changes, not just picking one.

questions.question: What is `git stash` and when do you use it?
questions.answer: `git stash` saves your uncommitted changes and clears the working directory, letting you switch branches or do other work, then restore later with `git stash pop`. I use it when I'm mid-task and need to fix an urgent bug on another branch without losing or committing work-in-progress.

questions.question: What is the difference between `git reset` and `git revert`?
questions.answer: `reset` moves the current branch pointer backward, undoing commits — it rewrites history, so it's dangerous if commits are already pushed. `revert` creates a NEW commit that undoes the changes of a previous commit — safe, non-destructive, and the right choice for already-pushed history. I use revert for anything shared and reset only for local, unpublished mistakes.

questions.question: What is `git cherry-pick`?
questions.answer: `cherry-pick` takes a specific commit from one branch and applies it onto another — without merging the whole branch. Useful for hotfixes: you fix a bug on main and cherry-pick that commit onto the release branch. It's a surgical tool that should be used sparingly, since overuse creates duplicate commits across branches.

questions.question: What is the difference between `HEAD`, `origin`, and `master`/`main`?
questions.answer: `HEAD` is a pointer to the current commit you're working on. `origin` is the default name for the remote repository. `main` (or master) is the primary branch. So `HEAD` is local state, `origin/main` is the remote's main branch, and your local main is where you integrate work. Understanding these three resolves a lot of 'why is it behind/ahead' confusion.

questions.question: What is a detached HEAD state?
questions.answer: You're in detached HEAD when HEAD points directly at a commit instead of a branch — like after `git checkout <commit>`. New commits here belong to no branch and are at risk of being lost. If I find myself detached and want to keep work, I create a branch immediately. It's a warning sign interviewers like you to recognize.

questions.question: What is `git log` and what useful options exist?
questions.answer: `git log` shows commit history. Useful options: `--oneline` (compact), `--graph` (visual branch tree), `--stat` (file changes), `--author=` (filter by author), `-p` (show patches), `--grep=` (search messages). It's my first tool when answering 'what changed recently.' Combined with `git show <sha>` for details.

questions.question: What is `.gitignore` and why is it important?
questions.answer: `.gitignore` lists files and patterns Git should never track — node_modules, .env with secrets, build output, OS files. It keeps the repo clean and prevents committing secrets. A good .gitignore is one of the first files I create in a project. Committing secrets because .gitignore was missing is a classic painful mistake.

questions.question: What is `git remote` and how do you add one?
questions.answer: `git remote` manages remote repository aliases. `git remote add origin <url>` links your local repo to a remote. `origin` is just the conventional name. `git remote -v` shows the URLs. Then push/pull talk to that remote. For my projects, one origin on GitHub is the usual setup.

questions.question: What is the difference between `git clone` and `git init`?
questions.answer: `git init` creates a brand-new repository from scratch — it adds version control to a new project. `git clone` copies an existing repository (including history) from a remote to your machine — you get a ready-to-work local copy. So init is for starting fresh, clone for joining existing work.

questions.question: What is a pull request and what is its purpose?
questions.answer: A pull request is a proposal to merge a branch into another, usually with a review process — GitHub's collaborative feature. It lets teammates review code, discuss, run CI checks, and then merge. PRs are where quality happens: they're the enforced checkpoint. My workflow is always feature branch → PR → review → merge.

questions.question: What are the benefits of code review?
questions.answer: Code review catches bugs before they ship, spreads knowledge across the team, enforces consistency, and improves the original author's code. I've caught real production bugs in review and learned patterns from reviewers. The best reviews are kind but thorough, focused on behavior and maintainability rather than style nitpicks.

questions.question: What is the difference between a fork and a clone?
questions.answer: A fork is a copy of a repository on the remote (GitHub) that lives under your account — common for open-source contributions where you can't push to the original. A clone copies a repository to your local machine. The workflow: fork on GitHub, clone locally, push to your fork, open a PR to the original.

questions.question: What is `git blame` and how do you use it?
questions.answer: `git blame` shows, for each line of a file, which commit and author last changed it. It's the forensic tool for 'who wrote this and when' — useful when tracking when a bug was introduced. I use it with `git log -p` on a file to understand the history of a problematic change.

questions.question: What is `git bisect`?
questions.answer: `git bisect` is a binary search over commit history to find the commit that introduced a bug. You mark a known-good and known-bad commit, then Git checks out the midpoint repeatedly while you test each one. For 'it broke somewhere in the last 200 commits,' bisect finds it in about 8 steps. It's one of the most underrated debugging tools.

questions.question: What is a Git tag and when do you use it?
questions.answer: A tag is a named reference to a specific commit — usually a release version like `v1.2.0`. Unlike branches, tags don't move. Releases are tagged so you can always rebuild or compare a specific version. My convention: tag every release and let CI/CD deploy from the tag.

questions.question: What is the difference between `git status` and `git diff`?
questions.answer: `git status` shows the state of the working directory — which files are modified, staged, or untracked. `git diff` shows the actual content changes — lines added and removed. Status is the map; diff is the detail. I use status constantly to know where I am, and diff to review what I'm about to commit.

questions.question: What is a Git workflow and name a few common ones?
questions.answer: A Git workflow is the team's convention for branches, merges, and releases. Common ones: GitFlow (develop/main plus feature/release/hotfix branches — good for versioned releases), GitHub Flow (main plus short feature branches, PRs, continuous deployment — simple and popular), and trunk-based (small commits directly to main with short-lived branches). I lean GitHub Flow for most projects and GitFlow when releases are versioned and frequent.

questions.question: What is GitFlow and when does it make sense?
questions.answer: GitFlow uses two long-lived branches — `main` for releases and `develop` for integration — plus feature, release, and hotfix branches. It's thorough but heavy. It makes sense for projects with scheduled versioned releases and multiple environments. For a fast-moving SaaS with continuous deployment it's overkill — that's when GitHub Flow wins.

questions.question: What is trunk-based development?
questions.answer: Trunk-based development means everyone integrates small, frequent changes directly into the main branch, with short-lived feature branches at most. It reduces merge pain, keeps main always deployable, and suits CI/CD. The key enablers are feature flags and small commits. It's the pattern behind the most productive CI/CD teams I've studied.

questions.question: What is `git reflog` and when do you need it?
questions.answer: `reflog` is Git's safety net — it records every movement of HEAD, even ones that normal log doesn't show, like after a reset or rebase. When I've accidentally 'lost' commits, `git reflog` shows where HEAD was and lets me recover. It's the tool for 'oh no, I broke my branch.'

questions.question: What is the difference between a shallow clone and a full clone?
questions.answer: A shallow clone (`git clone --depth 1`) downloads only the latest commit without full history — faster for large repos, good for CI. The cost: you can't browse history or switch to old branches easily. I use shallow clones in CI pipelines where only the latest code is needed, and full clones for real development.

questions.question: What is `git submodule` and when would you use it?
questions.answer: A submodule is a Git repository nested inside another, pinned to a specific commit — used to share a library across projects while tracking its version. The downside is complexity: you must update and commit submodule pointers explicitly, which confuses people. These days I'd prefer package managers or monorepos over submodules unless the workflow truly demands them.

questions.question: What is a monorepo and its pros and cons?
questions.answer: A monorepo holds multiple projects in one repository with shared tooling and one history. Pros: atomic changes across packages, unified builds, easier refactoring. Cons: scale issues, permission granularity, and CI complexity. Many large teams run monorepos successfully with tools like Nx or Bazel. For small teams, a single repo is often simplest.

questions.question: What is `.gitkeep`?
questions.answer: `.gitkeep` is an empty file committed to force Git to track an otherwise-empty directory — Git doesn't track empty folders. It's a convention, not a Git feature. I use it for directories like uploads or logs that need to exist in a fresh clone.

questions.question: How do you handle secrets in a Git repository?
questions.answer: Never commit secrets. Use `.gitignore` for `.env` files, inject secrets via environment variables or a secret manager (like AWS Secrets Manager), and if a secret was ever committed, rotate it immediately — removing it from history isn't enough because it's in the history. I've seen this lesson cost real companies. Prevention is the whole game.

questions.question: What is a commit message convention like Conventional Commits?
questions.answer: Conventional Commits standardizes messages: `type(scope): description` — like `feat(auth): add refresh token`. Types include feat, fix, docs, refactor, test, chore. Benefits: automated changelogs, semantic versioning, and clear history. I follow it because the discipline makes history readable and enables tooling.

questions.question: What is unit testing and why does it matter?
questions.answer: A unit test verifies the smallest piece of logic in isolation — a function, a method — with its dependencies mocked. It matters because it catches regressions at the cheapest point, documents behavior, and makes refactoring safe. I don't always reach 100% coverage, but I test the logic that's easy to get wrong — business rules, validation, calculations. For my MSS module, testing the capacity calculation prevented real factory planning errors.

questions.question: What is the difference between unit, integration, and end-to-end tests?
questions.answer: Unit tests check a single unit in isolation. Integration tests check that units work together — like an API talking to a real database. End-to-end tests run the whole app like a real user — browser clicks, form submissions. They form a pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, fewest slow E2E tests. My habit: heavy unit coverage on business logic, integration tests on the API, and a smoke E2E test on the critical path.

questions.question: What is Test-Driven Development (TDD)?
questions.answer: TDD is writing the test first, watching it fail, writing the minimum code to pass, then refactoring — red, green, refactor. The benefit is design pressure: you think about the interface before the implementation. I don't apply it everywhere, but for critical business logic I find the discipline genuinely produces better, simpler code.

questions.question: What is a mock and when do you use it?
questions.answer: A mock is a fake object that stands in for a real dependency — like a database or an HTTP service — and lets you control its behavior and assert on interactions. You use mocks to isolate the unit under test, so you're testing your logic, not your database or a network call. In my API tests I mock the DB layer so tests are fast and deterministic.

questions.question: What is the difference between a mock, a stub, and a spy?
questions.answer: A stub returns fixed data you set — canned responses. A mock also lets you assert that certain methods were called with certain arguments. A spy wraps a real object and records calls while letting the real behavior run. Stub = canned data, mock = behavior verification, spy = observation. Knowing the difference keeps tests honest.

questions.question: What is test coverage and is 100% coverage always good?
questions.answer: Coverage measures how much of your code the tests execute — lines, branches, functions. 100% coverage sounds ideal but isn't: it measures that code ran, not that behavior is correct. High coverage on trivial code is theater. I aim for meaningful coverage on risky logic and accept lower numbers elsewhere — coverage is a tool, not a goal.

questions.question: What is a flaky test and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: A flaky test passes and fails intermittently without code changes — usually caused by timing, order dependence, shared state, or network assumptions. To fix, I look for the nondeterminism: remove sleeps in favor of waits, isolate tests, seed data explicitly, and make tests not depend on execution order. Flaky tests destroy trust in the suite — I treat them as urgent.

questions.question: What is the testing pyramid?
questions.answer: The testing pyramid describes an ideal test distribution: a large base of fast unit tests, a middle layer of integration tests, and a small tip of slow E2E tests. The rationale: unit tests are cheap and fast, so you can have many; E2E tests are slow and brittle, so you keep them few. Teams that invert it — mostly E2E — end up with slow, flaky suites.

questions.question: What is a regression test?
questions.answer: A regression test targets a specific bug to make sure it doesn't come back — you write it for the exact failing scenario, watch it pass after the fix, and keep it forever. Every bug I fix should leave behind a regression test. That's the difference between fixing a bug once and fixing it repeatedly.

questions.question: What is testing in Angular and which tools do you use?
questions.answer: Angular comes with Jasmine and Karma for unit tests and TestBed for building test modules. I write component tests checking rendered output and interaction, service tests with HttpClientTestingModule for HTTP mocking. For E2E, Protractor historically, now Cypress or Playwright. Testing Angular means understanding TestBed, injectors, and how to isolate components.

questions.question: What is testing in Vue and which tools do you use?
questions.answer: Vue's official tooling is Vitest for unit tests and Vue Test Utils for mounting components — you can assert rendered output and emitted events, mock props and store. Component testing with Vitest is fast because it runs in Node with jsdom. For E2E, Playwright or Cypress. In my Vue projects I unit-test composables and components with Vitest.

questions.question: What is testing in Python (pytest vs unittest)?
questions.answer: `unittest` is the stdlib framework — class-based, similar to JUnit. `pytest` is the modern favorite: function-based, fixtures, parametrize, plugins, and far less boilerplate. I prefer pytest for everything. `pytest` fixtures handle setup/teardown elegantly, and `monkeypatch` mocks cleanly. For FastAPI/Frappe code, pytest is my default.

questions.question: What is a pytest fixture and how do you use it?
questions.answer: A fixture is a reusable setup/teardown function that provides data or objects to tests — declared with `@pytest.fixture` and injected by name as a parameter. It can yield, running teardown after the test. Examples: a database session, an authenticated client. Fixtures keep tests DRY and manage resources properly.

questions.question: What is a test double?
questions.answer: A test double is any object standing in for a real one during testing — the umbrella term covering stubs, mocks, fakes, spies. The name comes from 'stunt double.' When people say 'mocking everything,' they usually mean using various doubles. Understanding the taxonomy shows you think carefully about tests.

questions.question: What is mocking in JavaScript testing?
questions.answer: Mocking in JS means replacing a function or module with a controlled fake — via Jest's `jest.fn()`, `jest.mock()`, or Vitest's equivalents. `jest.mock('module')` replaces a whole module; `jest.fn()` creates a spy function. I mock HTTP services and time in frontend tests to make them fast and deterministic.

questions.question: What is snapshot testing?
questions.answer: Snapshot testing captures a component's rendered output as a saved snapshot and fails future tests if the output changes — useful for catching unintended UI changes. The danger: a giant snapshot is hard to review and people just update it on any change, making it noise. I use snapshots sparingly and keep them small, or prefer targeted assertions.

questions.question: What is the difference between a smoke test and a sanity test?
questions.answer: A smoke test is a quick check that the core flows work — often run on every deploy, like 'app loads and login works.' A sanity test is a narrower check after a specific change to confirm nothing broke in the touched area. Smoke is broad and shallow; sanity is targeted. I run smoke tests in CI after every deployment.

questions.question: What is CI testing and why do tests belong in CI?
questions.answer: CI testing means every push runs the test suite automatically in the pipeline — so failures surface immediately, not days later when someone merges. Tests in CI catch integration problems, enforce quality gates, and protect the main branch. My rule: if a PR breaks the build, it doesn't merge until it's green.

questions.question: What is performance testing?
questions.answer: Performance testing measures speed and resource use — load testing (many users), stress testing (beyond capacity), and latency profiling. It answers 'will this hold up.' In my projects I use it to verify the 500-transactions-a-day workloads and the 25% load-time improvement. Tools like k6 or JMeter for load, Lighthouse for frontend.

questions.question: What is the difference between load testing and stress testing?
questions.answer: Load testing verifies the system handles expected traffic at expected scale — does it meet response-time targets under normal load. Stress testing pushes beyond capacity to find the breaking point and how the system fails. Load answers 'can we handle today'; stress answers 'what's the ceiling and what breaks first.'

questions.question: What is a test plan and what does it contain?
questions.answer: A test plan is the strategy document — scope, features to test, approach, environments, schedule, risks, and exit criteria. It aligns the team on what 'done' means for quality. For small projects a one-page plan is enough; the value is in deciding what to test and how before you start.

questions.question: What is black-box vs white-box testing?
questions.answer: Black-box testing tests behavior without knowing the internals — you test the interface: inputs and outputs. White-box testing uses knowledge of the internals to design cases — covering branches and conditions. In practice, good testers blend both: white-box design for unit tests, black-box for API and UI testing.

questions.question: What is boundary testing?
questions.answer: Boundary testing targets the edges of valid ranges — for an age field of 18+, you test 17, 18, 19, and the empty case. Bugs cluster at boundaries. It's one of the highest-value-per-test techniques. I use boundary thinking constantly in validation: off-by-one errors are the most common class of bug I've caught.

questions.question: What is cross-browser testing and why does it matter?
questions.answer: Cross-browser testing verifies the app works in Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge, and mobile browsers, since each engine differs slightly in rendering and JS behavior. Tools: Playwright, BrowserStack, Cypress. I test the critical flows on the browsers my users actually use, and keep CSS defensive so engine differences don't break layout.

questions.question: What is Playwright and how is it different from Selenium?
questions.answer: Playwright is a modern browser automation framework that drives Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit with a single API, auto-waits for elements, and runs fast and reliably. Selenium is the older standard but requires more manual waiting and config. Both do E2E, but Playwright's auto-waiting and stability make it my choice for E2E suites.

questions.question: What is the difference between Selenium and Cypress?
questions.answer: Selenium runs in a real browser process with a WebDriver protocol, works across many languages and browsers, but can be slow and flaky. Cypress runs in the browser with the app, is fast and developer-friendly, but historically only Chrome-family and has limitations with multiple tabs. For Angular/Vue E2E I'd pick Playwright or Cypress; Selenium when a team demands multi-language/multi-browser coverage.

questions.question: What is contract testing?
questions.answer: Contract testing verifies that two services — like a frontend and a backend — agree on the shape of the API they exchange, using a shared contract (like Pact). It catches breaking API changes before they reach production, without expensive full E2E tests. In microservices teams it's the pragmatic middle ground between unit and E2E tests.

questions.question: What is mutation testing?
questions.answer: Mutation testing deliberately introduces small bugs (mutations) into your code and checks whether your tests catch them. If a test suite passes with a mutation present, that code isn't effectively tested. It measures test quality, not just coverage. Tools like Stryker do this. It's heavy but revealing — it shows which tests actually protect you.

questions.question: What is the difference between verification and validation in testing?
questions.answer: Verification asks 'did we build it right' — does the software meet the spec and work correctly. Validation asks 'did we build the right thing' — does it meet the user's actual need. In practice, verification is technical testing; validation is product-level checking. A technically perfect feature that nobody needs fails validation.

questions.question: What is exploratory testing?
questions.answer: Exploratory testing is unscripted testing where the tester learns the system and designs tests on the fly — no fixed test cases. It's excellent for finding issues that scripted tests miss, because it follows curiosity and real-user thinking. I do a light exploratory pass before release alongside the automated suite — the two find different bugs.

questions.question: What is Object-Oriented Programming?
questions.answer: OOP is a programming paradigm that organizes code around objects — bundles of state (attributes) and behavior (methods). Its four pillars are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, and polymorphism. It helps model real-world entities and keeps related data and behavior together. I use OOP heavily in Python and Java — like Frappe controller classes that model ERP documents.

questions.question: What are the four pillars of OOP?
questions.answer: Encapsulation — hiding internal state behind an interface; abstraction — exposing only what's needed; inheritance — building new classes from existing ones; polymorphism — treating different types through a common interface, so one call behaves differently per object. These four are the standard answer, and interviewers usually want a real example of each.

questions.question: What is encapsulation and how do you achieve it in Python?
questions.answer: Encapsulation bundles data and the methods that operate on it, and hides internal state. In Python it's by convention: `_private` is a convention, `__name_mangled` is stronger. In Java, `private`/`public` enforce it. The benefit: you can change internals without breaking callers. My controllers expose a small public API while keeping the logic private.

questions.question: What is abstraction?
questions.answer: Abstraction means exposing only the essential interface and hiding implementation details — you use a car without knowing engine internals. In code, abstract base classes and interfaces define 'what' without 'how.' It reduces coupling and cognitive load. Frameworks like FastAPI and Frappe are abstractions — I use their API without reading their source.

questions.question: What is inheritance and when should you avoid it?
questions.answer: Inheritance lets a class reuse and extend a parent's behavior — `class DiscountedItem(Item)`. It's good for clear 'is-a' relationships. Avoid it when the relationship is really 'has-a' — prefer composition. Deep inheritance hierarchies become rigid and fragile. In Frappe I extend core DocTypes sparingly, preferring composition and hooks for customization.

questions.question: What is polymorphism and give an example?
questions.answer: Polymorphism lets different classes be used through a common interface — the same method name behaves differently per type. In Python, duck typing gives it naturally: `for shape in shapes: shape.draw()` works for any object with a `draw` method. In Java, interfaces enable it. It's what lets my code handle many ERP document types through one code path.

questions.question: What is the difference between an interface and an abstract class?
questions.answer: An interface declares a contract — methods without implementation — and a class implements it. An abstract class can also have concrete methods and state, and a class extends it. A class can implement many interfaces but extend one abstract class. Interfaces describe capability; abstract classes share implementation. In Python, ABCs (`abc` module) play both roles.

questions.question: What is method overloading vs method overriding?
questions.answer: Overloading is defining multiple methods with the same name but different parameters — resolved at compile time. Overriding is redefining a parent method in a child — resolved at runtime. Python doesn't do traditional overloading (you use default args); Java does. Overriding is everywhere in frameworks — I override `validate` in Frappe controllers.

questions.question: What is constructor overloading and how do you handle it in Python?
questions.answer: Constructor overloading is multiple constructors with different parameters. Java supports it. Python has one `__init__`, so you achieve overloading with default arguments, classmethods as alternative constructors, or `*args`. A `@classmethod` like `User.from_email(...)` is the clean Python pattern.

questions.question: What is a static method vs an instance method vs a class method?
questions.answer: An instance method takes `self` and operates on instance state. A class method takes `cls` and can access class state — often used as alternative constructors. A static method takes neither — it's just a function namespaced in the class, for related utilities. In Python, `@classmethod` and `@staticmethod` decorate them; Java has `static` methods.

questions.question: What is `super()` in Python and how do you use it?
questions.answer: `super()` calls methods from a parent class — typically `super().__init__()` in a child's `__init__` to run parent initialization before extending it. It also handles multiple inheritance via MRO correctly. In Frappe, custom controllers call `super().validate()` to keep core validation then add their own.

questions.question: What is the difference between composition and inheritance?
questions.answer: Composition means a class holds other objects ('has-a') — `Car has-an Engine`. Inheritance means 'is-a' — `Dog is-an Animal`. Composition is more flexible, easier to test, and avoids fragile hierarchies. The guidance 'prefer composition over inheritance' is a staple. I build services that compose repositories, rather than deep class trees.

questions.question: What are SOLID principles?
questions.answer: SOLID is five design principles: Single Responsibility (one reason to change per class), Open/Closed (open for extension, closed for modification), Liskov Substitution (subtypes replace their parents), Interface Segregation (small specific interfaces), Dependency Inversion (depend on abstractions, not concretions). Together they keep systems maintainable. I apply them when classes start growing reasons to change.

questions.question: Explain the Single Responsibility Principle.
questions.answer: SRP says a class should have exactly one reason to change — one job. A class that parses data AND writes to the database AND renders output breaks when any of those change. Splitting responsibilities makes each piece testable and understandable. In my API code, controllers, services, and repositories each have one job — that's SRP in practice.

questions.question: Explain the Open/Closed Principle.
questions.answer: OCP says code should be open for extension but closed for modification — add new behavior by adding new code, not editing existing tested code. Achieved with inheritance, interfaces, or strategy patterns. In Frappe, hooks and overrides let me extend behavior without touching core — that's the open/closed idea in a framework.

questions.question: Explain the Liskov Substitution Principle.
questions.answer: LSP says if a subtype is used where its parent is expected, the program must behave correctly — no surprising failures. A square shouldn't subclass a rectangle if the square breaks rectangle's width/height contract. Violating LSP produces bugs where `isinstance` checks or behavior assumptions creep in. I follow it by making overrides honor the parent's contract.

questions.question: Explain the Interface Segregation Principle.
questions.answer: ISP says clients shouldn't depend on interfaces they don't use — prefer several small interfaces over one fat one. A class forced to implement methods it ignores has a smell. In practice, split capabilities into focused contracts. Python's duck typing makes this natural — my services expose small, specific methods rather than a god-object interface.

questions.question: Explain the Dependency Inversion Principle.
questions.answer: DIP says high-level modules shouldn't depend on low-level details — both should depend on abstractions. Concretely: your service depends on a repository interface, not a concrete MySQL class, so you can swap implementations and test with mocks. Dependency injection is the mechanism that implements DIP. FastAPI's dependency system and Angular's DI are DIP in action.

questions.question: What is dependency injection and why is it useful?
questions.answer: DI is handing a component its dependencies rather than letting it create them — the dependency is injected, often by a framework. Benefits: testability (inject mocks), flexibility (swap implementations), and decoupling. Angular is built on DI; FastAPI resolves dependencies from type hints. I've used DI everywhere without always naming it — it's how good frameworks are designed.

questions.question: What is inversion of control (IoC)?
questions.answer: IoC flips the flow of control: instead of your code calling the framework, the framework calls your code. DI is the common implementation. You register components and the container wires them. Frameworks like Spring and Angular are IoC containers. The benefit is that components stay loosely coupled and testable.

questions.question: What is the difference between IoC and DI?
questions.answer: IoC is the broad principle — the framework controls the flow and object lifecycle. DI is a specific technique — passing dependencies into an object instead of creating them internally. DI is one way to achieve IoC. So 'Spring uses IoC' is about the container controlling wiring; 'constructor injection' is the DI detail. People use them almost interchangeably, but the distinction is worth being precise about.

questions.question: What is a design pattern and why are they useful?
questions.answer: A design pattern is a proven, reusable solution to a common problem in software design — a vocabulary for solving recurring architecture problems. They're useful because they package battle-tested approaches: you don't reinvent, and teammates recognize the pattern immediately. The GoF book catalogued the classics. I use patterns as tools, not dogma — the right pattern solves a real problem, not a hypothetical one.

questions.question: Name some creational design patterns.
questions.answer: Creational patterns deal with object creation: Singleton (one instance), Factory Method (delegate creation to subclasses), Abstract Factory (families of related objects), Builder (step-by-step construction), Prototype (clone). I use Factory for object creation behind an interface and Builder for complex objects like a query builder.

questions.question: What is the Singleton pattern and when should you avoid it?
questions.answer: Singleton ensures one instance globally — often a config or connection object. But it's also global mutable state that hides dependencies and complicates testing. Modern advice: prefer DI with a single registered instance — you get one instance without the global. I avoid hand-rolled singletons and let DI containers manage lifecycle.

questions.question: What is the Factory pattern?
questions.answer: Factory centralizes object creation behind a method or class — callers ask for a product and the factory decides the concrete type. It decouples creation from usage. Example: a report factory that returns different report types based on a type parameter. I use it when creation logic has branching that shouldn't live in every caller.

questions.question: What is the Builder pattern?
questions.answer: Builder separates constructing a complex object from its representation — you chain steps and call build. It handles objects with many optional parts. Examples: query builders, request builders. Benefits: readable construction and validation at the end. I appreciate it for building complex test data.

questions.question: What is the Prototype pattern?
questions.answer: Prototype creates new objects by cloning an existing one rather than by construction — expensive or complex setup is copied. In Python, `copy.copy`/`deepcopy` are prototypes. It's niche in web dev, but the concept (clone a template object) shows up in config and templating. Interviewers ask it mostly to test pattern breadth.

questions.question: Name some structural design patterns.
questions.answer: Structural patterns organize classes and objects: Adapter (make incompatible interfaces work together), Decorator (add behavior without changing the class), Facade (simplified interface to a complex system), Proxy (control access), Composite (tree structures). I use Adapter to wrap third-party APIs and Decorator for adding behavior like caching or logging.

questions.question: What is the Adapter pattern?
questions.answer: Adapter converts one interface to another so incompatible classes can cooperate — like a power plug adapter. Example: wrapping a legacy vendor API in an interface your app expects. It's invaluable for integrations, which is a big part of my ERP work — biometric devices and third-party APIs all need adapting.

questions.question: What is the Decorator pattern?
questions.answer: Decorator wraps an object to add behavior without modifying its class — you stack wrappers. In Python, `@` decorators and `functools.wraps` are examples; in OOP, a Decorator class wraps and forwards. Use: adding logging, caching, auth to an existing component. It's the open/closed principle applied.

questions.question: What is the Facade pattern?
questions.answer: Facade provides a simple interface to a complex subsystem — a single entry point hiding the mess. Example: an `OrderService` facade that internally coordinates payment, inventory, and email services. Clients get one clean call instead of orchestrating five things. I use facades at API boundaries to keep controllers thin.

questions.question: What is the Proxy pattern and how is it different from Adapter?
questions.answer: Proxy provides the same interface as its subject but controls access — lazy loading, caching, access control, remote calls. Adapter changes the interface to make things compatible. Proxy keeps the interface and adds behavior around it; Adapter translates a different interface. Example: a lazy-loading proxy for an expensive service.

questions.question: Name some behavioral design patterns.
questions.answer: Behavioral patterns manage interaction and responsibility: Observer (notify dependents on change), Strategy (swap algorithms at runtime), Command (encapsulate a request as an object), Template Method (skeleton with overridable steps), State (behavior changes with state), Iterator. I use Strategy for interchangeable algorithms and Observer via event systems like Frappe hooks.

questions.question: What is the Observer pattern?
questions.answer: Observer lets objects subscribe to events and get notified when the subject changes — one-to-many. Your email is notified when you post. In web dev it's everywhere: event emitters, RxJS, Vue reactivity, publish/subscribe systems. Frappe's hooks and scheduler are observer-like. I've used it for sync systems that notify multiple consumers of a change.

questions.question: What is the Strategy pattern?
questions.answer: Strategy defines a family of interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface, selected at runtime. Example: a payment processor with different payment strategies — UPI, card, netbanking — swapped without changing the caller. It's the clean way to replace big if-else chains. Python makes it easy with callables and dicts.

questions.question: What is the Command pattern?
questions.answer: Command encapsulates a request as an object — with parameters and an execute method — enabling queuing, undo, and logging of actions. Example: an action queue where each task is a command object. In Frappe, enqueued jobs are essentially commands. It's valuable for undo/redo and task systems.

questions.question: What is the Template Method pattern?
questions.answer: Template Method defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class and lets subclasses override specific steps. The base controls the flow; children fill in details. Frameworks use this constantly — Frappe's validate/on_submit flow is a template method that I override specific steps of. It's the 'inheritance for algorithms' pattern.

questions.question: What is the State pattern?
questions.answer: State pattern makes an object's behavior change when its internal state changes — the object delegates to a state object. It's like a state machine: an order behaves differently in Draft, Submitted, and Cancelled. Frappe's workflow system implements exactly this. It removes giant switch statements on status by encapsulating per-state behavior.

questions.question: What is the difference between MVC and MVVM?
questions.answer: MVC splits into Model (data/logic), View (presentation), and Controller (input handling). MVVM splits into Model, View, and ViewModel (state the view binds to, with the framework syncing view and viewmodel). Angular and Vue are more MVVM-ish — components bind to a view model. MVC is the classic server pattern; MVVM is the common modern frontend architecture.

questions.question: What is the Repository pattern?
questions.answer: Repository mediates between the domain and the data layer — it presents a clean collection-like interface (`getByID`, `save`, `find`) over the actual database. The data source can be swapped and tested. It's the data-access layer's abstraction. In my API services I use repositories so business logic never touches SQL directly.

questions.question: What is the Unit of Work pattern?
questions.answer: Unit of Work tracks changes to multiple objects and commits them together in one transaction — one place for save/commit/rollback. It complements the repository pattern; ORMs like SQLAlchemy and Hibernate implement it via sessions that flush at the right time. It ensures a multi-object operation is atomic. In ERP work, this guarantees no partial saves.

questions.question: What is a DAO pattern and how does it differ from Repository?
questions.answer: DAO (Data Access Object) abstracts database access — each entity has a DAO with CRUD methods. Repository is similar but focuses on a domain-model interface and doesn't necessarily mean one-per-entity. Practically they overlap heavily; Repository is the more modern domain-centric framing. Interviewers want to know both and that they're both 'hide the persistence details' patterns.

questions.question: What is the N+1 query problem?
questions.answer: N+1 happens when you load N records and then make one extra query per record to fetch related data — 100 posts means 101 queries. It wrecks performance. Fixes: eager loading (join or fetch related data in one query), or using an ORM's `select_related`/`prefetch_related`, or raw SQL with joins. I hit this in internship work with indexed tables and learned to batch queries.

questions.question: What is ORM and why do developers use it?
questions.answer: ORM, object-relational mapping, maps database tables to objects so you work with classes instead of raw SQL. Benefits: productivity, type safety, portability, and safety from injection. Costs: it can hide what the database actually does and encourage inefficient queries. Frappe's ORM is how I write ERP logic; SQLAlchemy and Hibernate are the general-purpose ones.

questions.question: What is lazy loading vs eager loading in ORMs?
questions.answer: Lazy loading fetches related data only when accessed — convenient but risky for N+1. Eager loading fetches related data upfront in one query — efficient when you know you'll need it. In Django, `select_related` vs `prefetch_related`; in SQLAlchemy, relationships with lazy/eager settings. My rule: eager-load anything the view will use; avoid lazy surprise queries.

questions.question: What is Hibernate and what role does it play in Java?
questions.answer: Hibernate is a Java ORM implementing JPA — it maps Java classes to database tables, manages the session/transaction, and provides the query API. It's the standard Java persistence layer. In my Java/Spring work it's how Java objects become rows. I know its mapping annotations, session lifecycle, and the N+1 pitfalls.

questions.question: What is JPA and how does it relate to Hibernate?
questions.answer: JPA is the Java specification — the standard API for persistence. Hibernate is the most popular implementation of that spec. So you write JPA interfaces/annotations and Hibernate provides the engine. This spec/implementation split is a classic Java interview question, and it matters because code written to JPA can run on other implementations.

questions.question: What is the difference between a design pattern and a framework?
questions.answer: A design pattern is a reusable solution concept you apply in code — small, language-agnostic, no code provided. A framework is a concrete, shipped codebase that provides structure and calls your code (IoC). You write a pattern; you extend a framework. Angular is a framework; MVVM is a pattern it follows. Patterns describe, frameworks provide.

questions.question: What is an operating system and what does it do?
questions.answer: An OS is the software layer between hardware and applications. It manages processes, memory, files, devices, and user interaction — and it's what lets multiple programs share the CPU safely. Understanding it matters for backend work: threads, processes, scheduling, and memory explain real app behavior. When a Node app 'blocks,' it's the OS and event loop story.

questions.question: What is a process vs a thread?
questions.answer: A process is an independent program with its own memory space and resources — heavy to create, isolated. A thread is a lightweight unit of execution within a process, sharing the process's memory — cheaper to create, but threads in one process can interfere. Python threads share the GIL; Java threads are true OS threads. The tradeoff — isolation vs cost — decides the design.

questions.question: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism?
