questions.answer: Concurrency is dealing with many tasks at once — interleaving their execution, making progress on all of them. Parallelism is doing many tasks literally at the same time on multiple cores. You can have concurrency on one core (fast switching) but parallelism needs multiple cores. Node is concurrent via the event loop; multiprocessing in Python gives parallelism.

questions.question: What is a deadlock?
questions.answer: A deadlock is when two or more threads each hold a resource the other needs, so none can proceed — and they wait forever. Four conditions cause it: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait. Prevention: lock ordering, timeouts, or single locks. I've seen this in database transactions where two queries lock rows in opposite orders.

questions.question: What is a race condition?
questions.answer: A race condition is when the outcome depends on the unpredictable timing of threads or processes — two threads read the same value, both modify it, and one write is lost. It's a classic 'works in testing, fails in production' bug because timing differs. Fixes: locks, atomic operations, or transactional guarantees. My sync job bug was exactly this.

questions.question: What is mutual exclusion and how is it enforced?
questions.answer: Mutual exclusion means only one thread can enter a critical section at a time. It's enforced with locks — a thread acquires the lock, does its work, releases it. In Python, `threading.Lock`; in databases, row/table locks. The cost is serialization — overusing locks kills concurrency, so you scope critical sections tightly.

questions.question: What is a semaphore?
questions.answer: A semaphore is a counter that controls access to a limited resource — threads acquire (decrement) and release (increment), blocking when the counter is zero. A mutex is a binary semaphore (one holder). Semaphores are for pools: a connection pool of N connections uses a semaphore. I've used semaphore-like logic in DB connection pools.

questions.question: What is a mutex?
questions.answer: A mutex (mutual exclusion) is a lock allowing only one thread to hold it at a time — ownership-based. The thread that locks must unlock. It protects critical sections from concurrent corruption. The difference from a semaphore: a mutex is binary and owner-aware; a semaphore is a general counter. Classic OS question.

questions.question: What is context switching?
questions.answer: Context switching is the OS saving a running task's state and loading another's — the CPU changes what it's executing. It's how multitasking works, but it's not free: saving/restoring state costs time, so too many threads cause thrashing. Understanding it explains why thread pools are sized carefully and why the 'one thread per request' model has limits.

questions.question: What is virtual memory?
questions.answer: Virtual memory lets programs use more memory than physically available by mapping virtual addresses to physical ones, with pages swapped to disk when needed. Each process sees a clean, contiguous address space. It's why a process can have a huge address space. Performance suffers when pages thrash to disk — a reason to watch memory pressure on servers.

questions.question: What is paging and swapping?
questions.answer: Paging divides memory into fixed pages and moves them between RAM and disk — virtual memory's mechanism. Swapping moves entire processes in and out. When memory is overcommitted, the OS constantly pages/swaps, destroying performance — the server 'thrashes.' On Linux I check `free` and swap usage; high swap means add memory or reduce load.

questions.question: What is the difference between stack and heap memory?
questions.answer: The stack is fast, small, LIFO memory for function calls and local variables — automatically managed, thread-local. The heap is larger, shared memory for dynamically allocated objects — managed by the programmer or a GC, slower. In Python, objects live on the heap; in C, `malloc` uses the heap. Memory leaks come from heap mismanagement.

questions.question: What is garbage collection?
questions.answer: Garbage collection automatically reclaims memory no longer referenced — the language tracks objects and frees unreachable ones. Python uses reference counting plus a cycle collector; Java uses tracing GCs. The benefit: fewer manual memory bugs. The cost: pauses and overhead. Knowing GC behavior explains memory spikes in long-running services.

questions.question: What is the difference between a kernel and a shell?
questions.answer: The kernel is the core of the OS — manages hardware, processes, memory. The shell is the user interface to the OS — bash, PowerShell — where you type commands that ask the kernel to do things. I work in the shell daily on Ubuntu, and the kernel is the layer beneath that I interact with indirectly.

questions.question: What is a file system and what are common types?
questions.answer: A file system organizes how data is stored and retrieved on disk — directories, files, permissions, metadata. Common types: ext4 (Linux default), NTFS (Windows), APFS (macOS), plus network ones. It matters operationally: `df -h` shows disk, `inodes` can run out, and mounting wrong types breaks things. Most deployment issues I've seen were storage-related.

questions.question: What is an inode?
questions.answer: An inode is the metadata record for a file — permissions, owner, size, timestamps, and disk block pointers. Files without space but 'no space left' can actually be an inode exhaustion. When I diagnose disk issues on Ubuntu, I check both `df -h` (blocks) and `df -i` (inodes). It's a subtle but real deployment gotcha.

questions.question: What is a port and what are common ports?
questions.answer: A port is a numbered endpoint for network communication on a host — 0-65535. Common ones: 80 (HTTP), 443 (HTTPS), 22 (SSH), 3306 (MySQL), 5432 (PostgreSQL), 27017 (MongoDB), 6379 (Redis), 3000/8080 (dev apps). Knowing ports matters for firewalls, Docker publishing, and debugging why a service isn't reachable.

questions.question: What is the OSI model and what are its layers?
questions.answer: The OSI model is a 7-layer framework for networking: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. In practice, the TCP/IP model (Link, Internet, Transport, Application) is what the internet uses. Interviewers like it because it organizes thinking — a DNS problem is Application layer, a routing problem is Network layer.

questions.question: What is TCP and what are its key features?
questions.answer: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is a connection-oriented, reliable transport protocol. Key features: three-way handshake to establish, sequencing and acknowledgments, retransmission of lost packets, flow control, and congestion control. It guarantees ordered, error-checked delivery — the price is latency. HTTP runs on TCP. When reliability matters, TCP is the answer.

questions.question: What is UDP and how is it different from TCP?
questions.answer: UDP is connectionless and unreliable — no handshake, no guarantee of delivery or order. It's fast and low-overhead, used for real-time media, DNS, and gaming where a dropped packet beats a delayed one. TCP for reliability, UDP for speed/latency. The classic comparison: TCP is a phone call, UDP is a postcard.

questions.question: What is the TCP three-way handshake?
questions.answer: The handshake establishes a connection: client sends SYN, server replies SYN-ACK, client sends ACK. After that, data flows. It's why TCP connections cost a round trip before any data — one reason HTTP/2 and keep-alive reuse connections. Debugging slow first loads often leads back to handshake and connection setup.

questions.question: What is the difference between TCP and HTTP?
questions.answer: TCP is a transport protocol — the reliable pipe that moves bytes between machines. HTTP is an application protocol that defines how requests and responses are structured, running on top of TCP. So TCP is the road, HTTP is the rules for how mail moves on it. Same distinction for TLS: it's another layer on top of TCP.

questions.question: What is DNS and how does it work?
questions.answer: DNS translates domain names to IP addresses — the internet's phonebook. When you type a domain, a resolver queries root servers, TLD servers, then authoritative servers to find the IP. It's hierarchical and cached at every level. DNS issues — propagation, wrong records, TTL — are a whole class of deployment problems. I've debugged 'why doesn't my subdomain work' with DNS records.

questions.question: What is an IP address and the difference between IPv4 and IPv6?
questions.answer: An IP address identifies a device on a network. IPv4 is 32-bit, dotted-decimal — like 192.168.1.1 — with about 4.3 billion addresses, which ran out. IPv6 is 128-bit, hexadecimal — vastly more addresses, with built-in features. Modern servers support both; the transition matters for any system that handles addresses. For debugging, understanding IPv4/IPv6 duality explains odd connection failures.

questions.question: What is the difference between a public and private IP address?
questions.answer: A public IP is routable on the internet — globally unique. A private IP (like 192.168.x, 10.x, 172.16-31.x) is used inside a local network and translated to the public address by NAT. My EC2 instances get both: a public IP for the internet and a private one for VPC-internal traffic. Understanding this is basic cloud networking.

questions.question: What is NAT?
questions.answer: NAT (Network Address Translation) maps private addresses to a public one — a router lets many devices share one public IP. In the cloud, instances in a private subnet reach the internet via NAT. It's also why home networks work with one ISP address. It's the translation layer between internal and external addressing.

questions.question: What is a subnet mask?
questions.answer: A subnet mask defines which part of an IP address is the network and which is the host — 255.255.255.0 means the first three octets are network. CIDR notation (/24) is the modern form. When configuring AWS VPCs or firewalls, getting the subnet right determines reachability. It's a foundational networking concept.

questions.question: What is HTTP and how does it work?
questions.answer: HTTP is the application protocol for web communication — a request/response cycle between client and server. A client sends a request (method, path, headers, body), the server returns a response (status, headers, body). It's stateless — each request is independent, which is why auth tokens or cookies are needed. Understanding HTTP deeply is core to being a full stack developer.

questions.question: What is HTTPS and how does it work?
questions.answer: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS — the traffic is encrypted so eavesdroppers can't read it, and the server identity is verified via certificates. The handshake exchanges keys using public-key crypto, then symmetric encryption secures the rest. Modern practice is HTTPS everywhere — I configure TLS at Nginx for all my deployments.

questions.question: What is TLS and how does it differ from SSL?
questions.answer: SSL is the old encryption protocol (now deprecated and insecure). TLS is its successor — the modern secure layer. People say 'SSL' casually but they mean TLS 1.2/1.3. Certificates, handshake, encryption — same ideas. I configure TLS 1.2+ on Nginx and disable old protocols.

questions.question: What is a certificate in HTTPS?
questions.answer: A certificate is a digital identity for a server — it binds a public key to a domain, signed by a trusted Certificate Authority. The browser verifies the signature and the domain match, establishing trust. Certificates expire and must renew — Let's Encrypt automates that. 'Certificate expired' is a classic production outage.

questions.question: What is an HTTP status code? Name the categories.
questions.answer: Status codes communicate the result of a request: 1xx informational, 2xx success (200, 201, 204), 3xx redirection (301, 302, 304), 4xx client error (400, 401, 403, 404, 422), 5xx server error (500, 502, 503). Using the right code is API design basics — a 404 for missing, 401 for unauthenticated, 403 for unauthorized, 422 for validation. I care about these because my frontends branch on them.

questions.question: What is the difference between 401 and 403?
questions.answer: 401 Unauthorized means you aren't authenticated — no valid credentials, login needed. 403 Forbidden means you're authenticated but don't have permission — you can't access this even logged in. So 401 is 'who are you?' and 403 is 'you're not allowed.' In my auth middleware, invalid token → 401, valid but wrong role → 403.

questions.question: What is the difference between 404 and 410?
questions.answer: 404 means the resource isn't found — it may never have existed. 410 Gone means the resource existed but was intentionally removed and won't come back. 410 helps search engines stop indexing. It's niche but precise API design. I'd use 410 for a permanently retired endpoint.

questions.question: What is a redirect and what is the difference between 301 and 302?
questions.answer: A redirect tells the client to go to a different URL. 301 is permanent — browsers and search engines cache it, updating the address. 302 is temporary — the browser goes there now but keeps the original. Using the wrong one matters for SEO and for clients that cache. E.g., HTTPS migration uses 301; a temporary maintenance page uses 302.

questions.question: What is HTTP caching and what headers control it?
questions.answer: HTTP caching stores responses to reuse them, controlled by headers: `Cache-Control` (max-age, no-cache, no-store, immutable), `ETag` (revalidation), `Last-Modified`, `Expires`. Correct caching separates fast from slow sites — static assets cache long, dynamic content short. I tune these in deployments to cut load.

questions.question: What is a cookie and how do cookies work in HTTP?
questions.answer: A cookie is a small piece of data the server sets via `Set-Cookie`, stored by the browser and sent back on subsequent requests to that domain. It enables state on stateless HTTP — sessions, preferences, tracking. Attributes matter: `HttpOnly` (not readable by JS — safer), `Secure` (HTTPS only), `SameSite` (CSRF protection), expiry. In auth, httpOnly cookies are my preference over storing tokens in localStorage.

questions.question: What is a session?
questions.answer: A session is server-side state tied to a user, identified by a session ID in a cookie. The server stores session data (login state, cart) in memory or Redis. It's how servers remember users across stateless requests. Sessions are easy to revoke; the tradeoff is server-side storage. I've used both sessions and stateless JWT depending on scale needs.

questions.question: What is the difference between stateful and stateless protocols?
questions.answer: A stateful protocol keeps state between requests — the server remembers you (like a session-based app). Stateless means each request is independent and complete (like HTTP/REST by design). Stateless scales horizontally easily because any server can serve any request. My design default is stateless APIs with explicit tokens, sessions pushed to Redis when needed.

questions.question: What is the OSI transport layer responsible for?
questions.answer: The transport layer (layer 4) provides end-to-end communication between applications — segmentation, reliability (TCP), flow control, and port addressing. It's where TCP and UDP live. Understanding it as the 'delivery layer' between the network (routing) and application (content) clarifies what errors at each layer mean.

questions.question: What is latency and bandwidth, and how are they different?
questions.answer: Latency is the delay — how long data takes to travel (measured in ms). Bandwidth is the capacity — how much data can flow per second (Mbps/Gbps). A high-bandwidth but high-latency link (like a satellite) moves lots of data but slowly per round trip. Optimizing web apps means addressing both: fewer round trips reduce latency impact; smaller payloads need less bandwidth.

questions.question: What is a round trip time (RTT)?
questions.answer: RTT is the time for a packet to travel to a destination and back. It's the latency you feel per request. Lowering RTT — via CDNs, edge locations, keeping servers near users — directly improves perceived speed. Each additional request costs an RTT, which is why bundling and fewer requests matter.

questions.question: What is CDN in networking terms?
questions.answer: A CDN is a distributed network of edge servers that cache content close to users. Requests hit the nearest edge instead of the origin server, cutting RTT dramatically. It's both a performance and an architecture tool. For a global product, the frontend assets on a CDN is table stakes.

questions.question: What is HTTP/2 and how is it different from HTTP/1.1?
questions.answer: HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one connection, uses binary framing, header compression (HPACK), and server push. HTTP/1.1 opens multiple connections and suffers head-of-line blocking. The practical win: faster page loads, especially for many small resources. HTTP/3 goes further with QUIC over UDP. Modern servers enable HTTP/2 by default.

questions.question: What is WebSocket?
questions.answer: WebSocket is a protocol providing full-duplex, persistent communication over a single TCP connection — the server can push data without the client polling. Use cases: chat, live notifications, dashboards, real-time sync. It starts as an HTTP upgrade, then switches protocol. For real-time updates, WebSocket beats polling. My alternative for simpler cases is SSE (server-sent events) — one-way push over HTTP.

questions.question: What is the difference between WebSocket and SSE (Server-Sent Events)?
questions.answer: WebSocket is bidirectional — both sides send freely. SSE is one-way — server pushes to client over plain HTTP, with auto-reconnect and simpler implementation. For notifications and feeds, SSE is often enough and simpler; for interactive apps like chat, WebSocket is needed. My default: SSE unless bidirectional is required.

questions.question: What is long polling?
questions.answer: Long polling is a technique where the client requests, and the server holds the response open until there's data or a timeout — then the client immediately re-requests. It simulates push over HTTP but is inefficient and chatty. It was the pre-WebSocket way to do real-time. It's a good answer for 'how did real-time work before WebSockets.'

questions.question: What is a reverse proxy vs load balancer?
questions.answer: A reverse proxy forwards client requests to backend servers — it can also cache, compress, terminate TLS, and hide backend topology. A load balancer specifically distributes traffic across multiple servers for scale and availability. Nginx is often both. In my setups, Nginx terminates TLS and routes to app containers — that's reverse proxy; adding multiple app instances makes it a load balancer too.

questions.question: What is the difference between a firewall and a security group?
questions.answer: A firewall filters traffic based on rules — typically at network boundaries. In AWS, security groups are instance-level stateful filters — you allow specific ports from specific sources, and the cloud enforces them. Practically they're the same idea at different scopes. I lock EC2 instances to only 22/80/443 via security groups.

questions.question: What is SSH and how does it work?
questions.answer: SSH is a secure protocol for remote shell access, encrypted. It uses key pairs — the client authenticates with its private key against the server's authorized public key, and the server proves identity with its host key. I use SSH daily to manage Ubuntu servers, and I always disable password auth in favor of keys.

questions.question: What is a subnet and what is a VPC?
questions.answer: A subnet is a network segment of an IP range. A VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) is your isolated network in AWS — you define CIDR ranges, subnets, route tables, and gateways. Instances in a VPC get private IPs, and you control internet access via gateways. My deployments put app servers in subnets with controlled access. It's the foundation of cloud networking.

questions.question: What is the difference between HTTP request methods GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE?
questions.answer: GET retrieves (read-only, no body usually). POST creates or triggers an action (server decides the new resource's identity). PUT replaces a resource entirely (idempotent). PATCH applies a partial update. DELETE removes. The key interview points: idempotency — GET, PUT, DELETE, and HEAD should be idempotent; POST and PATCH are not guaranteed.

questions.question: What is idempotency in HTTP?
questions.answer: An operation is idempotent if repeating it produces the same result — no side effects multiplied. GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent by design; POST is not. This matters for retries: retrying a PUT safely overwrites with the same value, retrying a POST could duplicate an order. That's why payment APIs use idempotency keys. I designed the MSS Sales Order generation to be idempotent for the same reason.

questions.question: What is the difference between a URL, a URI, and a URN?
questions.answer: A URI is the umbrella term for identifying a resource. A URL locates it — scheme + host + path (https://example.com/page). A URN names it persistently (urn:isbn:...). So every URL is a URI, but not every URI is a URL. It's a precision question that shows you know the vocabulary precisely.

questions.question: What is a query string?
questions.answer: The query string is the part of a URL after `?` — `?page=2&sort=price` — used to pass parameters to the server, especially for GET requests. In APIs it's how filters, pagination, and sorting are passed. Servers parse it; I also validate it since it's user input.

questions.question: What is a path parameter vs a query parameter in REST?
questions.answer: A path parameter identifies a specific resource within the URL — `GET /users/42` (the 42). A query parameter filters or configures the request — `GET /users?role=admin`. Both are common in APIs. Path params for identity, query params for options. Mixing them up is a design smell.

questions.question: What is JSON and why is it the standard for APIs?
questions.answer: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a lightweight text format for structured data — objects and arrays, readable by humans and machines. It became the API standard because it's simple, language-agnostic, and maps naturally to programming structures. In all my APIs, JSON is the exchange format, validated with Pydantic or similar.

questions.question: What is XML and how does it differ from JSON?
questions.answer: XML is an older, verbose markup format for structured data with attributes and nested tags — used in SOAP, configs, and some legacy systems. JSON is compact and maps directly to code structures. XML has namespaces and schemas (XSD) that JSON lacks; JSON is the modern default for APIs. Interviewers often ask the REST-vs-SOAP angle: REST/JSON vs SOAP/XML.

questions.question: What is serialization?
questions.answer: Serialization converts an in-memory object into a storable or transmittable format — JSON, XML, bytes. Deserialization reverses it. It's the bridge between code objects and the network/disk. In Python, `json.dumps`/`loads`; in Java, Jackson/Gson. FastAPI does serialization automatically via Pydantic. Getting this right matters at every API boundary.

questions.question: What is the difference between client-server and peer-to-peer?
questions.answer: Client-server has a centralized server that serves multiple clients — the classic web model, easy to control and scale vertically. Peer-to-peer has equal nodes communicating directly — no central server, resilient and distributed, but hard to secure and manage. Web apps are client-server; my work is all in that model. Knowing P2P shows breadth.

questions.question: What is the Internet Protocol (IP)?
questions.answer: IP is the network-layer protocol responsible for addressing and routing packets across networks — it gets each packet to the right destination using IP addresses. It's best-effort: packets can be lost, so TCP (or apps) handle reliability on top. IP is the 'which street' layer of networking.

questions.question: What is a packet?
questions.answer: A packet is a unit of data transmitted over a network — headers with addressing/control info plus the payload. Networks break data into packets, route them independently, and reassemble at the destination. Understanding packets explains headers, MTU, and why large transfers are chunked. It's the atomic unit of network communication.

questions.question: What is an HTTP request header? Name common ones.
questions.answer: Headers carry metadata about the request — `Content-Type` (body format), `Authorization` (auth token), `Accept` (response format wanted), `User-Agent` (client), `Origin`/`Referer`, `Cookie`, `Cache-Control`, `Host`. Headers matter for security and correctness: CORS checks Origin, auth reads Authorization, content negotiation reads Accept. I set and read headers daily in API work.

questions.question: What is `Content-Type` and what is `application/json`?
questions.answer: `Content-Type` tells the server/client what format the body is in. `application/json` means the body is JSON. On responses it tells the client how to parse; on requests it tells the server how to interpret. If the client sends JSON but the server reads it as form data, nothing works. Mismatched content types are a common integration bug I've fixed.

questions.question: What is a status line in an HTTP response?
questions.answer: The status line is the first line of an HTTP response — protocol version, status code, and reason phrase: `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`. It's the fastest way to know what happened. Tools like curl show it immediately. It's the beginning of parsing any HTTP response.

questions.question: What is an application server vs a web server?
questions.answer: A web server serves static content and routes requests — Nginx, Apache. An application server runs your dynamic logic — your Python/Node/Java app. In practice the web server sits in front and proxies to the app server. Understanding the split helps architecture: static to Nginx, dynamic to the app. My deployments run exactly this way.

questions.question: What is Apache vs Nginx?
questions.answer: Both are web servers. Nginx is event-driven, handles high concurrency with low memory, excels as a reverse proxy and for static serving. Apache is module-based, highly configurable, with `.htaccess` per-directory config. Nginx is the modern choice for high-concurrency reverse proxy work; Apache persists in legacy and shared-hosting setups. I use Nginx.

questions.question: What is the difference between hosting and deployment?
questions.answer: Hosting is where the app lives — the infrastructure: a VPS, managed cloud, or PaaS. Deployment is the process of getting your code onto that infrastructure — build, ship, run, and manage releases. Hosting is the home; deployment is moving in. Both matter: good deployment practice on good hosting is what makes software reliable in production.

questions.question: What is the role of the Domain Name System in a deployment?
questions.answer: DNS connects your domain to your infrastructure — A records point to IPs, CNAMEs alias domains, MX for mail, TXT for verification. After deploying, DNS is how users find you. Getting records right — and waiting out propagation and TTLs — is a standard post-deploy step. I've pointed subdomains to EC2 with A records and to CDNs with CNAMEs.

questions.question: What is the difference between a static and a dynamic IP?
questions.answer: A static IP never changes — needed for servers, DNS stability, and services that accept connections. A dynamic IP changes — typical for home connections; the provider reassigns. Cloud instances can have both; elastic IPs in AWS are static public IPs you attach. For a public-facing server, static addressing is essential.

questions.question: What is the difference between wired and wireless networking? (concept)
questions.answer: Wired uses physical cables — reliable, fast, low interference. Wireless uses radio waves — convenient but subject to interference, range, and security concerns (encryption like WPA2/3 needed). For servers and datacenters, wired is standard; for users, wireless dominates. The interview angle is usually about understanding the tradeoffs, not trivia.

questions.question: What is a firewall rule?
questions.answer: A firewall rule defines what traffic is allowed or blocked — source, destination, port, protocol, and action (allow/deny). Rules combine into policies. On Ubuntu I use ufw; in AWS, security groups. A common misconfiguration: a port open to the world instead of a specific source. Firewall rules are the first thing I review when a service is unexpectedly public or unreachable.

questions.question: What is the `hosts` file and when is it used?
questions.answer: The hosts file maps hostnames to IPs locally, before DNS — `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` or `/etc/hosts`. It's used for local development overrides and blocking. I use it for testing domain behavior before DNS is set up. It overrides DNS, so a stale entry can cause 'why is this pointing at the old server' confusion.

questions.question: What is SSL termination and where does it happen?
questions.answer: SSL/TLS termination is decrypting HTTPS traffic at a point — typically the reverse proxy — so backend servers handle plain HTTP internally. The proxy holds the certificate and re-encrypts if needed. Benefits: one place for certificates and offloading encryption work. Nginx is my termination point, with a certificate issued via Let's Encrypt.

questions.question: What is the difference between an inbound and outbound firewall rule?
questions.answer: An inbound rule controls traffic coming to your server; an outbound rule controls traffic leaving. Often only inbound is locked down while outbound stays open. In AWS, security groups are stateful and both directions are considered. Locking inbound to only needed ports while leaving outbound open is the common secure default.

questions.question: What is a proxy server?
questions.answer: A proxy server sits between a client and the internet — forwarding requests on the client's behalf. It can cache, filter, anonymize, and control access. A forward proxy serves clients; a reverse proxy serves servers. Web proxies at work, Nginx as reverse proxy in deployments. The direction of the proxy — which side it represents — is the key distinction.

questions.question: What is a VPN and how does it work?
questions.answer: A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel between a device and a private network over the public internet — remote users appear on the corporate network. It protects traffic from snooping and grants network access. For servers, VPNs restrict admin access to trusted networks. It's a security tool for remote access and private connectivity.

questions.question: What is the difference between a LAN and a WAN?
questions.answer: LAN (Local Area Network) covers a small area — an office or building — with low latency and high speed. WAN (Wide Area Network) spans large distances — cities, countries — like the internet itself. Cloud VPCs are LAN-like; connecting regions is WAN-like. It's basic taxonomy that frames networking discussions.

questions.question: What is a MAC address?
questions.answer: A MAC address is the hardware address of a network interface — burned into the card, unique per device, used at the link layer for local communication. Unlike IP (logical, can change), MAC is physical and local. In ARP, MACs map to IPs on a LAN. Knowing the IP/MAC distinction is a foundational networking question.

questions.question: What is ARP?
questions.answer: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) maps an IP address to a MAC address on a local network — 'who has 192.168.1.5?' 'I do, here's my MAC.' It's how frames get delivered to the right device on a LAN. It's below the routing layer — IP gets you to the network, ARP gets the frame to the device.

questions.question: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
questions.answer: A hub broadcasts to all ports (dumb, obsolete). A switch forwards frames intelligently to the right port using MAC addresses (local, efficient). A router forwards packets between networks using IP addresses — the gateway to the internet. Switch connects devices within a network; router connects networks. This is a classic three-way comparison.

questions.question: What is a gateway?
questions.answer: A gateway is a node that connects different networks — typically your router, the exit point to the internet. In cloud terms, an internet gateway in a VPC provides outbound/inbound internet access. Your default route points at the gateway. When an instance 'has no internet,' the first suspect is gateway/routing configuration.

questions.question: What is bandwidth throttling and rate limiting?
questions.answer: Both limit traffic. Throttling caps speed or throughput — often by the network or provider. Rate limiting caps the number of requests in a window — an application-level control. Throttling is about speed; rate limiting is about count. Rate limiting protects APIs from abuse; I've configured it with express-rate-limit and Redis.

questions.question: What is the difference between a host and a node in networking?
questions.answer: A host is any device that sends or receives traffic — computers, phones, servers. A node is a broader term for any device on a network that can process traffic — hosts plus routers and switches. So every host is a node, but not every node is a host. The distinction matters for precise network diagrams.

questions.question: What is an endpoint in API terms?
questions.answer: An endpoint is a specific URL + method combination that performs a function — `POST /api/orders` is an endpoint. It's the contract your API exposes. Designing endpoints well — naming, methods, status codes — is API design. My APIs are organized around resource endpoints following REST conventions.

questions.question: What is the Python MRO (Method Resolution Order)?
questions.answer: MRO is the order in which Python looks up methods in a class hierarchy — critical for multiple inheritance. It follows the C3 linearization algorithm, ensuring consistency and that each class appears once. You inspect it with `ClassName.__mro__` or `ClassName.mro()`. When overriding with multiple inheritance, MRO determines which parent's method runs.

questions.question: What is the `__init__` vs `__new__` in Python?
questions.answer: `__new__` creates the instance — it's a static method that returns the new object. `__init__` initializes an already-created instance. So `__new__` runs first and is rarely overridden except for immutable types or singleton control. Most of the time you only write `__init__`. Interviewers like this distinction to check deep Python knowledge.

questions.question: What are dunder methods? Give examples.
questions.answer: Dunder (double underscore) methods define Python's behavior for operators and built-ins — `__str__` for string representation, `__repr__` for debugging representation, `__eq__`/`__lt__` for comparison, `__len__`, `__getitem__` for indexing, `__call__` to make objects callable. They're what make objects behave like language built-ins. I use `__str__`/`__repr__` and `__eq__` on model classes.

questions.question: What is the difference between `__str__` and `__repr__`?
questions.answer: `__repr__` is the unambiguous developer representation — meant for debugging, ideally showing how to recreate the object. `__str__` is the readable human representation — used by `print()` and `str()`. Rule: `__repr__` for developers, `__str__` for users; fallback is `__repr__` when `__str__` is missing. Good classes define both.

questions.question: What is a metaclass?
questions.answer: A metaclass is a class of a class — it controls how classes themselves are created, like a class is a template for objects. `type` is the default metaclass. Metaclasses let you customize class creation — adding methods, validating definitions. They're powerful but rarely needed; frameworks use them. I know them but reach for simpler tools like decorators first.

questions.question: What is the `contextlib` module and what is `contextmanager`?
questions.answer: `contextlib` provides tools for working with context managers. `@contextmanager` turns a generator function into a context manager — `yield` in the middle, and code after yield runs on exit. It's how I write clean `with` blocks for DB sessions and temporary state without writing a full class.

questions.question: What is `__enter__` and `__exit__`?
questions.answer: They're the methods that make an object a context manager — `__enter__` sets up and returns the resource used in `with`, `__exit__` cleans up and handles exceptions (returning True suppresses them). The `with` statement guarantees `__exit__` runs. For database connections I rely on this so sessions always close.

questions.question: What is `functools.lru_cache`?
questions.answer: `lru_cache` caches a function's results based on arguments — repeated calls with the same args hit the cache. It's a one-line memoization: `@lru_cache(maxsize=128)`. It's great for pure, expensive functions. The gotcha: args must be hashable, and cached results go stale if the underlying data changes — so I only use it for genuinely pure computations.

questions.question: What is `functools.wraps` and why is it important in decorators?
questions.answer: `functools.wraps` copies the wrapped function's metadata (name, docstring, signature) onto the wrapper. Without it, a decorated function loses its name and docstring, breaking introspection and debugging. It's the first thing you add to any real decorator. I use it in every decorator I write for API logging and validation.

questions.question: What is the `typing` module and why is type hinting useful?
questions.answer: The `typing` module provides type hints — `List[int]`, `Optional[str]`, `Dict[str, int]`, `Union`, `Callable`. Type hints make code self-documenting, enable static analysis with mypy, and give IDEs autocomplete. At runtime they're ignored unless you use `Annotated` with validators. FastAPI uses them for validation and docs. I type-hint every function in my Python code.

questions.question: What is `Optional` vs `Union` in typing?
questions.answer: `Optional[X]` is shorthand for `X | None` — the value is either X or None. `Union[X, Y]` means the value can be X or Y. So `Optional[int]` = `Union[int, None]`. Modern Python also allows `int | None` syntax (3.10+). I use Optional for nullable fields and Union for genuinely multi-type values.

questions.question: What is a dataclass in Python?
questions.answer: `@dataclass` automatically generates `__init__`, `__repr__`, `__eq__`, and more from annotated fields — removing boilerplate for data-holding classes. You can freeze them (immutable), add defaults, and order them. I use dataclasses for DTOs and config objects — they read clearly and behave predictably.

questions.question: What is `__slots__` and when should you use it?
questions.answer: `__slots__` declares a fixed set of instance attributes, preventing `__dict__` and reducing memory per instance — significant for many instances. It also prevents accidentally adding attributes. I'd use it for high-volume objects, but it's an optimization with constraints (no arbitrary attributes, careful with inheritance).

questions.question: What is the `collections` module? Name useful classes.
questions.answer: `collections` provides specialized containers: `deque` (fast appends/pops both ends — great queue), `Counter` (count elements), `defaultdict` (auto-default missing keys), `OrderedDict` (ordered, though dicts are now ordered), `namedtuple` (lightweight immutable records). I use `Counter` for frequency counts and `defaultdict` for grouping — both are bread-and-butter.

questions.question: What is `namedtuple` and when is it better than a tuple?
questions.answer: `namedtuple` creates tuple subclasses with named fields — `Point(x=1, y=2)`. Fields are accessible by name, and it's immutable like a tuple. It's better than a plain tuple when position gets confusing. I use it for lightweight, immutable records where a full class is overkill.

questions.question: What is the `itertools` module?
questions.answer: `itertools` provides fast, memory-efficient iteration tools: `chain` (combine iterables), `product` (cartesian product), `combinations`/`permutations`, `groupby`, `cycle`, `count`, and `islice`. They're lazy and composable. For processing large data without loading everything, itertools is the standard toolkit.

questions.question: What is a lambda and where is it appropriate?
questions.answer: A lambda is an anonymous one-line function — `lambda x: x * 2`. It's appropriate as a short inline function for `sorted(key=...)`, `filter`, `map`. For anything non-trivial it hurts readability — I convert to a named function. The line between lambda-ok and lambda-too-far is roughly 'fits on one line and is obvious.'

questions.question: What is the difference between `map`, `filter`, and `reduce`?
questions.answer: `map` applies a function to every element and returns a new iterable. `filter` keeps elements for which a predicate returns true. `reduce` (in `functools`) accumulates elements into a single value — like sum. List comprehensions cover map/filter in clearer syntax; reduce is the one with no direct comprehension equivalent. I use comprehensions mostly, reduce for genuine accumulation.

questions.question: What is a list comprehension and when is it better than a for loop?
questions.answer: A list comprehension builds a list in one expression — `[x * 2 for x in items if x > 0]`. It's better when the operation is a simple transformation or filter — faster and clearer. A for loop is better when you need multiple statements, side effects, or complex logic. Comprehensions can get unreadable when nested — then I switch back to loops.

questions.question: What is a generator expression?
questions.answer: A generator expression is a list-comprehension syntax that produces a lazy iterator instead of a list — `(x * 2 for x in items)`. It doesn't build the whole collection in memory, so it's for large streams. It differs from a generator function (which uses `yield`). Both save memory; I use generator expressions for big data and one-off iteration.

questions.question: What is the difference between `deepcopy` and `copy` with nested structures?
questions.answer: `copy.copy` creates a shallow copy — the outer object is new, but nested objects are shared references. `copy.deepcopy` recursively copies everything, so nothing is shared. For nested structures like a list of dicts, shallow copy shares the inner dicts — mutating them affects the original. I use deepcopy when I need true independence.

questions.question: What is the `json` module and common pitfalls?
questions.answer: The `json` module serializes/deserializes JSON — `dumps`/`loads`, with `ensure_ascii`, `indent`, `sort_keys` options. Pitfalls: `None` → `null`, tuples → arrays (can't round-trip), `datetime` isn't JSON-serializable by default, and non-string dict keys become strings. I handle datetime with a custom encoder or ISO strings.

questions.question: What is the `os` module vs `pathlib`?
questions.answer: `os` provides OS-level functions — file operations, environment, process info. `pathlib` is the modern object-oriented path handling — `Path('a/b')`, with operators like `/` for joining and methods like `.exists()`, `.glob()`. I prefer pathlib for any path work; `os` for env vars and process-level things.

questions.question: What is the difference between `open('r')`, `open('rb')`, and encoding?
questions.answer: `open('r')` reads text — with the default or specified encoding, decoding bytes to strings. `open('rb')` reads raw bytes without decoding. Text mode matters for cross-platform line endings and encoding errors. When dealing with binary data or unknown encodings, binary mode is safer. I specify `encoding='utf-8'` explicitly to avoid platform differences.

questions.question: What is the `re` module and what are common patterns?
questions.answer: `re` is Python's regular expression module — `search`, `match`, `findall`, `sub`, `split`, with compiled patterns via `re.compile`. Common patterns: `\d+`, `[a-z]+`, `^...$` anchors, groups `(...)`, and named groups `(?P<name>...)`. I use it for validation and parsing — like extracting structured data from resumes and logs.

questions.question: What is the difference between `search` and `match` in re?
questions.answer: `re.match` matches only at the beginning of the string; `re.search` finds the pattern anywhere. So `re.match('cat', 'a cat')` fails but `re.search` succeeds. When you want 'contains,' use search; when you want 'starts with,' use match. It's a small distinction that causes real bugs.

questions.question: What is `subprocess` and how do you run shell commands from Python?
questions.answer: `subprocess` runs external programs from Python — `subprocess.run(['git', 'status'], capture_output=True, text=True)` is the modern way (shell=False by default, avoiding injection). I use it for deployment automation and invoking tools. Always prefer a list of args over a shell string when possible.

questions.question: What is the `sys` module used for?
questions.answer: `sys` provides interpreter-level access: `sys.argv` (command-line args), `sys.path` (import path), `sys.stdout/stderr`, `sys.exit()`, `sys.getrecursionlimit()`. It's the module for program-to-interpreter communication. In CLI tools I read args from `sys.argv` or prefer `argparse` for structured parsing.

questions.question: What is the difference between `import module` and `from module import x`?
questions.answer: `import module` imports the whole module under its name — `module.func()`. `from module import x` imports the specific name directly — `func()`. The latter can cause name collisions and makes the source less obvious. Both fine; I prefer explicit imports of what I use and avoid `import *`.

questions.question: What is `__name__ == '__main__'` and why use it?
questions.answer: It's the idiom to run code only when the file is executed directly, not when imported: `if __name__ == '__main__': main()`. Imported modules get `__name__` as their module name; the executed script gets `'__main__'`. It makes scripts importable and testable. Every CLI script I write uses it.

questions.question: What is a wheel vs a source distribution in packaging?
questions.answer: A source distribution (sdist) is the raw source — `tar.gz` — requiring build on install. A wheel is a pre-built binary package — `.whl` — installs fast without compilation. Wheels are the modern standard for distributing Python packages. When I package internal tools, building wheels makes installs reliable and quick.

questions.question: What is `pip freeze` and how do you manage dependencies?
questions.answer: `pip freeze` lists installed packages with versions — the raw snapshot for requirements.txt. The modern approach is a lockfile or `pip-tools` for reproducible builds, since bare `pip install` ranges can drift. For my projects I pin exact versions or use lockfiles so environments match.

questions.question: What is the difference between a virtual environment and `pip install` globally?
questions.answer: A virtual environment isolates dependencies per project — a local Python with its own site-packages. Installing globally pollutes the system and causes version conflicts between projects. I create a venv for every project — `python -m venv .venv` — and activate it. It's non-negotiable for sane dependency management.

questions.question: What is the `logging` module and why is it better than `print`?
questions.answer: The `logging` module provides leveled, configurable, timestamped logging — debug/info/warning/error, handlers to console and files, formatters, and propagation. `print` has no levels, no structured output, and pollutes stdout. In production code I log with context — request IDs, errors with stack traces — so issues are diagnosable.

questions.question: What is structured logging?
questions.answer: Structured logging emits logs as structured data — JSON with keys — instead of free text: `{"level": "error", "event": "payment_failed", "order_id": 42}`. It makes logs searchable and parseable by tools like ELK. Correlation IDs tie a request across services. I prefer structured logs in any system I operate.

questions.question: What is the difference between `asyncio`, `threading`, and `multiprocessing`?
questions.answer: `asyncio` is cooperative concurrency — single thread, event loop, async/await — best for I/O-bound with many tasks. `threading` uses OS threads — also I/O-bound, with GIL limits for CPU work. `multiprocessing` runs separate processes — true parallelism for CPU-bound. My choice: asyncio for network-heavy code, multiprocessing for number crunching.

questions.question: What is `async` and `await` in Python?
questions.answer: `async def` declares a coroutine; `await` suspends it until an awaited coroutine completes, letting the event loop run other tasks meanwhile. It's the modern way to write non-blocking concurrent I/O. FastAPI supports async endpoints; SQLAlchemy has async support. I use async for I/O-heavy endpoints so one slow call doesn't block others.

questions.question: What is the `asyncio` event loop?
questions.answer: The event loop is the core of asyncio — it runs coroutines, watches I/O, and schedules callbacks, all in one thread. Awaiting suspends, the loop moves on, and resumes when the awaited operation is ready. It's how Python gets concurrency without threads for I/O. Understanding it explains why blocking calls inside async code are a bug.

questions.question: What is the difference between a coroutine and a thread?
questions.answer: A coroutine is a function that can suspend and resume cooperatively within one thread — lightweight, explicit suspension points (await). A thread is an OS-level unit that the kernel schedules preemptively — heavier, can be interrupted anywhere. Coroutines scale to thousands easily; threads have overhead. For network-heavy apps, coroutines are my default.

questions.question: What is the `datetime` module and timezone handling?
questions.answer: `datetime` provides dates, times, and timedeltas. Timezone handling: always work in UTC internally (`datetime.now(timezone.utc)`), attach timezone to stored times, convert to local only for display. Naive datetimes cause the classic 'off by some hours' bug. For complex scheduling I use `pytz` or `zoneinfo`. In ERP attendance work, timezone correctness was essential.

questions.question: What are the new features in ES6+ (ES2015+) and later?
questions.answer: ES6 brought let/const, arrow functions, template literals, destructuring, classes, modules, promises, default params, and spread/rest. Later additions: async/await (ES2017), object spread, optional chaining `?.` and nullish coalescing `??` (ES2020), private class fields `#`, and modern array methods. I use most of these daily — they made JavaScript far more pleasant to write.

questions.question: What is the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)?
questions.answer: TDZ is the period where a `let` or `const` variable exists but can't be accessed — from the start of the scope to the declaration line. Accessing it throws a ReferenceError. Unlike `var` (hoisted as undefined), `let`/`const` stay in the TDZ until initialized. It prevents using variables before they're declared — a strictness that catches bugs.

questions.question: What is destructuring and give examples?
questions.answer: Destructuring unpacks values from arrays or objects into variables: `const { name, age } = user` and `const [first, second] = items`. It also works with defaults, renaming, and nested values. It's cleaner than dot-chain access, especially for API responses. I destructure props and state constantly in Angular and Vue code.

questions.question: What is optional chaining (`?.`)?
questions.answer: `?.` safely accesses nested properties without throwing when an intermediate is null/undefined — `user?.address?.city` returns undefined instead of crashing. It short-circuits: if a link is missing, the rest isn't evaluated. It replaces the old `user && user.address && user.address.city` chains. I use it whenever I handle data that may be incomplete, like API responses.

questions.question: What is nullish coalescing (`??`)?
questions.answer: `??` returns the right side only when the left is null or undefined — not for other falsy values like `0` or `''`. That's the key difference from `||`, which treats all falsy values as absent. So `count ?? 10` keeps a legitimate 0; `count || 10` would replace it. I use `??` for defaults with meaningful falsy values.

questions.question: What is the difference between `??` and `||`?
questions.answer: `||` returns the right operand when the left is falsy — 0, '', false, null, undefined, NaN. `??` returns the right only for null/undefined. So `??` is the safer default for numeric or string values where 0 or '' are meaningful. Using the wrong one is a subtle but real bug — a price of 0 becoming the default price.

questions.question: What are arrow functions and how do they differ from regular functions?
questions.answer: Arrow functions are concise: `const f = (x) => x * 2`. Key differences: no own `this` (lexical), no `arguments` object, can't be constructors, no `prototype`, and can't be generators with `function*` syntax. The lexical `this` is the big one — it captures the surrounding scope, which solves callback context problems. I default to arrows for callbacks and short functions.

questions.question: Why should arrow functions not always be used as methods?
questions.answer: Because they don't have their own `this` — using an arrow as an object method means `this` refers to the outer scope, not the object. So `obj.method = () => this.x` won't see `obj`. Also, arrow functions can't be used as constructors. The rule: arrows for callbacks and short functions, regular functions for methods and constructors.

questions.question: What is a Promise and what are its states?
questions.answer: A Promise represents an eventual result of an async operation. States: pending (initial), fulfilled (resolved with a value), rejected (failed with a reason), and settled (fulfilled or rejected — final). You consume with `.then`, `.catch`, `.finally`, or await. Understanding states matters for debugging 'is this pending forever?' — usually a promise that never settles.

questions.question: What is Promise chaining and how does it work?
questions.answer: Promise chaining sequences async steps: `.then()` returns a new promise, so you can chain — `fetchUser().then(format).then(render)`. Each step receives the previous result. Errors propagate down to the nearest `.catch`. It replaces callback nesting. I prefer async/await for readability, but chaining is still common in utility code.

questions.question: What is `Promise.all` vs `Promise.race` vs `Promise.allSettled`?
questions.answer: `all` waits for all to resolve (rejects fast if any rejects). `race` resolves/rejects with the first settled promise. `allSettled` waits for all, reporting each as fulfilled or rejected without failing. So: all for parallel-dependency, allSettled for parallel-when-you-can-handle-failures, race for timeouts and first-wins. I use allSettled when loading data where some sources may fail gracefully.

questions.question: What is `Promise.any`?
questions.answer: `Promise.any` resolves with the first promise that fulfills, ignoring rejections — only rejects if ALL reject (with AggregateError). It's for 'give me the first successful one' scenarios, like trying multiple CDN endpoints. It complements race (which settles on first regardless of outcome) and all (which needs all). Modern ES2021 addition.

questions.question: What is async/await and how does it relate to promises?
questions.answer: async/await is syntactic sugar over promises — an async function returns a promise, and await pauses execution until a promise settles, unwrapping the value or throwing the error. It reads like synchronous code and error-handles with try/catch. Under the hood it's still promises — `await promise` is just a `.then`. I use it as my primary async pattern.

questions.question: What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous code?
questions.answer: Synchronous code runs top-to-bottom, blocking until each operation finishes. Asynchronous code defers operations — the program continues while I/O happens and handles the result via callbacks/promises when ready. Async is essential for web I/O — a sync fetch would freeze the UI. JavaScript's event loop makes async the norm.

questions.question: What is a callback and what is callback hell?
questions.answer: A callback is a function passed to be called later, usually after an async operation. Callback hell is deeply nested callbacks where each depends on the previous — unreadable, unmaintainable, hard to handle errors. Fixes: promises, async/await, and named functions instead of anonymous nesting. Recognizing callback hell and refactoring it is a common interview scenario.

questions.question: What is the event loop, microtasks, and macrotasks?
questions.answer: The event loop processes tasks in phases. After each macrotask (setTimeout, I/O, events), it drains the entire microtask queue (promise callbacks, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver) before the next macrotask. So promise callbacks run before the next timer callback. Understanding this ordering explains why `Promise.resolve().then(...)` runs before a setTimeout even if declared after.

questions.question: What is the order of `console.log` execution with setTimeout and promises?
questions.answer: Consider: synchronous logs first; then all microtasks (promises) in order; then macrotasks (setTimeout) by timer. So a sync log, a promise .then, and a setTimeout will run: sync first, then .then, then setTimeout. It's the event loop's microtask-before-macrotask rule. I've used this in interviews to show real understanding.

questions.question: What is `setTimeout` vs `setInterval` vs `setImmediate` vs `requestAnimationFrame`?
questions.answer: setTimeout runs once after a delay; setInterval repeats every interval; setImmediate (Node) runs after the current I/O phase; requestAnimationFrame runs before the next repaint (browser). For animations use rAF (synced to display), for one-off delays setTimeout, for periodic tasks setInterval (careful with overlap), and setImmediate for Node ordering. In Node, setImmediate vs setTimeout(0) ordering depends on phase.

questions.question: What is the `this` keyword in different contexts?
questions.answer: `this` depends on call context: in a regular function, it's the caller (or global in sloppy mode / undefined in strict); in a method, the object; in an arrow, the lexical scope; in a constructor, the new instance; with `.call`/`.apply`/`.bind`, whatever you pass. This is the most confusing part of JS for people — and arrows fixed the common cases.

questions.question: What is `bind`, `call`, and `apply`?
questions.answer: All three set `this`: `fn.call(obj, a, b)` invokes with arguments individually; `fn.apply(obj, [a, b])` with an array; `fn.bind(obj)` returns a new function permanently bound. bind is for pre-setting context (like event handlers); call/apply for one-off invocation. Modern code uses arrows instead, but knowing these is classic JS interview material.

questions.question: What is `prototype` and how does inheritance work in JS?
questions.answer: Every function has a `prototype` object, and instances inherit from it via the prototype chain — `obj.method` looks up the prototype chain if not on the object itself. `Object.create(proto)` and `class` (syntactic sugar over prototypes) use this. Unlike class-based languages, JS inheritance is delegation through a chain. Understanding it demystifies how objects share behavior.

questions.question: What is the difference between `class` and a constructor function?
questions.answer: A constructor function (`function Car() {}` + `new`) is the pre-ES6 way; `class` is modern syntax that does the same under the hood but cleaner — with `constructor`, `super`, static methods, and getters. Classes aren't a new paradigm, just nicer syntax over prototypes. I use classes for anything needing OOP structure, functions for stateless utilities.

questions.question: What is a `Proxy` object in JavaScript?
questions.answer: `Proxy` wraps an object and intercepts operations — get, set, has, deleteProperty — letting you add behavior like validation, logging, or reactivity. Vue 3's reactivity is built on Proxy. It's the modern metaprogramming tool. Use: observing changes, access control, virtualized properties. Powerful but can confuse debugging, so use deliberately.

questions.question: What is `Reflect` and how does it relate to Proxy?
questions.answer: `Reflect` provides the default implementations of object operations as functions — `Reflect.get`, `Reflect.set`. In Proxy traps, calling `Reflect.set(target, prop, value)` performs the default behavior, letting you intercept without breaking semantics. `Reflect` also fixes subtle issues like `delete` returning booleans. Vue's reactivity uses Proxy + Reflect together.

questions.question: What is `WeakMap` and `WeakSet`?
questions.answer: A WeakMap holds key-value pairs where keys are objects and references are weak — they don't prevent garbage collection when the key object is otherwise unreachable. Use: private data per object, caching, metadata. The catch: no iteration or size. WeakSet is the analogous set. I use WeakMap for per-instance caches that shouldn't leak memory.

questions.question: What is a `Set` vs a `Map`?
questions.answer: A Set stores unique values; a Map stores key-value pairs (any type keys). Both have O(1) average lookups. Use Set for deduplication and membership, Map when you need arbitrary key-value associations. In Vue, a reactive Map/Set tracks collections. `Array.from(new Set(arr))` is my dedup one-liner.

questions.question: What is `Symbol` and when do you use it?
questions.answer: A Symbol is a unique, immutable primitive — `Symbol('desc')` is never equal to another Symbol. Uses: object keys that can't collide, hidden metadata, and well-known symbols like `Symbol.iterator`. I use Symbol.iterator to make objects iterable. Symbols are niche but the iterator protocol depends on them.

questions.question: What is the Iterator protocol and `Symbol.iterator`?
questions.answer: The iterator protocol defines how objects produce sequences: an object with a `[Symbol.iterator]()` method returning an iterator with `.next()` that yields `{value, done}`. Arrays, strings, Maps are iterable. `for...of` uses it. Generators implement it elegantly. Understanding it explains spread, destructuring, and for...of.

questions.question: What is a generator function in JavaScript?
questions.answer: A generator (`function*`) is a function that can pause and resume — it yields values, and each `.next()` resumes until the next yield. It's lazy and stateful. Use: producing infinite sequences, custom iterators, pausing async flows (via async generators). Generators are the foundation of how some state machines and async libraries work.

questions.question: What is `async` iterator and `for await...of`?
questions.answer: An async iterator yields promises — `for await (const chunk of stream)` awaits each. It's for consuming async streams, like reading a file in chunks or paginated API data. Async generators (`async function*`) produce them. I'd use it for streaming large data without loading everything.

questions.question: What is `module.exports` vs `export default`?
questions.answer: `module.exports` is CommonJS (Node) — `module.exports = { ... }`, imported with `require`. `export default` is ES modules — imported with `import x from`. ES modules are static (enabling tree shaking) and the standard; CommonJS is still in Node. In Frappe/Node server code I've worked with CommonJS; in frontend, ES modules.

questions.question: What is a dynamic import?
questions.answer: Dynamic import loads a module at runtime: `const mod = await import('./heavy.js')`. It enables code splitting — heavy modules load only when needed. I use it for route-level lazy loading and on-demand features. It returns a promise, so it works with async/await. It's the modern replacement for `require`-on-demand patterns.

questions.question: What is `Intl` and how does it help with internationalization?
questions.answer: `Intl` provides locale-aware formatting: `Intl.NumberFormat`, `Intl.DateTimeFormat`, `Intl.RelativeTimeFormat`, `Intl.Collator`. It handles number/date/currency formatting per locale without manual logic. For i18n, Intl is the built-in foundation. I'd use it for currency and date display in multi-locale apps.

questions.question: What is the difference between `toLocaleString` and custom formatting?
questions.answer: `toLocaleString` delegates formatting to the runtime's Intl implementation per locale — handles currency, dates, and number grouping correctly. Custom formatting is manual string logic you own — flexible but easy to get wrong per locale. For production i18n, Intl-based formatting beats hand-rolled for correctness.

questions.question: What is a TypedArray and when is it used?
questions.answer: TypedArrays are views over binary data — `Uint8Array`, `Float64Array`, etc., used for WebGL, audio, files, and anything performance-sensitive with binary. They work with ArrayBuffer and are what `Buffer` in Node and Web APIs expose. For handling binary files efficiently, TypedArrays are the tool.

questions.question: What is the `structuredClone` function?
questions.answer: `structuredClone` deeply clones objects — including Date, Map, Set, typed arrays — which JSON.parse(JSON.stringify()) can't handle. It's the modern deep clone. Limitations: can't clone functions, DOM nodes, or symbols as keys. I use it for duplicating complex state safely instead of JSON hacks.

questions.question: What is `Object.freeze` vs `Object.seal`?
questions.answer: `freeze` makes an object immutable — no property changes, additions, or deletions. `seal` prevents adding/removing properties but existing ones can still be modified. Both are shallow. freeze is useful for constants; seal for 'fixed shape but mutable values.' They're defense-in-depth, not real immutability.

questions.question: What is the difference between `deep` and `shallow` equality in JS objects?
questions.answer: Shallow equality compares references for objects — two different objects with identical content aren't equal. Deep equality compares contents recursively — no built-in, so you write it or use a library (lodash isEqual). Reference comparison is fast; deep equality is correct for value semantics. Frameworks rely on this: changing a ref triggers updates.

questions.question: What is memoization and how do you do it in JS?
questions.answer: Memoization caches function results by arguments so repeated calls skip recomputation. In JS: a Map keyed by args, or `useMemo` in React. It's for pure, expensive functions. The tradeoff is memory and stale results. I use memoization for expensive derivations in components.

questions.question: What is debouncing and throttling? Give examples.
questions.answer: Debouncing delays a function until a quiet period — 'run after 300ms of no input' — for search-as-you-type. Throttling limits execution to once per interval — 'at most once per second' — for scroll/resize handlers. Debounce waits for the pause; throttle caps the rate. I've used both for input handling and resize listeners.

questions.question: How do you implement a debounce in JavaScript?
questions.answer: The pattern: on each call, clear the previous timer and set a new one — only the final call (after the quiet period) runs. `return function(...args) { clearTimeout(t); t = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), wait); }`. I've written debounce for search inputs and form auto-save.

questions.question: What is `AbortController` and how do you cancel a fetch?
questions.answer: `AbortController` provides a signal you pass to fetch; calling `.abort()` cancels it, triggering an AbortError. It's how you cancel requests on unmount, timeouts, or user cancellation. I use it to cancel stale requests when components unmount, preventing race conditions where an old response overwrites new data.

questions.question: What is the difference between `fetch` and `XMLHttpRequest`?
questions.answer: `fetch` is the modern promise-based API — cleaner, streaming support, works in workers, and uses ReadableStream for bodies. `XMLHttpRequest` is the legacy callback-based API with more verbose handling. fetch is the standard; XHR only remains for specialized cases like progress events. All my frontend HTTP uses fetch or an HTTP client built on it.

questions.question: What is `FormData` and when do you use it?
questions.answer: `FormData` builds form payloads for submission — it encodes files and fields for `multipart/form-data`. It's the way to upload files via fetch. I use it for file uploads and complex form submissions in Angular/Vue apps. It pairs with `fetch` bodies directly.

questions.question: What is `URLSearchParams`?
questions.answer: `URLSearchParams` manipulates query strings — create, append, get, set, delete, toString. It builds query parameters correctly (URL-encoding) instead of string concatenation. I use it for API query building — filters and pagination — and parsing `location.search`. It's the correct tool for query strings.

questions.question: What is React and how does it differ from Angular?
questions.answer: React is a library for building UIs — you compose components, manage state, and let React update the DOM efficiently via the virtual DOM. Angular is a full framework — it includes routing, DI, forms, HTTP, and opinionated structure. React gives freedom (you pick libraries); Angular gives batteries. My resume leans Angular/Vue, but I've used React for the Resume Lens tool, so I can compare them honestly.

questions.question: What is JSX?
questions.answer:
JSX is JavaScript with HTML-like syntax — `const el =

Hi

` — that compiles to `React.createElement` calls. It makes component markup readable. JSX isn't HTML: `class` becomes `className`, attributes are camelCase, and you embed expressions with `{}`. Browsers can't run it directly — a build step transforms it.

questions.question: What is the virtual DOM and how does it work?
questions.answer: The virtual DOM is an in-memory representation of the UI. When state changes, React builds a new virtual tree, diffs it against the previous one (reconciliation), and applies the minimal changes to the real DOM. This minimizes expensive real-DOM mutations. Vue does the same; Angular uses its own change detection. The diffing strategy — keys and tree comparison — is what makes it fast.

questions.question: What is reconciliation and how do keys help?
questions.answer: Reconciliation is React's diffing algorithm — comparing old and new element trees to figure out minimal updates. Keys let React identify which list items changed rather than re-rendering all of them. Using stable, unique keys (like an id) is critical; using the index breaks identity when the list reorders. The same key discipline applies in Vue's `v-for`.

questions.question: What is the difference between the Shadow DOM and the Virtual DOM?
questions.answer: The Shadow DOM is a browser feature for encapsulating styles and markup within a component — real DOM scoping (used by web components). The Virtual DOM is a JavaScript-level optimization that diffs trees and updates the real DOM efficiently. Shadow DOM is about encapsulation; Virtual DOM is about performance. They solve different problems.

questions.question: What are React hooks and why were they introduced?
questions.answer: Hooks let functional components use state and lifecycle behavior — `useState`, `useEffect`, `useContext`, `useMemo`, `useRef`. They were introduced to remove the class/function split, make stateful logic reusable (custom hooks), and avoid class boilerplate and `this` confusion. Hooks are the modern way to write React.

questions.question: What is `useState` and how does it work?
questions.answer: `useState` declares state in a functional component: `const [count, setCount] = useState(0)`. It returns the current value and a setter that triggers a re-render when called. The setter accepts a value or an updater function. Unlike class `this.state`, each call is scoped to the component. State changes are what drive React's re-renders.

questions.question: What is `useEffect` and when does it run?
questions.answer: `useEffect` runs side effects — fetching data, subscriptions, timers — after render. With no dependency array it runs after every render; with `[]` once after mount; with `[deps]` when deps change. Cleanup functions run before the next effect and on unmount. Effect dependency bugs — missing deps causing stale closures or infinite loops — are the most common React issues.

questions.question: What is `useRef` and what is it for?
questions.answer: `useRef` holds a mutable value that persists across renders without triggering re-renders — `useRef(initial)`. Uses: referencing DOM elements, storing mutable values like intervals or previous values. Changing `.current` doesn't cause a re-render. It's the escape hatch for values that shouldn't trigger UI updates.

questions.question: What is `useMemo` vs `useCallback`?
questions.answer: `useMemo` memoizes a computed value — `useMemo(() => expensiveCalc(a), [a])`. `useCallback` memoizes a function reference — `useCallback(() => doSomething(a), [a])` — so children with memoized props don't re-render needlessly. useMemo for values, useCallback for functions. Both optimize performance but only where the computation or re-render cost justifies it.

questions.question: What is `useContext` and how does it help with state?
questions.answer: `useContext` reads context — a way to pass data to many components without prop drilling: a provider wraps the tree, and any descendant consumes it. It's built-in and fine for medium-scale state. For larger apps or frequent updates, context can cause broad re-renders, so a state library often complements it. I'd use context for theme/auth-type data.

questions.question: What is prop drilling and how do you avoid it?
questions.answer: Prop drilling is passing props through many intermediate components that don't use them, just to reach a deep consumer. Avoid with: context, a state library (Redux, Zustand), or component composition (passing the component itself). The refactor to composition or context removes the noise. It's a common smell and a favorite interview topic.

questions.question: What is Redux and how does it work?
questions.answer: Redux is a predictable state container: a single store holds the state; actions are dispatched; pure reducers compute the new state. Components select what they need and dispatch to change it. The discipline — unidirectional data flow, pure reducers, immutable updates — makes state changes traceable. For React apps I'd consider Redux Toolkit or Zustand depending on complexity.

questions.question: What is the difference between Redux and Context API?
questions.answer: Context is a built-in mechanism for passing data down the tree — simple, but updates cause all consumers to re-render and it's not built for frequent updates. Redux is a state management library with a store, devtools, time-travel, and performance optimizations via selectors. Use Context for simple shared data; Redux/Zustand for complex, frequently-updated global state.

questions.question: What is a higher-order component (HOC)?
questions.answer: A HOC is a function that takes a component and returns an enhanced component — `withAuth(Component)`. It's the old pattern for cross-cutting concerns (auth, logging, data loading) by wrapping. Hooks have largely replaced HOCs for these. Recognizing them matters for reading legacy code.

questions.question: What is a controlled vs uncontrolled component?
questions.answer: A controlled component's value comes from state and updates via handlers — React owns the input value. An uncontrolled component keeps its value in the DOM, read via a ref. Controlled is more predictable and testable; uncontrolled is simpler for one-off cases. React's docs recommend controlled for most forms.

questions.question: What is lifting state up?
questions.answer: Lifting state up means moving shared state to the nearest common ancestor so multiple children can read and update it through props. It's the React pattern for sibling communication. The child receives value + setter as props. When it gets unwieldy, that's the signal to introduce context or a store.

questions.question: What is React Router and why do you need it?
questions.answer: React Router is the standard routing library for SPAs — it maps URLs to components with `<Route>` and handles navigation, parameters, and history. It's needed because a single-page app still needs deep links and back/forward behavior. Angular and Vue have equivalent routers (Angular Router, Vue Router). I know the pattern across all three.

questions.question: What is lazy loading in React and how do you implement it?
questions.answer: Lazy loading defers component loading until needed — `const Lazy = React.lazy(() => import('./Lazy'))` wrapped in `<Suspense>`. It splits the bundle so the initial load is smaller. I use it for routes and heavy components. Combined with code splitting, it's one of the highest-impact React performance levers.

questions.question: What is a key in React lists and why does it matter?
questions.answer: A key gives each list item a stable identity so React can match items across re-renders — updating the changed ones instead of rebuilding all. Using the array index as a key breaks when items are added/removed/reordered because identity shifts. I use unique ids as keys. It's the same principle as `trackBy` in Angular and `:key` in Vue.

questions.question: What is `React.memo`?
questions.answer: `React.memo` memoizes a component so it only re-renders when its props change — a performance optimization for components that render often with unchanged props. It's shallow comparison by default. Combined with useCallback for function props, it prevents cascading re-renders. I'd apply it to leaf components in large lists.

questions.question: What is Server-Side Rendering (SSR) and how does React do it?
questions.answer: SSR renders React components to HTML on the server first, sending a complete page — better SEO and faster first paint — then hydrates on the client for interactivity. Frameworks like Next.js implement it. The tradeoff: more server work and hydration complexity. I've used SSR thinking for pages where SEO and load speed matter.

questions.question: What is Next.js and what are its main features?
questions.answer: Next.js is a React framework providing SSR/SSG, file-based routing, API routes, image optimization, and more.
