questions.answer: SQS is a queue — each message is consumed by one worker (point-to-point, pull-based). SNS is pub/sub — each message fans out to all subscribers (push-based). Queue for work distribution, topic for notifications. They combine: SNS → SQS to fan out to queues. The pull vs push model is the core distinction.

questions.question: What is CloudFormation / Infrastructure as Code?
questions.answer: CloudFormation defines AWS resources in YAML/JSON templates — infrastructure as code — so environments are reproducible, reviewable, and version-controlled. IaC removes 'works on my machine' from infrastructure. Terraform is the multi-cloud alternative. I value IaC because it makes deployments deterministic and auditable.

questions.question: What is the difference between CloudFormation and Terraform?
questions.answer: Both are IaC. CloudFormation is AWS-native — tight integration, but AWS-only. Terraform is multi-cloud (AWS, GCP, Azure) with its own state management and a broader community. Choose CloudFormation for pure AWS, Terraform for multi-cloud or to avoid lock-in. I know the concepts from both; Terraform's state file model is worth understanding.

questions.question: What is AWS cost management and how do you control costs?
questions.answer: Cost control: right-size instances (don't over-provision), use auto-scaling to run only what's needed, lifecycle S3 policies, reserved instances for steady loads, and alarms on spend. The 'forgot to stop an instance' bill is a rite of passage. I set budgets and use tags to track cost per project.

questions.question: What is containerization and why is it useful?
questions.answer: Containerization packages an app with its runtime and dependencies into a portable unit that runs consistently anywhere. It solves the 'works on my machine' problem, makes scaling replicas trivial, and isolates apps. Docker is the standard container runtime. It's the backbone of my deployments — I build once, run anywhere.

questions.question: What is the difference between a container and an image?
questions.answer: An image is the immutable template — the filesystem snapshot with the app and config. A container is a running instance of an image — with its own writable layer and lifecycle. You can run many containers from one image. The image is the recipe; the container is the dish being served.

questions.question: What is a Docker image layer?
questions.answer: Image layers are the incremental filesystem changes that compose an image — each instruction (RUN, COPY) adds a layer, and layers are cached and shared. Rebuilding with unchanged layers is fast (cache hits). The final image is the stack of layers. Multi-stage builds drop unneeded layers. Layer caching is why Docker builds are so fast after small changes.

questions.question: What is the Dockerfile and give common instructions?
questions.answer: The Dockerfile is the build recipe: FROM (base), WORKDIR, COPY/ADD (files), RUN (build commands), ENV, EXPOSE (document ports), VOLUME, CMD/ENTRYPOINT (startup). Order matters for caching — put stable instructions first so frequent changes don't invalidate the cache. I keep images small and layer-ordered for fast builds.

questions.question: What is the difference between `CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT`?
questions.answer: `ENTRYPOINT` is the fixed command that always runs; `CMD` provides default arguments (or the default command) that can be overridden. Combined, ENTRYPOINT sets the executable and CMD the default args. If you want users to override the command, use CMD; for a fixed entry, ENTRYPOINT. It's a common Docker interview question.

questions.question: What is a multi-stage build and why use it?
questions.answer: A multi-stage build uses multiple FROM statements — compile in one stage, copy only artifacts to a slim final stage. The result: production images without build tools, much smaller and safer. Example: build a Node/Go app, then copy the binary to a runtime image. I use multi-stage builds to cut image size significantly.

questions.question: What is Docker Compose and when would you use it?
questions.answer: Docker Compose defines multi-container apps in a YAML file — services, networks, volumes, environment — and manages them together with `docker compose up`. It's for local development and single-host deployments. I use it to run app + database + Redis + Nginx together reproducibly. For multi-host orchestration, Kubernetes takes over.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Docker volume and a bind mount?
questions.answer: A volume is Docker-managed storage in its own directory — portable, recommended for persistent data, easy to back up. A bind mount maps a host directory directly — handy for dev (live code) but less isolated. Volumes are the right default for databases and persistent data; bind mounts for development workflows.

questions.question: What is Docker networking?
questions.answer: Docker networks connect containers — bridge (default, isolated on one host, containers talk by name), host (share host network), overlay (across hosts in Swarm). Containers on the same bridge network resolve each other by service name. I use networks so the app reaches the DB and Redis by name, not IP.

questions.question: What is `docker-compose.yml`'s role in a deployment?
questions.answer: It's the deployment definition for a single host — services with images, ports, volumes, env, and dependencies. It makes deployments reproducible with one file. For a small app, compose IS the deployment. It's the stepping stone to orchestrators for multi-host scale.

questions.question: What is container orchestration?
questions.answer: Orchestration manages containers at scale — deployment, scaling, networking, service discovery, health checks, and updates. Kubernetes is the standard orchestrator; Docker Swarm and ECS are alternatives. Orchestration is what makes containers a platform, not just packaging.

questions.question: What is Kubernetes (K8s) and its core concepts?
questions.answer: Kubernetes orchestrates containerized apps across a cluster. Core concepts: Pods (smallest unit — one or more containers), Deployments (desired state of replicas), Services (stable network access), ConfigMaps/Secrets (config), Ingress (HTTP routing), and Nodes (cluster machines). It's the industry standard for container platforms. I know the concepts and use Docker-focused stacks, with K8s as the scale-up path.

questions.question: What is a Pod in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit — one or more containers sharing network and storage, scheduled together on a node. Containers in a pod share localhost and volumes. Deployments manage pods. It's the atom of K8s scheduling. Understanding pods explains how containers are grouped in the cluster.

questions.question: What is a Kubernetes Deployment?
questions.answer: A Deployment declares the desired state — how many replicas of a pod, which image, update strategy. The controller works to make reality match: rolls out new versions, rolls back on failure, and maintains replica counts. It's the declarative model — you say what you want, K8s does the work. That declarative approach is the heart of K8s.

questions.question: What is a Kubernetes Service?
questions.answer: A Service provides a stable network endpoint for a set of pods — pods are ephemeral (IPs change), services give a fixed name/IP and load-balance across the pods. Types: ClusterIP (internal), NodePort (expose on nodes), LoadBalancer (cloud LB). It's how clients reach pods reliably. I think of services as the 'phone number' for a pod group.

questions.question: What is an Ingress in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: Ingress is the entry point for HTTP(S) traffic into the cluster — routing, TLS termination, and path-based routing to services. It's the cluster's reverse proxy with rules. It's how external traffic reaches your apps with nice URLs and certificates. In my mental model, Ingress is Nginx-like but cluster-native.

questions.question: What is a ConfigMap and a Secret in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: ConfigMap holds non-sensitive config — env vars, config files — injectable into pods. Secret holds sensitive data — base64-encoded, with better protection options. Separating config from images is the point: same image, different environments. I use ConfigMaps for settings and Secrets for credentials, never baking them into images.

questions.question: What is a liveness probe and a readiness probe?
questions.answer: Liveness probes check if the container is alive — K8s restarts it if it fails. Readiness probes check if it's ready to serve traffic — K8s stops routing to it until ready. Both are health checks with different purposes: liveness = restart, readiness = traffic gate. They enable zero-downtime rolling updates. I define them for every service I deploy.

questions.question: What is a rolling update in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: A rolling update replaces old pods with new gradually — new pods become ready while old ones drain, keeping the service available. The Deployment controls max unavailable and max surge. Combined with readiness probes, updates happen with no downtime. It's the standard safe deployment strategy.

questions.question: What is a helm chart?
questions.answer: Helm is Kubernetes' package manager — a chart is a packaged template of K8s resources with values for customization. `helm install` deploys a full app from a chart. Charts make complex deployments reusable and parameterized. It's how K8s apps are shared and versioned.

questions.question: What is the difference between Docker Swarm and Kubernetes?
questions.answer: Swarm is Docker's native orchestrator — simpler, integrated with Docker, good for small/medium single-org clusters. Kubernetes is the industry standard — more features, ecosystem, and complexity, steeper learning curve. Choose Swarm for simplicity, K8s for scale and ecosystem. I know both at the conceptual level.

questions.question: What is ECS vs EKS?
questions.answer: ECS is AWS's container orchestrator — deeply integrated with AWS (ALB, IAM, CloudWatch), simpler to run. EKS is managed Kubernetes on AWS — the full K8s platform with AWS running the control plane. ECS for AWS-first simplicity; EKS when you need standard Kubernetes or portability. I've used Docker-oriented setups and understand both as managed options.

questions.question: What is a container registry?
questions.answer: A registry stores and serves container images — Docker Hub, ECR, GHCR. You push images, and deployment pulls them. Registries support tagging, scanning, and access control. CI builds images and pushes them; deploys pull them. It's the artifact store for containerized apps.

questions.question: What is image scanning and why is it important?
questions.answer: Image scanning checks images for known vulnerabilities — base image CVEs, outdated packages — before they reach production. Registries and CI do it automatically. It's supply-chain security for containers. I make scanning part of CI so vulnerable images never deploy.

questions.question: What is the difference between Kubernetes and Docker Compose?
questions.answer: Compose defines multi-container apps on ONE host — simple, great for dev and small deploys. Kubernetes orchestrates across a CLUSTER — scaling, self-healing, rolling updates, service discovery — with far more power and complexity. Compose for single-host simplicity, K8s for distributed production scale. They're not competitors; they're different scopes.

questions.question: What is system design and why do interviews test it?
questions.answer: System design tests how you architect a system — components, data flow, scaling, tradeoffs — for a given requirement. It matters because real engineering is mostly design: choosing the right shape before writing code. Interviewers look for structured thinking: requirements → estimates → data model → components → scaling → tradeoffs. I approach it like I'd approach a real client module.

questions.question: What are the first steps in designing a system?
questions.answer: Clarify requirements first — features, users, scale, latency, consistency needs. Then rough capacity estimates — QPS, storage, bandwidth. Then the high-level architecture — clients, services, database, cache, queues. Then dive into components and, finally, talk tradeoffs and bottlenecks. Skipping requirements is how designs go wrong — I always confirm scope before whiteboarding.

questions.question: What is throughput and latency in system design?
questions.answer: Throughput is how much work the system does per unit time — requests per second. Latency is how long one request takes — milliseconds. They're related but distinct: a system can have high throughput with high latency. The design goal is usually both, but the tradeoff — batching raises throughput but adds latency. I state both numbers when estimating capacity.

questions.question: How do you estimate QPS (queries per second)?
questions.answer: QPS = daily users × requests per user ÷ seconds per day, with a peak factor (peaks are often 2-3x average). For example, 100k DAU × 20 requests ÷ 86400 ≈ 23 avg, ~50-70 peak. Peak matters for capacity — you size for peaks, not averages. I always compute both average and peak and check what single-instance capacity is.

questions.question: What is load balancing and what types exist?
questions.answer: Load balancing distributes traffic across servers. Types: DNS load balancing (round-robin at DNS level), L4 (network-level, IP/port, fast), L7 (application-level, path/header-aware — ALB, Nginx). L7 enables smart routing like path-based and sticky sessions. A load balancer also does health checks, removing unhealthy servers. It's the front door of any scaled system.

questions.question: What is the difference between a single point of failure and redundancy?
questions.answer: A single point of failure (SPOF) is a component whose failure takes down the whole system — one database, one load balancer. Redundancy means having backups — a second instance, a replica, failover — so no single component is fatal. Design removes SPOFs by adding redundancy at each layer. The load balancer itself should be redundant.

questions.question: What is a health check in a distributed system?
questions.answer: A health check probes whether a server is alive and ready — an endpoint returning 200 when healthy. The load balancer or orchestrator uses it to stop routing to unhealthy instances and remove them. Types: HTTP, TCP, custom. Health checks are what make automatic failover and rolling updates safe.

questions.question: What is service discovery?
questions.answer: Service discovery is how services find each other's addresses in a dynamic environment — containers move, IPs change. Options: DNS-based, a registry (Consul, Eureka), or K8s Services. In my Docker setups, Compose networks provide name-based discovery; in K8s, Services do it. Without it, config becomes a mess of hardcoded addresses.

questions.question: What is a message broker?
questions.answer: A message broker is the middleman for async communication — producers publish messages, consumers process them — decoupling services. Examples: RabbitMQ, Kafka, Redis Streams, SQS. Benefits: load leveling, reliability (retries), and independent scaling. In my designs, heavy or async work goes through a broker so the API stays responsive.

questions.question: What is the difference between a message queue and a message topic?
questions.answer: A queue delivers each message to one consumer (competing consumers — work distribution). A topic delivers each message to all subscribers (fan-out). Queues for task processing; topics for events everyone cares about. Kafka's model is log-based with consumer groups — both patterns available. Choosing right depends on one-worker vs many-watchers.

questions.question: What is Kafka and what makes it different from RabbitMQ?
questions.answer: Kafka is a distributed event log — append-only, partitioned, durable, with replay and high throughput. RabbitMQ is a message broker — routing, flexible exchanges, per-message delivery. Kafka for event streaming, replay, and high-volume logs; RabbitMQ for task queues with routing. Kafka's replay (consumers can re-read) is the defining difference.

questions.question: What is a distributed cache?
questions.answer: A distributed cache is a shared in-memory store across servers — Redis or Memcached — so all app instances read the same cached data, not their own copies. It keeps caches consistent and scales horizontally. Without it, each instance's local cache diverges and cache hits drop. It's a core scaling component.

questions.question: What is a cache and why is it important in design?
questions.answer: A cache stores frequently-accessed data near the consumer to avoid expensive recomputation or DB reads. It cuts latency and protects the database — the usual bottleneck. Cache layers: browser, CDN, app-level, distributed (Redis). The design questions are what to cache, TTL/invalidation, and consistency. A good cache design is often the biggest performance lever.

questions.question: What is database partitioning?
questions.answer: Partitioning splits a table's data into segments — by range, hash, or list — for manageability and performance. Horizontal partitioning (sharding) distributes rows across machines; vertical splits columns. Partitioning is about scale and query pruning — queries touch only relevant partitions. I'd use it for large time-series tables where queries filter by date.

questions.question: What is the difference between vertical and horizontal partitioning?
questions.answer: Vertical partitioning splits a table by COLUMNS — hot columns separate from cold ones, on one machine. Horizontal partitioning splits by ROWS — across machines (sharding). Vertical reduces width and I/O; horizontal distributes load and storage. The terms overlap with scaling (vertical = bigger machine, horizontal = more machines), so I clarify the context.

questions.question: What is a CDN and where does it fit in system design?
questions.answer: A CDN caches static content at edge locations near users — images, JS, CSS, videos. It cuts latency and offloads origin servers. In design, static assets go to a CDN while dynamic content stays on the origin. It's a cheap, high-impact layer for global users.

questions.question: What is a two-phase commit and when would you use it?
questions.answer: Two-phase commit coordinates a transaction across multiple databases or services — prepare phase (everyone votes) then commit phase (everyone commits if all agree). It gives atomicity across systems. The cost: blocking and complexity — if a participant hangs, the transaction blocks. Modern systems often prefer sagas or eventual consistency instead. It's the classic distributed-transaction answer.

questions.question: What is a saga pattern?
questions.answer: A saga breaks a distributed transaction into local transactions with compensating actions — if a step fails, earlier steps undo. Unlike 2PC (blocking), sagas are non-blocking and eventually consistent. Orchestration (one coordinator) or choreography (each service reacts to events). It's the modern answer for distributed consistency in microservices.

questions.question: What is eventual consistency vs strong consistency?
questions.answer: Strong consistency — every read sees the latest committed write; you wait for confirmation. Eventual consistency — writes propagate asynchronously; reads may briefly be stale but converge. Distributed systems trade them off. Money needs strong; a news feed can be eventual. My designs choose per-feature — not one size fits all.

questions.question: What is a CAP theorem and its implications?
questions.answer: CAP says a distributed system can have at most two of: Consistency (all nodes agree), Availability (every request gets a response), Partition tolerance (works despite network splits). Since partitions are unavoidable, the real choice is consistency vs availability during a partition. Databases advertise their trade — Cassandra prefers availability, Spanner consistency. Understanding CAP frames every distributed design.

questions.question: What is the difference between CP and AP systems?
questions.answer: CP systems choose consistency during a partition — they may refuse requests rather than serve stale data (HBase, ZooKeeper, some DBs). AP systems choose availability — they serve possibly-stale data rather than error (Cassandra, DynamoDB, CouchDB). The choice depends on whether stale data or unavailable service is worse for your domain.

questions.question: What is an idempotency key and where do you use it?
questions.answer: An idempotency key is a client-generated unique token sent with a request so the server can deduplicate retries — if the same key comes again, return the same result instead of repeating the action. It's critical for payments and order creation where retries would duplicate side effects. I designed the MSS Sales Order generation around exactly this.

questions.question: What is rate limiting in system design?
questions.answer: Rate limiting caps requests per client in a window to protect the system. Implementations: token bucket (refill tokens), fixed window (reset counters), sliding window (smooth). Where: API gateway, Nginx, or app middleware backed by Redis for distributed counting. The design questions are limits per user/IP, responses (429 with Retry-After), and sharding the counter. It's both security and stability.

questions.question: What is a token bucket vs a leaky bucket algorithm?
questions.answer: Token bucket: tokens refill at a rate; each request consumes one; bursts up to bucket size allowed. Leaky bucket: requests enter a queue processed at a fixed rate — smooths bursts but forces constant output. Token bucket allows bursts; leaky bucket enforces steady rate. Token bucket is the common choice for APIs.

questions.question: What is a circuit breaker pattern?
questions.answer: A circuit breaker prevents a failing dependency from cascading failures — three states: closed (normal), open (fail fast after threshold), half-open (test recovery). When a dependency fails repeatedly, the breaker opens and calls fail fast instead of timing out, letting the dependency recover. Libraries: Hystrix, resilience4j. It's resilience for inter-service calls.

questions.question: What is a bulkhead pattern?
questions.answer: Bulkhead isolates failures by partitioning resources — like ship compartments — so a failure in one part doesn't drain shared resources for others. In services: separate connection pools per dependency so one slow dependency doesn't consume all threads. It limits blast radius. I apply it to dependency pools and thread limits.

questions.question: What is a retry strategy and what's the problem with naive retries?
questions.answer: Retries re-attempt failed operations — with backoff (exponential) and jitter (randomness) to avoid synchronized retry storms. Naive retries hammer a failing system, amplifying load — 'retry storm.' The backoff + jitter + circuit breaker combo prevents that. Timeouts also matter — a request that hangs forever is worse than one that fails fast.

questions.question: What is exponential backoff?
questions.answer: Exponential backoff increases retry delay exponentially — 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s — so a failing service gets recovery time. Jitter adds randomness so clients don't retry in lockstep. It's how clients behave politely under failures. I configure it in API clients and SDKs.

questions.question: What is a hot partition / hot key problem?
questions.answer: A hot partition is when one node holds most of the load — a popular user, a viral item — while others idle. Causes: poor shard key, skewed data. Fixes: re-keying (hash distribution), splitting hot keys (add suffix), caching the hot data. It's the classic sharding failure mode — my design questions always include 'what if one key is huge.'

questions.question: What is a read-heavy vs write-heavy system design?
questions.answer: A read-heavy system (content, product catalog) is solved with caching, CDNs, and read replicas — the DB rarely touched on reads. A write-heavy system (logs, sensors, orders) needs queues to buffer writes, batching, and possibly append-only storage. The bottleneck differs, so the design differs. I always identify read/write ratio first.

questions.question: What is backpressure and why is it important?
questions.answer: Backpressure is a consumer signaling a producer to slow down — because it can't keep up. Without it, producers overflow consumer queues and memory, causing cascading failure. Mechanisms: bounded queues, flow control, consumer acknowledgment. In stream and queue designs, bounded buffers and ack-based processing are the backpressure answer.

questions.question: What is a dead letter queue (DLQ)?
questions.answer: A DLQ is where messages that repeatedly fail processing go — instead of blocking the queue forever. You inspect, fix, and replay them. It isolates poison messages so the main queue keeps flowing. I'd pair every real queue with a DLQ and alerting — silent message loss is worse than a visible failure.

questions.question: What is graceful degradation?
questions.answer: Graceful degradation means a system continues to function, partially, when a component fails — showing cached content when the live feed is down, or returning a simplified response instead of an error. Feature flags, fallbacks, and timeouts enable it. It's the difference between a degraded but usable product and a hard outage.

questions.question: What is a blue/green deployment?
questions.answer: Blue/green runs two environments — blue (current) and green (new). You deploy to green, test, then switch the load balancer to green. Rollback is instant — flip back to blue. It gives zero-downtime releases with trivial rollback. The cost is double infrastructure. It's one of the deployment strategies I'd choose when downtime is unacceptable.

questions.question: What is a canary deployment?
questions.answer: Canary releases the new version to a small subset of users first — monitoring errors before rolling to everyone. It's gradual, with automatic or manual rollout based on health. It catches problems with real traffic but limited blast radius. Blue/green is all-at-once with instant rollback; canary is incremental with validation. Both beat a big-bang deploy.

questions.question: What is A/B testing?
questions.answer: A/B testing serves different versions to different user segments and measures which performs better on a metric — conversion, engagement. The infrastructure: feature flags or routing a percentage of traffic, with metrics collection and statistical analysis. It's product decisions driven by data. In system design it's usually a small component — traffic split + analytics.

questions.question: What is a feature flag?
questions.answer: A feature flag is a runtime switch that turns a feature on/off without a deploy — enabling gradual rollouts, instant rollback, and per-segment releases. Flags are powerful but need hygiene — dead flags get cleaned up. They're the enabler for trunk-based development and canary releases.

questions.question: What is a sidecar pattern?
questions.answer: A sidecar is a helper process deployed alongside the main service in the same pod/host — handling cross-cutting concerns like logging, proxying, TLS, or metrics. The main app stays focused; the sidecar handles the plumbing. It's a K8s-native pattern (e.g., service meshes use sidecars). It's the modern take on 'do one thing in each process.'

questions.question: What is a service mesh?
questions.answer: A service mesh is a dedicated infrastructure layer handling inter-service communication — proxies (sidecars) handle routing, TLS, retries, observability — so app code doesn't. Tools: Istio, Linkerd. Benefits: uniform resilience and tracing. Costs: complexity and overhead. I'd consider it when microservice communication needs advanced features; for smaller systems it's overkill.

questions.question: How do you design for failure (fault tolerance)?
questions.answer: Design for failure assumes components WILL fail and makes failures survivable: redundancy and failover, health checks, circuit breakers, timeouts with retries/backoff, queues that buffer, and observability that surfaces issues. The principle: no single point of failure, and failure should degrade gracefully. I design with the mindset that the thing I'm building will break — and that's okay if it breaks gracefully.

questions.question: What is the OWASP Top 10 and why does it matter?
questions.answer: The OWASP Top 10 is the standard list of the most critical web application security risks — updated regularly. It includes injection, broken authentication, sensitive data exposure, XXE, broken access control, security misconfiguration, XSS, insecure deserialization, vulnerable components, and insufficient logging. It matters because it's the shared vocabulary for web security. I use it as my security checklist.

questions.question: Explain how parameterized queries prevent SQL injection at the database layer. Why is sanitizing input alone not enough?
questions.answer: A parameterized (prepared) statement sends the SQL skeleton and the values separately over the wire, so the database treats user input as data, never as executable SQL. Sanitizing alone is not enough because it is easy to miss an edge case or an encoding trick, and it never fully protects dynamic identifiers or ORDER BY columns. Defense in depth: parameterize everything, validate types and lengths, use least-privilege DB accounts, and escape only when a dynamic identifier is truly unavoidable.

questions.question: What is XSS and what are the types?
questions.answer: XSS (cross-site scripting) injects scripts into pages that run in other users' browsers. Types: stored (persisted in DB, served to all — worst), reflected (in a URL/response), DOM-based (client-side manipulation). Prevention: escape output, sanitize HTML (DOMPurify), use a CSP, and avoid innerHTML with untrusted data. My frontend rule: treat all user content as untrusted on output.

questions.question: What is CSRF and how do you prevent it?
questions.answer: CSRF (cross-site request forgery) tricks a logged-in user's browser into making a request the attacker wants — the victim's session cookie does the rest. Prevention: CSRF tokens (unpredictable per-session values verified server-side), SameSite cookies, and checking Origin/Referer. Frameworks like Angular and Spring include CSRF protection by default. I keep SameSite and token checks in place.

questions.question: What is the difference between XSS and CSRF?
questions.answer: XSS exploits a trust in the site's content — injecting scripts that run in the browser. CSRF exploits trust in the user's browser — forging requests using the user's session. XSS is an injection of code; CSRF is a forgery of actions. They're different attack classes with different defenses — output escaping for XSS, tokens/SameSite for CSRF.

questions.question: What is authentication vs authorization?
questions.answer: Authentication verifies WHO you are — credentials, tokens, MFA. Authorization verifies WHAT you can do — roles, permissions, policies. You authenticate first, then authorize actions. A user is authenticated but denied (403) if not authorized. Getting them confused is a common interview mistake — they're distinct stages.

questions.question: What is a brute-force attack and how do you defend against it?
questions.answer: A brute-force attack tries many passwords/keys until one works. Defenses: rate limiting and lockout, strong password policy, multi-factor authentication, and captcha. The goal is to make guessing impractical. I'd combine account lockout with rate limiting and MFA — a layered defense slows attacks to useless.

questions.question: What is a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack?
questions.answer: MITM is an attacker intercepting and possibly altering communication between two parties — eavesdropping on unencrypted HTTP, or impersonating a server. Defense: TLS everywhere (HTTPS), certificate validation, and HSTS. An attacker between the browser and a plain-HTTP server sees everything. TLS is the baseline mitigation.

questions.question: What is a session hijacking and how do you prevent it?
questions.answer: Session hijacking steals a valid session to impersonate the user — via stolen cookies, XSS, or sniffing. Prevention: HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookies, HTTPS, session regeneration on login, rotating tokens, and short-lived sessions. The HttpOnly flag stops JavaScript from reading the session cookie — a first line of defense against XSS-based theft.

questions.question: What is a JWT and what are its security concerns?
questions.answer: JWT is a signed token for stateless auth — header, payload, signature. Concerns: it's not encrypted (don't put secrets in payload), the signature must use a strong algorithm and secret (algorithm confusion attacks), and revocation is hard — a stolen JWT is valid until expiry. Keep expiry short, use refresh tokens, store carefully, and validate signature + expiry + issuer.

questions.question: What is a clickjacking attack?
questions.answer: Clickjacking hides malicious UI under a transparent iframe, tricking users into clicking something they don't see — like approving a payment. Defense: the `X-Frame-Options: DENY` header or `frame-ancestors` CSP, preventing your page from being embedded. I set frame protection headers on every deployment.

questions.question: What is a Content Security Policy (CSP)?
questions.answer: CSP is a header restricting what the browser may load — scripts, styles, images, frames — via allowlists: `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'`. It blocks XSS and injection by preventing untrusted sources from executing. It's one of the strongest modern defenses. The caveat is tuning — strict CSPs break inline scripts and third-party widgets, so I tune carefully.

questions.question: What is a DDoS attack and how do you mitigate it?
questions.answer: DDoS floods a service with traffic until it's unavailable. Mitigation: rate limiting, load balancing, CDNs absorbing traffic, and cloud DDoS protection (AWS Shield). At the app level you can't stop the flood — you absorb and filter it. The goal is availability during attack. I mention rate limits and CDN absorption as the practical layers.

questions.question: What is input validation and why is it critical?
questions.answer: Input validation rejects malformed or malicious data before it's processed — validating types, lengths, ranges, and formats on both client and server. It's the first line against injection, XSS, and logic bugs. Client validation is UX; server validation is security — never trust the client. Pydantic in FastAPI and schema validation are how I enforce it.

questions.question: What is output encoding and where does it apply?
questions.answer: Output encoding converts data to a safe form for its context before rendering — HTML-escape for HTML, URL-encode for URLs, etc. It prevents injection by making user data inert. Context matters: encoding for HTML isn't enough for JavaScript or attribute contexts. I encode at every rendering boundary — the browser is only safe if output is safe.

questions.question: What is a supply chain attack?
questions.answer: A supply chain attack compromises a dependency or build tool instead of your code directly — malicious npm packages, compromised libraries, compromised CI. Mitigations: lock files, package integrity checks, auditing dependencies, and scanning images. My dependency hygiene — npm audit, lock files, scoped installs — is exactly this defense.

questions.question: What is HTTPS redirect and HSTS?
questions.answer: HTTPS redirect forces all HTTP traffic to HTTPS. HSTS is the header telling browsers to ONLY use HTTPS for a domain, preventing downgrade attacks. Together they make plain HTTP impossible. I configure both in Nginx — redirect plus `Strict-Transport-Security` header. It's the baseline transport security.

questions.question: What is password storage best practice?
questions.answer: Never store plaintext or reversible-encrypted passwords. Use a slow, salted hash — bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2. Salts prevent rainbow tables; slowness resists brute force. Store the hash and its parameters, not the password. On login, compare hashes. This is non-negotiable — a leaked password table is only survivable if passwords are properly hashed.

questions.question: What is a security misconfiguration?
questions.answer: A misconfiguration is an insecure default or setup — default passwords, open debug endpoints, exposed admin panels, verbose errors, permissive CORS, unpatched software. It's one of the most common vulnerabilities because it's easy to create and easy to miss. Mitigation: hardening checklists, secrets hygiene, least-privilege, and regular review.

questions.question: What is the principle of least privilege?
questions.answer: Least privilege means granting the minimum access needed to do the job — users, services, and IAM roles get only what's required. If compromised, the blast radius is limited. I apply it to DB users (app user can't drop tables), IAM roles, and file permissions. It's a foundational security principle that compounds every other defense.

questions.question: What is the difference between an array and a linked list?
questions.answer: An array stores elements contiguously — O(1) random access by index, cache-friendly, but O(n) insert/remove in the middle (shifting). A linked list stores nodes with pointers — O(1) insert/remove given the position, but O(n) access and worse cache locality. Arrays win for access; linked lists for structural changes. In practice arrays are the default.

questions.question: What is the difference between a stack and a queue in data structures?
questions.answer: A stack is LIFO — push/pop from the top, like undo history. A queue is FIFO — enqueue/dequeue, like a task queue. Both are O(1) for their core operations. Python: list for stack, `collections.deque` for queue. Choosing the right one for the access pattern is the point.

questions.question: What is a hash table and how does it achieve O(1)?
questions.answer: A hash table maps keys to values via a hash function into buckets. Lookup hashes the key, finds the bucket, and reads — O(1) average. Collisions (same bucket) are handled by chaining or open addressing. Good hash functions and load factors keep it fast. It's the workhorse data structure behind dictionaries and sets.

questions.question: What is a binary search tree (BST)?
questions.answer: A BST is a tree where each node's left subtree is smaller and right subtree is larger — enabling O(log n) search, insert, and delete (balanced). It maintains sorted order for in-order traversal. The catch: unbalanced trees degrade to O(n). Balanced variants — AVL, red-black — fix that. BSTs are the conceptual base for many structures.

questions.question: What is an AVL tree vs a red-black tree?
questions.answer: Both are self-balancing BSTs. AVL maintains stricter balance (height differences ≤ 1) — faster lookups, but more rotations on insert/delete. Red-black maintains looser balance — slightly slower lookups, fewer rotations, better for write-heavy. Java's TreeMap uses red-black; databases use B-trees. The tradeoff is lookup speed vs update cost.

questions.question: What is a B-tree and why do databases use it?
questions.answer: A B-tree is a self-balancing tree with many children per node — designed for disk/block storage. High branching factor means fewer disk reads; data stays sorted; O(log n) operations. Databases use B-trees for indexes because they minimize I/O — each node is a page. It's the reason DB lookups are fast even on huge tables.

questions.question: What is a heap and when do you use it?
questions.answer: A heap is a tree-based structure where the root is the min or max — O(log n) insert, O(log n) extract-min/max, O(1) peek. Uses: priority queues, top-K problems, Dijkstra, heap sort. Python's `heapq` provides min-heaps. I use heaps for 'k largest' and scheduling by priority.

questions.question: What is a priority queue?
questions.answer: A priority queue serves the highest-priority item first — implemented with a heap. Insert and extract are O(log n). Uses: task scheduling, Dijkstra, event handling. It's not FIFO — priority, not arrival order, decides. Python's `heapq` or `queue.PriorityQueue` provides it. The heap implementation is the standard answer.

questions.question: What is a trie and when is it useful?
questions.answer: A trie is a tree for storing strings by prefix — nodes are characters, and paths spell words. Lookup and prefix queries are O(length). Uses: autocomplete, spell check, IP routing. It's space-hungry but fast for prefix matching. For a search-as-you-type feature, a trie is the classic structure.

questions.question: What is a graph and what are the common representations?
questions.answer: A graph is nodes (vertices) connected by edges — directed/undirected, weighted/unweighted. Representations: adjacency list (each node lists neighbors — memory-efficient, common) and adjacency matrix (2D array — fast lookups, dense). The list is the practical default. Graphs model networks, dependencies, and social connections.

questions.question: What is BFS vs DFS?
questions.answer: BFS explores level by level using a queue — finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs, O(V+E). DFS explores deep first using a stack/recursion — for connectivity, cycles, topological sort. BFS for shortest path and level order; DFS for exploring all paths and tree traversal. Both visit everything once — the order and data structure differ.

questions.question: What is Dijkstra's algorithm?
questions.answer: Dijkstra finds the shortest path from a source to all nodes in a weighted graph with non-negative weights — using a priority queue to always expand the closest unvisited node. Complexity O((V+E) log V) with a heap. It's the standard shortest-path algorithm. For negative weights you'd use Bellman-Ford.

questions.question: What is the difference between Dijkstra and A*?
questions.answer: Both find shortest paths, but A* adds a heuristic guiding the search toward the goal — it explores fewer nodes in practice. Dijkstra explores in all directions; A* biases toward the target. A* needs a good heuristic (admissible). For games and maps A* wins; for general graphs Dijkstra is the safe default.

questions.question: What is topological sort?
questions.answer: Topological sort orders a DAG (directed acyclic graph) so every edge goes from earlier to later — used for dependency ordering: build order, course prerequisites, task scheduling. Implementations: Kahn's algorithm (in-degree counting) or DFS with a stack. It only works on acyclic graphs — a cycle means no valid order.

questions.question: What is dynamic programming?
questions.answer: DP solves problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems, storing results to avoid recomputation — memoization (top-down) or tabulation (bottom-up). It turns exponential brute force into polynomial. The pattern: define state, recurrence, base cases, and order. Classic problems: Fibonacci, knapsack, LCS, coin change. Recognizing the overlapping-subproblem structure is the skill.

questions.question: What is the difference between memoization and tabulation?
questions.answer: Memoization is top-down — recursion with a cache, computes only needed subproblems. Tabulation is bottom-up — iterative table filling, computes all subproblems in order, no recursion stack. Memoization is easier to write; tabulation is often faster and avoids stack limits. Both are DP; the choice is style and constraints.

questions.question: What is the knapsack problem?
questions.answer: The knapsack problem: given items with weights and values and a capacity, pick the maximum value subset without exceeding capacity. The 0/1 version uses DP — O(nW) with a table. It's the canonical DP problem that appears across interviews. Understanding it demonstrates DP pattern recognition.

questions.question: What is the Longest Common Subsequence (LCS)?
questions.answer: LCS finds the longest subsequence common to two strings (preserving order, not necessarily contiguous). Classic DP — a 2D table comparing characters, O(n·m). It's used in diff tools and bioinformatics. The DP table and backtracking to reconstruct the sequence is the standard solution.

questions.question: What is the sliding window technique?
questions.answer: Sliding window maintains a window over an array/substring, expanding and contracting it to track a condition in O(n) — for 'longest substring with k distinct chars,' 'max sum subarray of size k.' It avoids the O(n²) nested loop. Two pointers manage the window. It's one of the most common interview patterns.

questions.question: What is the two-pointer technique?
questions.answer: Two pointers traverse an array from ends or with an offset — for sorted-array problems (pair sum, reverse, remove duplicates) and linked-list cycles (fast/slow). It reduces O(n²) to O(n) by using sortedness. It's a pattern I reach for early when I see sorted input or palindrome-type problems.

questions.question: What is backtracking and give an example?
questions.answer: Backtracking explores decisions, undoing (backtracking) when a path fails — brute force with pruning. Classic: N-Queens, Sudoku, permutations, subsets. The pattern: choose, explore, un-choose. It's exponential worst-case but correct. Recognizing when brute-force-with-pruning is acceptable is part of the answer.

questions.question: What is greedy algorithm and when does it work?
questions.answer: A greedy algorithm makes the locally optimal choice at each step, hoping it's globally optimal. It only works when the problem has optimal substructure with greedy choice property — activity selection, coin change with standard denominations, Huffman coding. It fails on knapsack (which needs DP). I mention when greed works and when it doesn't.

questions.question: What is divide and conquer?
questions.answer: Divide and conquer breaks a problem into smaller subproblems, solves them, and combines — recursion with a merge step. Examples: merge sort, quick sort, binary search, closest-pair. The efficiency comes from halving. It's distinct from DP (which has overlapping subproblems; D&C typically doesn't).

questions.question: What is the difference between merge sort and quick sort?
questions.answer: Merge sort divides, sorts, merges — guaranteed O(n log n), stable, but O(n) extra space. Quick sort partitions around a pivot — average O(n log n), worst O(n²) with bad pivots, in-place, faster in practice. Merge for guaranteed bounds and stability; quick for in-place speed. Both are the 'explain sorting' interview staples.

questions.question: What is binary search and what are the requirements?
questions.answer: Binary search halves the search space each step — O(log n). Requirements: sorted data (or a monotonic predicate). Implementation: check mid, adjust left/right. Variants: first/last occurrence, search in rotated array. The off-by-one on `mid` and loop conditions is the classic bug — I write it carefully.

questions.question: What is a hash function and what makes a good one?
questions.answer: A hash function maps arbitrary data to a fixed-size value. A good one: deterministic, fast, uniform (spreads values evenly), and avalanche (small input change → big output change). It's used in hash tables, password hashing (with slowness), and integrity checks. For tables you want speed and uniformity; for passwords you want deliberate slowness.

questions.question: What is a bloom filter?
questions.answer: A bloom filter is a probabilistic structure for membership tests — tells you 'definitely not present' or 'probably present' — using bits and multiple hashes. Small and fast, with a false-positive rate but zero false negatives. Uses: caching layers, spell checkers, dedup in databases. It's a classic design answer for avoiding expensive lookups.

questions.question: What is a LRU cache and how do you implement it?
questions.answer: LRU (least recently used) evicts the oldest-accessed item when the cache is full — implemented with a hash map (O(1) lookup) plus a doubly-linked list (O(1) move-to-front and eviction). It's the standard interview design question. Redis and browser caches use LRU-ish policies. The hash map + linked list combo is the canonical answer.

questions.question: What is amortized analysis and give an example?
questions.answer: Amortized analysis averages the cost of operations over a sequence — a single operation can be expensive, but averaged over many it's cheap. Example: dynamic array (ArrayList) doubling — most appends are O(1), the doubling append is O(n), but amortized it's O(1) per append. It explains why resizable structures are efficient in practice.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of common sorting algorithms?
questions.answer: Merge sort and heapsort: O(n log n) always. Quick sort: O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst. Insertion sort: O(n²) but O(n) on nearly-sorted. Counting/radix: O(n+k) for special cases. Python's `sorted()` uses Timsort — O(n log n), adaptive to sorted runs. Knowing these tradeoffs is the sorting interview.

questions.question: What is a two-sum problem and how do you solve it?
questions.answer: Given an array and a target, find two numbers that sum to it. The efficient solution: a hash map storing complements — for each number, check if `target - num` is already seen, O(n) time. The brute force is O(n²). It's the classic 'convert lookup to a hash map' lesson.

questions.question: What is the difference between a substring and a subsequence?
questions.answer: A substring is contiguous — 'abc' in 'xxabcxx'. A subsequence preserves order but need not be contiguous — 'ac' is a subsequence of 'abc' but not a substring. Substring problems use sliding window; subsequence problems often use DP. Interviewers test whether you know the distinction — the solution approaches differ entirely.

questions.question: What is a palindrome and how do you check efficiently?
questions.answer: A palindrome reads the same forward and backward. Check by two pointers from both ends comparing characters — O(n) time, O(1) space. The harder versions ask for the longest palindromic substring (expand around centers, O(n²)) or subsequence (DP). The basic check with two pointers is the standard first answer.

questions.question: What is the Kth largest element problem?
questions.answer: Find the kth largest in an array: sort and index (O(n log n)), or quickselect (average O(n)), or a min-heap of size k (O(n log k)). Quickselect and heap are the efficient answers. I'd mention the heap approach — it's clean and also works on streaming data.

questions.question: What is cycle detection in a linked list?
questions.answer: Detect if a linked list has a cycle using Floyd's tortoise-and-hare — two pointers, one moving twice as fast; if they meet, there's a cycle. It's O(n) time, O(1) space. A hash set also works (O(n) space). Floyd's is the classic answer — it demonstrates pointer technique elegantly.

questions.question: What is a spanning tree and a minimum spanning tree?
questions.answer: A spanning tree connects all vertices of a graph with the minimum edges (V-1) with no cycles. A minimum spanning tree is the one with minimum total edge weight — found by Kruskal (sort edges, union-find) or Prim (greedy growth). Uses: network design, clustering. It's a classic graph theory topic.

questions.question: What is union-find (disjoint set)?
questions.answer: Union-find tracks connected components — `find` (which set) and `union` (merge sets), optimized with path compression and union by rank — near O(1) amortized. Uses: cycle detection, Kruskal's MST, dynamic connectivity. It's a compact, powerful structure that appears in many interview problems.

questions.question: What is a string hashing technique like rolling hash?
questions.answer: Rolling hash computes hashes of substrings incrementally in O(1) per substring — used in Rabin-Karp string matching and duplicate-detection. It reuses the previous hash with a base and modulo. The catch is collisions — mitigated with a good base and double hashing. It's an advanced but classic technique.

questions.question: What is the difference between recursion and iteration?
questions.answer: Recursion calls itself on a subproblem — elegant for tree/graph traversal and divide-and-conquer, but uses the call stack (stack overflow risk). Iteration uses loops — no stack growth, often faster. Many recursive solutions can be converted to iteration (sometimes with an explicit stack). I use recursion for natural recursive structures and iteration for hot paths.

questions.question: What is the space complexity of an algorithm?
questions.answer: Space complexity is how much extra memory an algorithm uses relative to input size — O(1) for in-place, O(n) for a copy or table, O(log n) for balanced recursion. It's the counterpart to time complexity. Interviewers check that you consider both — a fast O(n²)-space solution can be unusable. I state both when presenting solutions.

questions.question: What is the difference between best, average, and worst-case complexity?
questions.answer: Best case is the easiest input (often trivial and not informative). Average case is typical input (usually what matters). Worst case is adversarial input (what bounds matter for guarantees). For quicksort: O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst. I present worst-case guarantees and mention average behavior.

questions.question: What is the `Timsort` algorithm?
questions.answer: Timsort is Python's (and Java's) sort — a hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort that exploits existing order in real data (runs). It's O(n log n) worst, near-linear on nearly-sorted data, and stable. It's why Python's sort is fast on real-world data. It's a good 'explain a real algorithm' answer.

questions.question: What is Dijkstra vs BFS for shortest path?
questions.answer: BFS gives shortest paths in UNWEIGHTED graphs — O(V+E). Dijkstra handles WEIGHTED graphs with non-negative weights — O((V+E) log V). BFS is Dijkstra specialized for uniform weights (a simple queue instead of a priority queue). If all edges have the same cost, BFS is simpler and faster.

questions.question: What is a divide and conquer example in sorting?
questions.answer: Merge sort is the purest example — split the array, sort each half recursively, merge the sorted halves. The merge step is the combining part. Quick sort also divides and conquers (partition then recurse), but the work happens in the partition (divide) step rather than the combine. Both show the pattern.

questions.question: What is a segment tree and when do you use it?
questions.answer: A segment tree supports range queries (sum, min, max) and point updates in O(log n) — storing aggregates over segments. It's for dynamic range queries where precomputation goes stale. Fenwick trees are a simpler subset. I'd use it for problems like range-sum-with-updates. It's an advanced structure that shows depth.

questions.question: What is a Fenwick tree (BIT)?
questions.answer: A Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) supports prefix sums and point updates in O(log n) — more compact and simpler than a segment tree. It's for cumulative range queries with updates. It's less general than a segment tree but faster and simpler for the prefix-sum family. The bit-twiddling in implementation is the fun part.

questions.question: What is the difference between an algorithm and a data structure?
questions.answer: An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure for solving a problem — the process. A data structure is a way of organizing and storing data — the container. They work together: the right data structure enables the efficient algorithm. Binary search (algorithm) needs a sorted array (data structure). Interview answers usually cover both.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of hash map operations?
questions.answer: Hash map operations — get, set, delete — are O(1) average, O(n) worst-case (pathological collisions/resize). The average-case constant-time lookup is why hash maps dominate. Worst case matters only for adversarial inputs or broken hash functions. I answer 'amortized O(1)' to be precise.

questions.question: What is a topological sort used for in real life?
questions.answer: Real uses: build systems (compile dependencies in order), course scheduling (prerequisites first), package managers (install in dependency order), and task DAGs in pipelines. In Frappe, DocType dependency and workflow ordering have similar logic. It's an algorithm with direct engineering applications.

questions.question: What is the difference between greedy and DP in coin change?
questions.answer: Greedy picks the largest coin first — works for standard denominations (Indian/US currency) but FAILS for arbitrary ones (e.g., coins {1,3,4}, amount 6 — greedy gives 4+1+1=3 coins, optimal is 3+3=2). DP explores all combinations — correct always, more expensive. The lesson: greedy is an assumption, DP is a guarantee.

questions.question: How would you implement a debounce from scratch?
questions.answer: Debounce delays a call until the input pauses: keep a timer, clear it on each call, and only fire when the timer completes without interruption. `return function(...args) { clearTimeout(timer); timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), wait); }`. I'd also mention the leading-edge variant and `this` handling. It's a common machine-coding question because it tests closure and timer understanding.

questions.question: How would you flatten a nested array?
questions.answer: Flatten recursively — for each element, if it's an array, flatten it; else push it. Depth-aware: `arr.flat(depth)` or `flat(Infinity)` exist, but interviewers want the manual version. Recursion with a result accumulator is the standard. I'd also handle the case of avoiding stack overflow for very deep arrays.

questions.question: How would you implement `Promise.all` from scratch?
questions.answer: `Promise.all` takes an array of promises, resolves with all results when all succeed, and rejects on the first rejection. Implementation: track remaining count, store results by index (order preserved), resolve when count hits zero, reject on first error. The subtleties: handle empty arrays, non-promise values, and index ordering. It tests async fundamentals.

questions.question: How would you write a function to group an array by a key?
questions.answer: Use a reduce or a loop building an object keyed by the group value: `arr.reduce((acc, item) => { const k = item[key]; (acc[k] ||= []).push(item); return acc; }, {})`. Or use `Object.groupBy` (modern). For data like sales by region, this is a daily pattern. The reduce version is the expected answer.

questions.question: How would you deep clone an object?
questions.answer: The simple answer is `structuredClone(obj)` — handles Date, Map, Set, typed arrays. Before that, JSON tricks failed on special types. If I had to hand-write: recursively copy, handling arrays, plain objects, and special types, with a WeakMap for cycles. `structuredClone` is the modern correct answer.

questions.question: How would you implement `setInterval` with `setTimeout`?
questions.answer: To make a timer that adapts to slow callbacks, implement setInterval via recursive setTimeout: `function setInterval(fn, ms) { const t = setTimeout(() => { fn(); t = setTimeout(...) }, ms) }` — the next tick is scheduled AFTER the work, avoiding overlap. It's the classic answer about why recursive setTimeout is safer than setInterval.

questions.question: How would you reverse a string without built-in reverse?
questions.answer: Two-pointer swap or a backward loop: `for (let i = s.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) result += s[i]`. In Python, `s[::-1]`. The point is understanding indexing and avoiding the built-in when asked. For Unicode, I'd mention character encoding considerations. Simple but shows fundamentals.

questions.question: How would you find the first non-repeating character?
questions.answer: Two passes: count frequencies in a hash map, then scan again to find the first char with count 1 — O(n) time, O(1) or O(k) space. The two-pass pattern is the standard. For huge strings, iterating with an ordered structure changes the answer. It's a common easy-medium question.

questions.question: How would you check if two strings are rotations of each other?
questions.answer: Check if the first string is a substring of the concatenation of the second with itself: `s2 + s2` contains `s1`. For 'abcd' and 'cdab', 'cdab'+'cdab' contains 'abcd'. The key is the concatenation trick plus length check. It's a neat trick question that tests insight.

questions.question: How would you implement a simple rate limiter?
questions.answer: Token bucket or sliding window: track timestamps per key and count within the window. A simple approach: a Map keyed by user id → timestamps, evict those outside the window, reject if count ≥ limit. For distributed, back it with Redis (INCR with expiry). The interview answer starts single-instance and mentions the Redis extension.

questions.question: How would you build a simple URL shortener?
questions.answer: API: POST to create a short code, GET redirects. Design: a counter or random code (base62) stored in a table with a unique index, plus caching hot mappings in Redis. The short code avoids collisions (unique index + retry). Redirects are read-heavy — caching handles most traffic. I'd walk through these decisions in order.

questions.question: How would you implement a LRU cache?
questions.answer: Hash map for O(1) lookup + doubly-linked list for O(1) move-to-front and eviction. On access, move the node to the head; on insert when full, evict the tail. This is the classic design. Interviewers check both the data structure combo and the O(1) reasoning.

questions.question: How would you merge two sorted arrays?
questions.answer: Two-pointer merge — compare heads, take the smaller, advance — O(n+m) time, O(n+m) or O(1) space. It's the merge step of merge sort. In-place merging (from the end) is the harder variant. The two-pointer merge is the base answer; I'd write it cleanly.

questions.question: How would you implement `Array.map` from scratch?
questions.answer: `map` creates a new array applying a callback to each element: iterate, call callback with (element, index, array), push the result. The subtleties: handle sparse arrays and the `thisArg` optional parameter. It tests knowledge of array iteration and callback signatures. The standard implementation is straightforward.

questions.question: How would you implement a simple event emitter?
questions.answer: An object storing event names → arrays of handlers. `on` pushes a handler, `emit` calls all handlers for an event, `off` removes one. It's the observer pattern from scratch. Node's EventEmitter works this way. Adding once-wrappers and error handling are extensions. It tests object design and closure skills.

questions.question: How would you throttle a function?
questions.answer: Throttle allows at most one call per interval: track the last run time; if enough time has passed, run and update; else schedule (or skip). The difference from debounce: throttle fires periodically during activity; debounce fires after the pause. I'd implement with a `lastRan` timestamp and timer.

questions.question: How would you find the intersection of two arrays?
questions.answer: Put one array in a Set, then filter the other for elements in the set — O(n+m). For duplicates, count frequencies. The Set-based approach is the standard efficient answer. It demonstrates using the right data structure for membership tests.

questions.question: How would you sum all numbers in an array without a loop?
questions.answer: `reduce`: `arr.reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, 0)`. Recursion is another way: `n === 0 ? 0 : arr[0] + sum(rest)`. The reduce answer is idiomatic; recursion shows algorithmic thinking. Interviewers usually want one or both.

questions.question: How would you remove duplicates from an array?
questions.answer: `Array.from(new Set(arr))` — the one-liner. Or a filter with an index-check, or a manual set loop. The Set approach preserves insertion order and is O(n). For objects you need a key function. Duplicate removal is a daily real task — I do it in data cleaning constantly.

questions.question: How would you implement a binary search?
questions.answer: Set low=0, high=len-1. While low ≤ high, mid = low + (high-low)/2; if arr[mid] === target return mid; if less, high = mid-1; else low = mid+1. The `low + (high-low)/2` avoids overflow. Return -1 if not found. I'd mention the two variants (first/last occurrence) as extensions. It's the most-asked algorithm question.

questions.question: How would you reverse a linked list?
questions.answer: Iterative: three pointers — prev, current, next — reversing links as you walk. Recursive: recurse to the end, then reverse links on the way back. The iterative version is the standard answer with O(1) space. It's a classic data-structure manipulation question.

questions.question: How would you check if a string has balanced parentheses?
questions.answer: A stack: push open brackets, pop on close, check the match, and ensure the stack is empty at the end. The stack is the natural structure because nesting is LIFO. Variants: multiple bracket types and the 'return invalid index' version. It's one of the first stack problems and a favorite interview question.

questions.question: How would you implement a debounce with leading edge?
questions.answer: Leading-edge debounce fires immediately on the first call, then suppresses until the quiet period ends. Implementation: track a `lastRan` timestamp; if enough time passed, run immediately; otherwise set a timer for the remainder. It's the version that keeps the first click responsive — useful for 'send now' type actions.

questions.question: How would you find the missing number in an array 1..n?
questions.answer: Sum of 1..n is `n(n+1)/2` — subtract the array sum to find the missing number, O(n) time O(1) space. XOR is the elegant alternative (works without overflow). The sum trick is the expected answer; XOR shows depth.

questions.question: How would you implement `Object.groupBy` behavior manually?
questions.answer: Build a map keyed by the callback result: `arr.reduce((acc, item) => { const k = keyFn(item); (acc[k] ||= []).push(item); return acc; }, {})` or with `Map`. It groups items by a computed key — used for categorizing data. The reduce version is the standard manual implementation.

questions.question: What is the difference between HTTP and HTTPS in one line?
questions.answer: HTTP is plaintext; HTTPS encrypts the connection with TLS so data can't be read or tampered with in transit.

questions.question: What is the difference between HTML and HTML5 in one line?
questions.answer: HTML5 adds semantic tags, native audio/video, canvas, and richer forms — modern HTML.

questions.question: What is a cookie in one line?
questions.answer: A small piece of data a server sets and the browser sends back with each request, enabling state like sessions.

questions.question: What is the difference between an IP address and a domain name?
questions.answer: An IP is the numeric address of a machine; a domain is the human-readable name that DNS resolves to that IP.

questions.question: What is DNS in one line?
questions.answer: DNS is the phonebook of the internet — it translates domain names into IP addresses.

questions.question: What is the difference between a compiler and an interpreter?
questions.answer: A compiler translates the whole program to machine code before running; an interpreter executes source line by line. JIT (like the JVM/V8) compiles at runtime for speed.

questions.question: What is the difference between a class and an object?
questions.answer: A class is a blueprint or template; an object is a concrete instance created from that blueprint.

questions.question: What is the difference between a variable and a constant?
questions.answer: A variable's value can change; a constant's value can't be reassigned after definition.

questions.question: What is the difference between a stack and the heap in one line?
questions.answer: Stack is fast, LIFO memory for function calls; heap is larger, dynamic memory for objects.

questions.question: What is the difference between front-end and back-end development?
questions.answer: Frontend is what runs in the browser — UI and interaction; backend is what runs on the server — logic, data, APIs.

questions.question: What is a database schema?
questions.answer: The structure of a database — its tables, columns, types, keys, and relationships.

questions.question: What is the difference between a primary key and a unique key in one line?
questions.answer: A primary key uniquely identifies rows and is non-null; a unique key also enforces uniqueness but can be null.

questions.question: What is the difference between a DELETE and a TRUNCATE in one line?
questions.answer: DELETE removes selected rows and can be rolled back; TRUNCATE removes all rows quickly and is harder to roll back.

questions.question: What is the difference between a WHERE and a HAVING in one line?
questions.answer: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. In practice: use WHERE to narrow raw rows, HAVING to filter the results of GROUP BY (like counts or sums).

questions.question: What is a foreign key in one line?
questions.answer: A column linking to another table's primary key to enforce referential integrity.

questions.question: What is the difference between a stack and a queue in one line?
questions.answer: A stack is LIFO (last in, first out) — the last item added is the first removed, like a pile of plates. A queue is FIFO (first in, first out) — items are processed in the order they arrive, like a checkout line. Stacks suit undo history and recursion; queues suit task processing and breadth-first traversal.

questions.question: What is the difference between O(n) and O(log n)?
questions.answer: O(n) grows linearly with input; O(log n) grows logarithmically — halving the work each step, much faster at scale.

questions.question: What is the difference between a binary tree and a binary search tree?
questions.answer: A binary tree has any left/right children; a BST additionally orders them (left smaller, right larger) enabling O(log n) search.

questions.question: What is the difference between a process and a thread in one line?
questions.answer: A process is an isolated program instance; a thread is a lightweight unit within a process sharing its memory.

questions.question: What is the difference between a deadlock and a livelock?
questions.answer: A deadlock waits forever with no progress; a livelock keeps acting but makes no progress (it's busy but stuck).

questions.question: What is the difference between an algorithm and a program?
questions.answer: An algorithm is the step-by-step method; a program is the concrete implementation of an algorithm in code.

questions.question: What is the difference between debugging and testing?
questions.answer: Testing verifies the software behaves correctly; debugging finds and fixes the specific cause of a failure.

questions.question: What is the difference between a bug and a defect?
questions.answer: Bug and defect are largely synonyms — an error in code causing wrong behavior. Some contexts distinguish a defect as a spec mismatch vs a bug as a coding error.

questions.question: What is the difference between validation and verification in one line?
questions.answer: Verification: did we build it right (does the product meet its spec/design)? Validation: did we build the right thing (does it meet the user's actual need)? Verification is about correctness against requirements; validation is about value and fit for the user.

questions.question: What is the difference between a deployment and a release?
questions.answer: Deployment ships the code to an environment; release makes a deployed feature available to users (often gated by flags).

questions.question: What is the difference between a rollback and a revert?
questions.answer: A rollback restores a previous state (often a deploy); a revert creates a new commit undoing a previous change.

questions.question: What is the difference between scaling up and scaling out?
questions.answer: Scaling up (vertical) uses a bigger machine; scaling out (horizontal) adds more machines.

questions.question: What is the difference between a hot and a cold backup?
questions.answer: A hot backup is taken while the system runs (online); a cold backup is taken while it's stopped (consistent but requires downtime).

questions.question: What is the difference between a full backup and an incremental backup?
questions.answer: A full backup copies everything; an incremental backup copies only changes since the last backup — smaller but needs the chain to restore.

questions.question: What is the difference between encryption and hashing?
questions.answer: Encryption is reversible with a key (for confidentiality); hashing is one-way (for integrity/passwords).

questions.question: What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption?
questions.answer: Symmetric uses one key for both encrypt/decrypt (fast); asymmetric uses a public/private key pair (secure key exchange).

questions.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization in one line?
questions.answer: Authentication proves who you are (verifying identity, e.g., password, token, biometrics); authorization decides what you can do once your identity is established (permissions, roles, scopes). AuthN comes first, then AuthZ.

questions.question: What is the difference between a token and a session?
questions.answer: A token is client-held proof of identity (stateless); a session is server-held state referenced by an id (stateful).

questions.question: What is the difference between OAuth and JWT?
questions.answer: OAuth is a delegation protocol (authorize a third party); JWT is a token format for carrying claims. They often combine — OAuth issues JWTs.

questions.question: What is the difference between a monolith and a modular monolith?
questions.answer: A monolith is one deployable unit; a modular monolith is a monolith internally organized into clear, loosely coupled modules — the middle ground before microservices.

questions.question: What is the difference between SOAP and REST?
questions.answer: SOAP is a strict XML protocol with contracts; REST is a lightweight style using HTTP verbs and JSON. REST is the modern default.

questions.question: What is the difference between JSON and JavaScript objects in one line?
questions.answer: JSON is a text format (serialized); a JS object is the in-memory structure. They look similar but aren't the same thing.

questions.question: What is the difference between HTTP status 200 and 201?
questions.answer: 200 means success (often for reads/updates); 201 Created specifically means a resource was created, with a Location header.

questions.question: What is the difference between a daemon and a service?
questions.answer: A daemon is a background process; a service is a managed background process with lifecycle management (systemd). In practice they overlap.

questions.question: What is the difference between a load balancer and a reverse proxy in one line?
questions.answer: A reverse proxy fronts and routes requests to backends; a load balancer specifically distributes traffic across multiple backends for scale.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you improved a process at work.
questions.answer: At Assimilate, sync jobs and imports used to be run manually and failures were discovered days later. I set up automated scheduled syncs with logging and an alert on failure — failures surfaced the same day instead of the week after. It changed how the team operated: fewer surprises, more trust in the data. I like process improvements that compound.

questions.question: How do you handle conflicting priorities between your manager and a client?
questions.answer: I'd clarify impact and deadlines first — often the conflict is about timing, not intent. Then I'd propose a plan that serves both as much as possible — sequence the work, communicate the tradeoff, and flag it early. What I don't do is quietly drop one of them. Transparency about conflicts is the professional move.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you showed leadership.
questions.answer: I didn't have a title change to show leadership — I led by taking ownership of an uncertain area. When the biometric sync integration was under-specified, I defined the approach, broke it into steps, and kept stakeholders updated — other people could plan around me. Leadership to me is being the person who makes the unclear clear.

questions.question: How do you handle a team member who isn't pulling their weight?
questions.answer: I'd first check if it's a skills, workload, or motivation issue — most 'not pulling weight' cases are one of those, and the fix differs. I'd have a direct, private conversation focused on the work and support they need, and I'd involve the manager if it persisted. The goal is helping, not punishing — but silent resentment helps no one.

questions.question: Describe a time you received criticism.
questions.answer: Early on, a senior pointed out that my code was correct but hard to follow — clever but not clear. It stung, but he was right. I started writing for the next person who'd read it: clearer names, smaller functions, and comments where the why was non-obvious. That feedback changed my standard for good code more than anything else.

questions.question: What would you do in your first 30 days at a new job?
questions.answer: Learn, don't change things. I'd ramp on the codebase and architecture, understand the product and the users, meet the team and their workflows, and pick up the team's conventions. I'd aim to deliver something small and real by the end of the month to prove I can ship. I'd ask a lot of questions early — that's when they're expected.

questions.question: How do you deal with a tight deadline on a complex feature?
questions.answer: I break the feature into the smallest vertical slice that delivers value, ship that first, then layer on more. I communicate scope tradeoffs with the stakeholder early rather than silently cutting. And I protect quality fundamentals — I won't skip tests or reviews under pressure, because debt compounds. Deadlines are met by sequencing, not heroics.

questions.question: What do you do when you disagree with a technical decision?
questions.answer: I bring data and alternatives rather than just objecting. I'd build a small prototype or reference docs, present the tradeoffs — not just my preference — and be willing to go with the decision once it's made. The goal is the best outcome for the project, and sometimes that means my idea loses. I've changed my own mind plenty of times with evidence.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to work outside your comfort zone.
questions.answer: Angular was my framework of choice, and a project needed React for a client tool. I could have resisted, but instead I treated it as a learning sprint — built a small sample first, then delivered the Resume Lens app. It turned out the patterns I knew from Vue carried over.
